query.original_query: multilingual language models spatial frames of reference cross-linguistic spatial reasoning representation

sub_queries.semantic_query: internal representation of spatial frames of reference and cross-linguistic spatial reasoning in multilingual language models, probing residual stream and attention heads for spatial encoding
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how multilingual language models encode spatial frames of reference across languages with differing spatial systems. Using causal probing and activation patching on the residual stream and attention heads, we analyze whether models like LLaMA and GPT-2 represent spatial relations (e.g., left/right, north/south, relative vs. absolute frames) in a language-specific or shared manner. Our analysis reveals that spatial encoding is distributed across early-to-middle layers, with attention heads in mid-layer transformers showing selective sensitivity to language-specific spatial cues. Probing the residual stream with linear classifiers indicates that absolute frame information (e.g., cardinal directions) is more robustly encoded in languages that grammatically require it, while relative frame representations are more polysemantic. Causal mediation analysis further shows that patching spatial features from one language to another partially transfers spatial reasoning, but with systematic errors reflecting cross-linguistic frame conflicts. Results suggest that multilingual models do not fully abstract spatial representations into a universal format, instead retaining language-specific spatial biases in intermediate representations.

sub_queries.semantic_query: spatial frames of reference in human cognition cross-linguistic spatial reasoning language and thought effects of language on spatial representation and navigation
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated the influence of linguistic framing on spatial memory and navigation strategies across speakers of languages with distinct spatial frames of reference. Participants, including native speakers of a geocentric language (Tzeltal) and an egocentric language (Dutch), completed a series of non-linguistic spatial tasks, including a reorientation paradigm and a path integration task in a virtual environment. We measured response latencies and directional accuracy in both static array recall and dynamic navigation contexts. Results indicate that language-specific preferences for absolute versus relative spatial encoding reliably predicted performance asymmetries: geocentric speakers showed faster and more accurate reorientation when using environmental landmarks, while egocentric speakers relied more heavily on body-based cues. Findings support the hypothesis that habitual use of a particular spatial frame of reference in language modulates the weighting of spatial cues during non-linguistic navigation, consistent with the Whorfian hypothesis of linguistic relativity. These effects persisted even when verbal interference tasks were introduced, suggesting a deep entrenchment of spatial schemas.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: More than Correlation: Do Large Language Models Learn Causal Representations of Space?
papers.research_question: Does the internal spatial representation in large language models have a causal effect on their behavior in geospatial tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models learn internal spatial representations of location words, and these representations causally influence the model's performance on geospatial tasks.
papers.conclusion: Through representational similarity analysis and probing, the paper shows that both DeBERTa-v2 and GPT-Neo learned spatial representations of location words, and intervention experiments demonstrate these representations have causal effects on model output.
papers.key_findings:
The hidden states of city names in DeBERTa and GPT-Neo correlate with real-world geospatial distances, as shown by representational similarity analysis.
Linear and non-linear probes can map hidden states to latitude and longitude with low error, indicating the presence of spatial information.
A novel GeoDist loss function, which accounts for spherical geometry, improves probing performance over mean squared error.
Causal intervention experiments show that aligning hidden states with true geographic coordinates improves accuracy in a country prediction task, while misaligning degrades it.
Perturbing hidden states with spatial information affects next-word prediction for country names, demonstrating causal use of spatial representations.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to location words and geospatial tasks; it is unclear how spatial representations affect other types of words and non-geospatial tasks.
future_direction: Investigate spatial representations for words without inherent geographical property
Study the effect of spatial representation perturbation on tasks that do not rely on geographical knowledge
papers.abstract: Recent work found high mutual information between the learned representations of large language models (LLMs) and the geospatial property of its input, hinting an emergent internal model of space. However, whether this internal space model has any causal effects on the LLMs' behaviors was not answered by that work, led to criticism of these findings as mere statistical correlation. Our study focused on uncovering the causality of the spatial representations in LLMs. In particular, we discovered the potential spatial representations in DeBERTa, GPT-Neo using representational similarity analysis and linear and non-linear probing. Our casual intervention experiments showed that the spatial representations influenced the model's performance on next word prediction and a downstream task that relies on geospatial information. Our experiments suggested that the LLMs learn and use an internal model of space in solving geospatial related tasks.

papers.title: Linear Spatial World Models Emerge in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models implicitly encode linear spatial world models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides empirical evidence that large language models encode linear spatial world models, showing that spatial relations are represented in a low-dimensional subspace with geometric structure and are functionally used by the model.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that large language models do encode a basic spatial world model linearly within their representations.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes achieve near-perfect accuracy in decoding spatial relations, indicating linear encoding.
PCA reveals a low-dimensional subspace where spatial relations are organized geometrically (inverse relations are antipodal, orthogonal relations are perpendicular).
Spatial representations are compositional: composed relations correspond to vector sums of atomic relations.
Object positions are consistently represented in the same spatial subspace.
Causal interventions (activation steering) show that the spatial subspace is functionally used by the model for prediction.
papers.limitation:
The work does not investigate other essential components of a full world model, such as temporal dynamics or object permanence.
The analysis focuses on a limited set of spatial relations.
The generality of the findings to other model types remains an open question.
future_direction: Extending the framework to cover a broader and more diverse set of spatial directions.
Investigating other components of world models such as temporal dynamics.
Testing generalization to other model types.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated emergent abilities across diverse tasks, raising the question of whether they acquire internal world models. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs implicitly encode linear spatial world models, which we define as linear representations of physical space and object configurations. We introduce a formal framework for spatial world models and assess whether such structure emerges in contextual embeddings. Using a synthetic dataset of object positions, we train probes to decode object positions and evaluate geometric consistency of the underlying space. We further conduct causal interventions to test whether these spatial representations are functionally used by the model. Our results provide empirical evidence that LLMs encode linear spatial world models.

papers.title: From Text to Space: Mapping Abstract Spatial Models in LLMs during a Grid-World Navigation Task
papers.research_question: How do different text-based spatial representations affect LLM performance and internal activations in a grid-world navigation task? Do LLMs develop abstract internal representations of space that are invariant to prompting?
papers.core_contribution: Cartesian spatial representations lead to better navigation performance in LLMs, and internal units in intermediate layers encode spatial features invariantly across representations and are also active in unrelated spatial reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop internal representations of spatial information that are partially invariant to prompting, with specific units in middle layers encoding spatial features and action correctness, which are also engaged in unrelated spatial reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Cartesian representations of spatial information yield higher success rates and path efficiency in grid-world navigation, with performance scaling with model size.
Linear probing reveals that grid configuration is represented in activations, with the best decoding in middle layers, and representations are partially specific to the spatial information representation (SIR) type.
Individual units (neurons) are found that encode the agent's x and y coordinates and border cells invariantly across SIR types.
A set of units in middle layers predict action correctness invariantly across SIR types and are also more active in unrelated spatial reasoning tasks.
Ablation of these invariant units does not significantly harm performance, suggesting spatial information is distributed and polysemantic.
papers.limitation:
The simple grid-world task limits generalizability to more complex spatial reasoning scenarios.
Ablation of core spatial units did not reduce performance, indicating that spatial information is distributed and polysemantic, making it hard to isolate.
future_direction: Extend experiments to larger models and more challenging tasks (obstacles, multiple goals, 3D spaces).
Investigate if Cartesian representation advantages extend to other non-spatial domains.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) represent and reason about spatial information is crucial for building robust agentic systems that can navigate real and simulated environments. In this work, we investigate the influence of different text-based spatial representations on LLM performance and internal activations in a grid-world navigation task. By evaluating models of various sizes on a task that requires navigating toward a goal, we examine how the format used to encode spatial information impacts decision-making. Our experiments reveal that cartesian representations of space consistently yield higher success rates and path efficiency, with performance scaling markedly with model size. Moreover, probing LLaMA-3.1-8B revealed subsets of internal units, primarily located in intermediate layers, that robustly correlate with spatial features, such as the position of the agent in the grid or action correctness, regardless of how that information is represented, and are also activated by unrelated spatial reasoning tasks. This work advances our understanding of how LLMs process spatial information and provides valuable insights for developing more interpretable and robust agentic AI systems.

papers.title: Beyond Semantics: Rediscovering Spatial Awareness in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language Models (VLMs) under-utilize spatial cues despite having positional encodings and spatially rich vision-encoder features?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a norm imbalance between vision and text token embeddings that suppresses positional encoding in VLMs, and provides interpretability tools and interventions to restore spatial reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Norm imbalance is a key mechanism behind poor spatial reasoning in VLMs, and interpretability tools can guide interventions to improve spatial awareness.
papers.key_findings:
Vision token embeddings have much larger norms than text tokens, suppressing the LLM's positional encoding (RoPE).
Random permutation of vision tokens causes only minor performance drops, indicating VLMs are largely insensitive to positional information.
Normalizing vision token embeddings restores positional sensitivity and improves spatial reasoning performance.
Intermediate layers of the vision encoder contain richer spatial information; combining them with normalization further improves spatial reasoning.
The system prompt absorbs a large portion of attention, masking vision use and skewing attention analysis.
papers.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) excel at identifying and describing objects but often fail at spatial reasoning. We study why VLMs, such as LLaVA, underutilize spatial cues despite having positional encodings and spatially rich vision encoder features. Our analysis reveals a key imbalance: vision token embeddings have much larger norms than text tokens, suppressing LLM's position embedding. To expose this mechanism, we developed three interpretability tools: (1) the Position Sensitivity Index, which quantifies reliance on token order, (2) the Cross Modality Balance, which reveals attention head allocation patterns, and (3) a RoPE Sensitivity probe, which measures dependence on rotary positional embeddings. These tools uncover that vision tokens and system prompts dominate attention. We validated our mechanistic understanding through targeted interventions that predictably restore positional sensitivity. These findings reveal previously unknown failure modes in multimodal attention and demonstrate how interpretability analysis can guide principled improvements.

papers.title: Why Is Spatial Reasoning Hard for VLMs? An Attention Mechanism Perspective on Focus Areas
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with spatial reasoning tasks, and how does attention mechanism contribute to this difficulty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that spatial reasoning errors in VLMs stem from misallocated attention to image tokens and proposes ADAPTVIS, a confidence-guided attention intervention method that dynamically adjusts attention distribution to significantly improve spatial reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Spatial reasoning in VLMs is hindered by attention misallocation, and adaptive intervention based on confidence can effectively guide the model's focus to improve performance.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs allocate only about 10% of their attention to image tokens despite images comprising around 90% of the input sequence.
Simply increasing attention to image tokens does not improve spatial reasoning; the geometric distribution of attention is critical.
The model's self-confidence (generation probability) correlates with the correctness of its attention pattern and can be used to guide intervention.
ADAPTVIS adaptively sharpens attention when confidence is high and smooths it when confidence is low, leading to substantial improvements on spatial reasoning benchmarks.
papers.limitation: The study primarily focuses on spatial reasoning tasks with simple relationships and does not address more complicated geometric structures or long-horizon spatial reasoning.
future_direction: Explore the mechanism of VLMs on complicated geometric structure understanding, such as long-horizon spatial reasoning.
Investigate other spatial reasoning bottlenecks.
papers.abstract: Large Vision Language Models (VLMs) have long struggled with spatial reasoning tasks. Surprisingly, even simple spatial reasoning tasks, such as recognizing "under" or "behind" relationships between only two objects, pose significant challenges for current VLMs. In this work, we study the spatial reasoning challenge from the lens of mechanistic interpretability, diving into the model's internal states to examine the interactions between image and text tokens. By tracing attention distribution over the image through out intermediate layers, we observe that successful spatial reasoning correlates strongly with the model's ability to align its attention distribution with actual object locations, particularly differing between familiar and unfamiliar spatial relationships. Motivated by these findings, we propose ADAPTVIS based on inference-time confidence scores to sharpen the attention on highly relevant regions when confident, while smoothing and broadening the attention window to consider a wider context when confidence is lower. This training-free decoding method shows significant improvement (e.g., up to a 50 absolute point improvement) on spatial reasoning benchmarks such as WhatsUp and VSR with negligible cost. We make code and data publicly available for research purposes at https://github.com/shiqichen17/AdaptVis.

papers.title: Linear Mechanisms for Spatiotemporal Reasoning in Vision Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether spatiotemporal reasoning in Vision Language Models (VLMs) can be explained by linear mechanisms (spatial IDs) that bind spatial/temporal information to object word activations, and how these mechanisms can be used to understand and improve VLMs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces spatial IDs, a linear mechanism by which VLMs bind spatial/temporal information to object word activations, and shows that these IDs causally mediate model beliefs and can be used to diagnose and improve VLMs.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that spatiotemporal IDs provide a linear mechanistic explanation for spatiotemporal reasoning in VLMs and offer ways to improve model design and diagnosis.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs encode object locations by linearly binding spatial IDs to textual activations.
Spatial IDs can causally mediate model beliefs about spatial relationships through interventions.
Spatial IDs reveal limitations in depth representation in VLMs.
Spatial IDs can diagnose failure modes in VLMs (e.g., vision encoder vs. crossmodal integration).
Analogous temporal IDs exist in video VLMs and similarly mediate temporal reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Limited to analyses in simple spatial queries or appearance-based temporal queries.
Only extract and steer models of sizes up to 14B parameters due to compute constraints.
Limited use cases for leveraging spatial IDs for VLM diagnostics or finetuning.
future_direction: Experimental design for more complex, open-ended queries.
Investigation into whether the spatial ID circuit plays a similarly prominent role in larger models.
Expanded use cases such as explicit temporal guidance at large scale.
papers.abstract: Spatio-temporal reasoning is a remarkable capability of Vision Language Models (VLMs), but the underlying mechanisms of such abilities remain largely opaque. We postulate that visual/geometrical and textual representations of spatial structure must be combined at some point in VLM computations. We search for such confluence, and ask whether the identified representation can causally explain aspects of input-output model behavior through a linear model. We show empirically that VLMs encode object locations by linearly binding \textit{spatial IDs} to textual activations, then perform reasoning via language tokens. Through rigorous causal interventions we demonstrate that these IDs, which are ubiquitous across the model, can systematically mediate model beliefs at intermediate VLM layers. Additionally, we find that spatial IDs serve as a diagnostic tool for identifying limitations in existing VLMs, and as a valuable learning signal. We extend our analysis to video VLMs and identify an analogous linear temporal ID mechanism. By characterizing our proposed spatiotemporal ID mechanism, we elucidate a previously underexplored internal reasoning process in VLMs, toward improved interpretability and the principled design of more aligned and capable models. We release our code for reproducibility: https://github.com/Raphoo/linear-mech-vlms.

papers.title: The Geometry of Multilingual Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, facilitating feature extraction for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual language models encode features along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, enabling targeted extraction of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, as shown by causal effects on language modeling performance and direct subspace comparisons.
Subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that encode information such as token vocabularies, and shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages.
Stable language-neutral axes encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech, and these axes are orthogonal to language-sensitive axes.
The identified axes (both language-sensitive and language-neutral) are relatively stable across middle layers of the model.
Token position information is encoded along nonlinear structures like spirals, toruses, and curves in the representation space.
future_direction: Investigate how nonlinear structures (e.g., spirals, toruses) arise from and interact with the dot product self-attention mechanism in Transformer models.
Conduct a more detailed analysis of how specific representational structures are retained across layers.

Assess how multilingual language models encode more complex linguistic features geometrically, and the extent to which representation spaces can be fully decomposed into orthogonal subspaces encoding different features.
papers.abstract: We assess how multilingual language models maintain a shared multilingual representation space while still encoding language-sensitive information in each language. Using XLM-R as a case study, we show that languages occupy similar linear subspaces after mean-centering, evaluated based on causal effects on language modeling performance and direct comparisons between subspaces for 88 languages. The subspace means differ along language-sensitive axes that are relatively stable throughout middle layers, and these axes encode information such as token vocabularies. Shifting representations by language means is sufficient to induce token predictions in different languages. However, we also identify stable language-neutral axes that encode information such as token positions and part-of-speech. We visualize representations projected onto language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, identifying language family and part-of-speech clusters, along with spirals, toruses, and curves representing token position information. These results demonstrate that multilingual language models encode information along orthogonal language-sensitive and language-neutral axes, allowing the models to extract a variety of features for downstream tasks and cross-lingual transfer learning.

papers.title: The Semantic Hub Hypothesis: Language Models Share Semantic Representations Across Languages and Modalities
papers.research_question: To what extent do language models learn and use a shared semantic representation space across different languages and modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the semantic hub hypothesis, which posits that language models learn a shared representation space across languages and modalities, and provides evidence through representation similarity and intervention experiments.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models learn a shared semantic representation space (the semantic hub) that is anchored by the dominant language and is causally involved in processing across languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in intermediate layers.
The shared representation space is scaffolded by the model's dominant language (e.g., English) and can be interpreted via the logit lens.
This phenomenon extends to other data types: arithmetic expressions, code, images, and audio.
Interventions in the shared space using the dominant language affect model outputs in other data types, indicating causal usage.
The shared space is not just a byproduct but actively used during processing.
papers.limitation:
Chameleon-7B cannot answer more sophisticated reasoning questions about images, such as asking for a country flag or spatial relationships, even without interventions.
The logit lens analysis for audio is a lower bound because many words in labels (e.g., prepositions) are unlikely to be represented in the audio hidden states.
future_direction: Future work aimed at better controlling models using insights from the semantic hub hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can process inputs across diverse languages and modalities. We hypothesize that models acquire this capability through learning a shared representation space across heterogeneous data types (e.g., different languages and modalities), which places semantically similar inputs near one another, even if they are from different modalities/languages. We term this the semantic hub hypothesis, following the hub-and-spoke model from neuroscience (Patterson et al., 2007) which posits that semantic knowledge in the human brain is organized through a transmodal semantic "hub" which integrates information from various modality-specific "spokes" regions. We first show that model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in the intermediate layers, and that this space can be interpreted using the model's dominant pretraining language via the logit lens. This tendency extends to other data types, including arithmetic expressions, code, and visual/audio inputs. Interventions in the shared representation space in one data type also predictably affect model outputs in other data types, suggesting that this shared representations space is not simply a vestigial byproduct of large-scale training on broad data, but something that is actively utilized by the model during input processing.

papers.title: Cognitive Maps in Language Models: A Mechanistic Analysis of Spatial Planning
papers.research_question: How do large language models solve spatial navigation tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on exploratory data develop a generalizable cognitive map for spatial navigation, while those trained on goal-directed data learn brittle, path-dependent algorithms, revealing a trade-off between generalization and optimization.
papers.conclusion: Training paradigms shape the algorithms learned by transformers for spatial navigation, with exploratory data encouraging generalizable world models and goal-directed data leading to optimized but brittle heuristics.
papers.key_findings:
The Foraging Model develops a robust, map-like representation of space (cognitive map) and shows a phase transition in layer 8 where it becomes independent of historical direction tokens.
The Foraging Model uses an adaptive strategy: local heuristics for short contexts and map-based reasoning for longer contexts.
The goal-directed SP models learn path-dependent algorithms that remain reliant on explicit directional inputs throughout all layers.
The hybrid SP-RW model improves generalization but retains the path-dependent algorithm of its parent.
Mechanistic analysis reveals a local spatial update circuit in Layer 1 of the Foraging Model and self-sufficient spatial representations from Layer 8 onwards.
papers.limitation:
Use of a simplified 4x4 grid and GPT-2 small architecture limits scalability to more complex environments and larger models.
Mechanistic analysis is incomplete; the exact circuit and transformation of spatial information across intermediate layers remains a black box.
Causal analysis focuses on the Foraging Model, leaving the brittleness of the SP models behaviorally observed but not mechanistically explained.
future_direction: Apply automated circuit discovery techniques to systematically map the transformations of spatial information across intermediate layers.
Prioritize a comparative mechanistic analysis to uncover the algorithmic failures in the SP models.
papers.abstract: How do large language models solve spatial navigation tasks? We investigate this by training GPT-2 models on three spatial learning paradigms in grid environments: passive exploration (Foraging Model- predicting steps in random walks), goal-directed planning (generating optimal shortest paths) on structured Hamiltonian paths (SP-Hamiltonian), and a hybrid model fine-tuned with exploratory data (SP-Random Walk). Using behavioural, representational and mechanistic analyses, we uncover two fundamentally different learned algorithms. The Foraging model develops a robust, map-like representation of space, akin to a 'cognitive map'. Causal interventions reveal that it learns to consolidate spatial information into a self-sufficient coordinate system, evidenced by a sharp phase transition where its reliance on historical direction tokens vanishes by the middle layers of the network. The model also adopts an adaptive, hierarchical reasoning system, switching between a low-level heuristic for short contexts and map-based inference for longer ones. In contrast, the goal-directed models learn a path-dependent algorithm, remaining reliant on explicit directional inputs throughout all layers. The hybrid model, despite demonstrating improved generalisation over its parent, retains the same path-dependent strategy. These findings suggest that the nature of spatial intelligence in transformers may lie on a spectrum, ranging from generalisable world models shaped by exploratory data to heuristics optimised for goal-directed tasks. We provide a mechanistic account of this generalisation-optimisation trade-off and highlight how the choice of training regime influences the strategies that emerge.

papers.title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What does 'linear representation' actually mean in the context of language models, and how can we make sense of geometric notions like cosine similarity and projection in the representation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the linear representation hypothesis using counterfactuals, connects it to linear probing and model steering, and introduces a causal inner product that unifies different notions of linear representation and respects semantic structure.
papers.conclusion: The paper formalizes linear representation and shows that all natural variants of this notion can be unified through a causal inner product, which plays a critical role in enabling interpretation and control of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Concepts are represented as directions in the unembedding space, supporting the linear representation hypothesis.
The proposed causal inner product respects causal separability, making causally separable concepts approximately orthogonal.
The unembedding representation of a concept can be used as a linear probe to predict the concept from context embeddings.
The embedding representation (obtained via the causal inner product) can be used for intervention, steering the model's output towards a target concept.
The Euclidean inner product does not always capture semantic structure, while the causal inner product does.
papers.abstract: Informally, the 'linear representation hypothesis' is the idea that high-level concepts are represented linearly as directions in some representation space. In this paper, we address two closely related questions: What does "linear representation" actually mean? And, how do we make sense of geometric notions (e.g., cosine similarity or projection) in the representation space? To answer these, we use the language of counterfactuals to give two formalizations of "linear representation", one in the output (word) representation space, and one in the input (sentence) space. We then prove these connect to linear probing and model steering, respectively. To make sense of geometric notions, we use the formalization to identify a particular (non-Euclidean) inner product that respects language structure in a sense we make precise. Using this causal inner product, we show how to unify all notions of linear representation. In particular, this allows the construction of probes and steering vectors using counterfactual pairs. Experiments with LLaMA-2 demonstrate the existence of linear representations of concepts, the connection to interpretation and control, and the fundamental role of the choice of inner product.

papers.title: State Design Matters: How Representations Shape Dynamic Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does inference-time state representation, along the axes of granularity (long-form trajectories versus summaries), structure (natural language versus symbolic encodings), and spatial grounding (text-only representations versus explicit spatial grounding via images or textual map encodings), affect performance on dynamic reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that design choices for representing state (granularity, structure, spatial grounding) are a decisive factor in performance on dynamic reasoning tasks, distinct from the availability of information itself.
papers.conclusion: State representation design matters as much as the information it contains; compact representations help when they preserve task-critical structure, but can be harmful if they omit necessary details. Future work should focus on verification and training for temporal spatial state tracking.
papers.key_findings:
Trajectory summarisation improves performance by reducing noise and stabilising long-horizon reasoning.
Natural language representations are the most robust across models.
Structured encodings help mainly for models with strong code or structured output priors.
Text-based spatial encodings (like Visualization-of-Thought) are most effective, primarily by inducing step-by-step spatial reasoning.
Even with improved representations, current LLMs and VLMs remain brittle over long horizons.
papers.limitation: Even with improved representations, current LLMs and VLMs remain brittle over long horizons, particularly when they must synthesise information to manage multiple subtasks to reach a goal.
future_direction: Pairing agents with verifiers during the process.
Training signals that directly encourage maintaining a consistent spatial state over many steps.
A shift toward dynamic evaluation to test true agentic competence.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) move from static reasoning tasks toward dynamic environments, their success depends on the ability to navigate and respond to an environment that changes as they interact at inference time. An underexplored factor in these settings is the representation of the state. Holding model parameters fixed, we systematically vary three key aspects: (1) state granularity (long form versus summary), (2) structure (natural language versus symbolic), and (3) spatial grounding (text-only versus images or textual map encodings) across sequential decision-making benchmarks. We find that trajectory summarisation improves performance by reducing noise and stabilising long-horizon reasoning. Second, natural language representations are the most robust across models, whereas structured encodings help mainly for models with strong code or structured output priors, such as JSON schemas. Third, while image-inputs show some benefit, text-based spatial encodings prove most effective. This advantage stems not from the spatial information itself, but from the act of construction, which compels the model to perform the spatial reasoning that static input does not elicit. Overall, we demonstrate that design choices for representing state are a decisive factor in performance, distinct from the availability of information itself. We note, however, that even with improved representations, current LLMs and VLMs remain brittle over long horizons, particularly when they must synthesise information to manage multiple subtasks to reach a goal.

papers.title: Geospatial Mechanistic Interpretability of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally represent and process geographical information?
papers.core_contribution: Establishes a novel framework for geospatial mechanistic interpretability, demonstrating that LLMs' internal representations for geographical information exhibit spatial autocorrelation and can be decomposed into interpretable features using sparse autoencoders.
papers.conclusion: The framework advances the understanding of how LLMs handle geographical information and opens up new research questions in geospatial mechanistic interpretability, contributing to AI safety and reliable geoAI tools.
papers.key_findings:
Internal representations handling geographical information in LLMs are often distributed across polysemantic neurons, consistent with the superposition hypothesis.
Spatial autocorrelation analysis shows that activations for placenames display geospatial patterns, indicating that the model encodes geographical relationships.
Sparse autoencoders can disentangle polysemantic structures into more interpretable, monosemantic features that reveal clearer geospatial patterns.
Features extracted via sparse autoencoders encode specific geographical regions or concepts, such as Wales or southern Italy, and urban areas like New York City and London.
Only a small percentage (0.2%) of features show significant spatial autocorrelation, suggesting that geographical information is sparsely encoded in the model.
papers.limitation:
Placename ambiguity impacts the interpretation and may require further handling.
The scale of geographical relationships encoded and their interaction with other types of relationships remain open questions.
Only a small fraction of features from the sparse autoencoder showed spatial autocorrelation, indicating room for improvement in decomposition methods.
future_direction: Exploring how placename ambiguity impacts LLMs' learning and interpretability.
Investigating what scale(s) of geographical relationships are encoded and at which model depths.
Examining how geographical relationships compare to and interact with other types of relationships (e.g., social, economic, historical).
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated unprecedented capabilities across various natural language processing tasks. Their ability to process and generate viable text and code has made them ubiquitous in many fields, while their deployment as knowledge bases and "reasoning" tools remains an area of ongoing research. In geography, a growing body of literature has been focusing on evaluating LLMs' geographical knowledge and their ability to perform spatial reasoning. However, very little is still known about the internal functioning of these models, especially about how they process geographical information. In this chapter, we establish a novel framework for the study of geospatial mechanistic interpretability - using spatial analysis to reverse engineer how LLMs handle geographical information. Our aim is to advance our understanding of the internal representations that these complex models generate while processing geographical information - what one might call "how LLMs think about geographic information" if such phrasing was not an undue anthropomorphism. We first outline the use of probing in revealing internal structures within LLMs. We then introduce the field of mechanistic interpretability, discussing the superposition hypothesis and the role of sparse autoencoders in disentangling polysemantic internal representations of LLMs into more interpretable, monosemantic features. In our experiments, we use spatial autocorrelation to show how features obtained for placenames display spatial patterns related to their geographic location and can thus be interpreted geospatially, providing insights into how these models process geographical information. We conclude by discussing how our framework can help shape the study and use of foundation models in geography.

papers.title: Left-Right Symmetry Breaking in CLIP-style Vision-Language Models Trained on Synthetic Spatial-Relation Data
papers.research_question: How does left–right relational understanding emerge in Transformer-based vision and text encoders trained with a CLIP-style contrastive objective on synthetic spatial-relation data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that label diversity, more than layout diversity, drives generalization in learning left-right relations in CLIP-style models, and mechanistically, an attention gradient from positional-token embedding interactions breaks left-right symmetry.
papers.conclusion: The study provides mechanistic insights into how CLIP-style models acquire spatial relational understanding through attention gradients driven by positional embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive training can learn left-right relations and generalize to unseen object pairs.
Label diversity is more important than layout diversity for generalization.
Attention decomposition reveals a horizontal attention gradient from positional-token embedding interactions that breaks left-right symmetry.
Ablating the positional-embedding contributions reduces left-right discrimination.
The text encoder also exhibits left-right symmetry breaking in attention patterns.
papers.limitation: The study uses a synthetic 1D image-text setting, which may not capture the complexity of real-world spatial reasoning.
future_direction: Further investigation of the role of multi-head attention in generalization.
Thorough investigation of attention dynamics in deeper models.
papers.abstract: Spatial understanding remains a key challenge in vision-language models. Yet it is still unclear whether such understanding is truly acquired, and if so, through what mechanisms. We present a controllable 1D image-text testbed to probe how left-right relational understanding emerges in Transformer-based vision and text encoders trained with a CLIP-style contrastive objective. We train lightweight Transformer-based vision and text encoders end-to-end on paired descriptions of one- and two-object scenes and evaluate generalization to unseen object pairs while systematically varying label and layout diversity. We find that contrastive training learns left-right relations and that label diversity, more than layout diversity, is the primary driver of generalization in this setting. To gain the mechanistic understanding, we perform an attention decomposition and show that interactions between positional and token embeddings induce a horizontal attention gradient that breaks left-right symmetry in the encoders; ablating this contribution substantially reduces left-right discrimination. Our results provide a mechanistic insight of when and how CLIP-style models acquire relational competence.

papers.title: Multimodal Function Vectors for Spatial Relations
papers.research_question: Whether the concept of function vectors can be extended from language-only transformer models to large multimodal models (LMMs) to support the extraction and manipulation of relational knowledge in images, and how architectural factors influence the effectiveness of function vector interventions.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that spatial relational knowledge in a vision-language model is encoded within a sparse subset of attention heads and can be extracted as 'multimodal function vectors'. These vectors can be fine-tuned and linearly combined to solve novel relational tasks, advancing understanding of model modularity and control over relational reasoning in LMMs.
papers.conclusion: The results confirm that function vectors can be extracted from LMMs, encode causally meaningful relational knowledge, and serve as flexible, optimizable modules that can be combined to enhance and control relational reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset of attention heads in OpenFlamingo-4B is causally responsible for transmitting representations of spatial relations.
Extracted relation-specific function vectors, when injected into zero-shot prompts, significantly improve relational prediction accuracy.
Fine-tuning these function vectors with a modest amount of data while keeping the LMM frozen outperforms few-shot in-context learning baselines.
Relation-specific function vectors can be linearly combined to form composite vectors that solve one-shot analogy problems involving novel, untrained spatial relations.
The effectiveness of function vector intervention depends on the injection layer and the number of heads used, peaking at intermediate layers and a small subset of heads.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted using a single, relatively lightweight architecture (OpenFlamingo-4B), and it remains to be seen whether findings generalize to larger, more complex models.
The scope of relational tasks investigated is restricted to a small set of spatial relations (e.g., above, next to), not capturing the full richness of real-world multimodal tasks.
future_direction: Explore whether the multimodal function vector framework generalizes to larger, more advanced multimodal architectures with different training regimes and fusion mechanisms.
Extend the analysis to a broader range of relational categories, including physical, agentic, and social relations.
papers.abstract: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) demonstrate impressive in-context learning abilities from limited multimodal demonstrations, yet the internal mechanisms supporting such task learning remain opaque. Building on prior work of large language models, we show that a small subset of attention heads in the vision-language model OpenFlamingo-4B is responsible for transmitting representations of spatial relations. The activations of these attention heads, termed function vectors, can be extracted and manipulated to alter an LMM's performance on relational tasks. First, using both synthetic and real image datasets, we apply causal mediation analysis to identify attention heads that strongly influence relational predictions, and extract multimodal function vectors that improve zero-shot accuracy at inference time. We further demonstrate that these multimodal function vectors can be fine-tuned with a modest amount of training data, while keeping LMM parameters frozen, to significantly outperform in-context learning baselines. Finally, we show that relation-specific function vectors can be linearly combined to solve analogy problems involving novel and untrained spatial relations, highlighting the strong generalization ability of this approach. Our results show that LMMs encode spatial relational knowledge within localized internal structures, which can be systematically extracted and optimized, thereby advancing our understanding of model modularity and enhancing control over relational reasoning in LMMs.

papers.title: Under the Shadow of Babel: How Language Shapes Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Do different languages lead LLMs to think differently? Do LLMs internalize the cognitive biases embedded in different languages, specifically in causal reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BICAUSE, a structured bilingual dataset for causal reasoning, and provides empirical evidence that LLMs internalize language-specific reasoning biases, showing typologically aligned attention patterns and a shared understanding when reasoning succeeds.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit language-specific biases in causal reasoning that impact performance, but when reasoning succeeds, they form a shared understanding that transcends surface linguistic form.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit typologically aligned attention patterns, focusing more on causes and sentence-initial connectives in Chinese, while showing a more balanced distribution in English.
Models internalize language-specific preferences for causal word order and often rigidly apply them to atypical inputs, leading to degraded performance, especially in Chinese.
When causal reasoning succeeds, model representations converge toward semantically aligned abstractions across languages, indicating a shared understanding beyond surface form.
Attention patterns over syntactic components show consistent layerwise trends but differ in absolute weights between Chinese and English, reflecting language-specific structural biases.
The similarity of layerwise attention patterns (measured by SVCCA) correlates with reasoning accuracy across different input structures and languages.
papers.limitation:
Focuses exclusively on Chinese and English, representing only a small portion of the world's linguistic diversity.
Does not encompass all model architectures or training paradigms.
Primarily focuses on attention patterns and hidden representations; does not incorporate additional interpretability methods.
future_direction: Extending BICAUSE to a broader set of languages.
Advancing research on multilingual interpretability and alignment mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Language is not only a tool for communication but also a medium for human cognition and reasoning. If, as linguistic relativity suggests, the structure of language shapes cognitive patterns, then large language models (LLMs) trained on human language may also internalize the habitual logical structures embedded in different languages. To examine this hypothesis, we introduce BICAUSE, a structured bilingual dataset for causal reasoning, which includes semantically aligned Chinese and English samples in both forward and reversed causal forms. Our study reveals three key findings: (1) LLMs exhibit typologically aligned attention patterns, focusing more on causes and sentence-initial connectives in Chinese, while showing a more balanced distribution in English. (2) Models internalize language-specific preferences for causal word order and often rigidly apply them to atypical inputs, leading to degraded performance, especially in Chinese. (3) When causal reasoning succeeds, model representations converge toward semantically aligned abstractions across languages, indicating a shared understanding beyond surface form. Overall, these results suggest that LLMs not only mimic surface linguistic forms but also internalize the reasoning biases shaped by language. Rooted in cognitive linguistic theory, this phenomenon is for the first time empirically verified through structural analysis of model internals.

papers.title: When Less Language is More: Language-Reasoning Disentanglement Makes LLMs Better Multilingual Reasoners
papers.research_question: Can reasoning and language processing in LLMs be disentangled to improve multilingual reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reasoning and language can be disentangled in LLMs by ablating language-specific components in hidden states, leading to improved multilingual reasoning performance across diverse models and languages.
papers.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that language and reasoning are separable in LLMs, and the proposed training-free intervention provides a lightweight and interpretable strategy for improving cross-lingual generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Language-reasoning disentanglement via activation ablation consistently improves multilingual reasoning performance across 10 open-weight LLMs and 11 typologically diverse languages.
There is a negative correlation between language-specific activation and reasoning accuracy; removing language-specific signals improves reasoning.
Middle layers are most effective for disentanglement, improving reasoning while preserving language fidelity, whereas upper-layer ablation degrades output fluency.
The training-free intervention achieves comparable or superior results to post-training methods like supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.
Low-resource languages show a trade-off: reasoning improves with ablation, but language fidelity drops more sharply than in high-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
After ablation, models tend to default to English, which may reduce language fidelity, especially for low-resource languages.
The exact ratios of pretraining data for different languages are unknown, which limits a definitive explanation of the convergence phenomenon.
future_direction: Further investigation into the convergence of non-English representations to English after ablation.
Exploring adaptive ablation strategies to balance reasoning improvement and language fluency for low-resource languages.
Combining the training-free intervention with post-training methods for enhanced multilingual reasoning.
papers.abstract: Multilingual reasoning remains a significant challenge for large language models (LLMs), with performance disproportionately favoring high-resource languages. Drawing inspiration from cognitive neuroscience, which suggests that human reasoning functions largely independently of language processing, we hypothesize that LLMs similarly encode reasoning and language as separable components that can be disentangled to enhance multilingual reasoning. To evaluate this, we perform a causal intervention by ablating language-specific representations at inference time. Experiments on 10 open-weight LLMs spanning 11 typologically diverse languages show that this language-specific ablation consistently boosts multilingual reasoning performance. Layer-wise analyses further confirm that language and reasoning representations can be effectively disentangled throughout the model, yielding improved multilingual reasoning capabilities, while preserving top-layer language features remains essential for maintaining linguistic fidelity. Compared to post-training methods such as supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning, our training-free language-reasoning disentanglement achieves comparable or superior results with minimal computational overhead. These findings shed light on the internal mechanisms underlying multilingual reasoning in LLMs and suggest a lightweight and interpretable strategy for improving cross-lingual generalization.

papers.title: The Transfer Neurons Hypothesis: An Underlying Mechanism for Language Latent Space Transitions in Multilingual LLMs
papers.research_question: How do multilingual LLMs transfer representations between language-specific latent spaces and a shared semantic latent space, and what neurons are responsible for this transfer?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes and empirically validates the Transfer Neurons Hypothesis, identifying specific MLP neurons that facilitate transitions between language-specific and shared semantic latent spaces in multilingual LLMs, and shows their critical role in reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that transfer neurons are a key mechanism for latent space transitions in multilingual LLMs, enabling language-agnostic reasoning and output generation in the input language.
papers.key_findings:
Internal representations in multilingual LLMs form language-specific latent spaces in initial and final layers, converging to a shared semantic latent space in middle layers.
Transfer neurons in the MLP module are responsible for moving representations between language-specific and shared latent spaces.
Type-1 transfer neurons shift inputs to the shared space, while Type-2 neurons shift outputs back to language-specific spaces.
Type-2 neurons exhibit language specificity and are similar to previously identified language-specific neurons.
Deactivating transfer neurons impairs representation alignment and reduces performance on multilingual QA tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have suggested a processing framework for multilingual inputs in decoder-based LLMs: early layers convert inputs into English-centric and language-agnostic representations; middle layers perform reasoning within an English-centric latent space; and final layers generate outputs by transforming these representations back into language-specific latent spaces. However, the internal dynamics of such transformation and the underlying mechanism remain underexplored. Towards a deeper understanding of this framework, we propose and empirically validate The Transfer Neurons Hypothesis: certain neurons in the MLP module are responsible for transferring representations between language-specific latent spaces and a shared semantic latent space. Furthermore, we show that one function of language-specific neurons, as identified in recent studies, is to facilitate movement between latent spaces. Finally, we show that transfer neurons are critical for reasoning in multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language when processing non-English prompts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that multilingual language models like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate representations favoring English before shifting to the target language.
papers.conclusion: The evidence suggests that the abstract 'concept space' in multilingual transformers lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding linguistic biases.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate embeddings in middle layers decode to English versions of the correct next token, even when the input and output are non-English.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space (high entropy, no language), concept space (low entropy, English dominates), and output space (target language dominates).
The concept space is biased towards English, indicating an internal pivot language.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The token energy metric shows that latent embeddings have low energy in middle layers and high energy in later layers when the target language is selected.
papers.limitation:
Focus on the Llama-2 family limits generalizability to other models.
Tasks are simple and provide a highly controlled, toy-like context.
Limited understanding of the structure of the concept space in its original high-dimensional form.
The logit lens only grants approximate access to internal beliefs about output; other information remains hidden.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias changes when decreasing the dominance of English during training, e.g., by using different language mixtures or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks, including more culturally sensitive problems and popular use-cases.
Better understand and map out the concept space in its high-dimensional form.
papers.abstract: We ask whether multilingual language models trained on unbalanced, English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language -- a question of key importance for understanding how language models function and the origins of linguistic bias. Focusing on the Llama-2 family of transformer models, our study uses carefully constructed non-English prompts with a unique correct single-token continuation. From layer to layer, transformers gradually map an input embedding of the final prompt token to an output embedding from which next-token probabilities are computed. Tracking intermediate embeddings through their high-dimensional space reveals three distinct phases, whereby intermediate embeddings (1) start far away from output token embeddings; (2) already allow for decoding a semantically correct next token in the middle layers, but give higher probability to its version in English than in the input language; (3) finally move into an input-language-specific region of the embedding space. We cast these results into a conceptual model where the three phases operate in "input space", "concept space", and "output space", respectively. Crucially, our evidence suggests that the abstract "concept space" lies closer to English than to other languages, which may have important consequences regarding the biases held by multilingual language models.

papers.title: Transformer Language Models without Positional Encodings Still Learn Positional Information
papers.research_question: Can transformer language models learn positional information without explicit positional encodings, and how do they do it?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models without explicit positional encodings (NoPos) can learn implicit positional information and achieve competitive performance, and this ability is due to the causal attention mask.
papers.conclusion: Transformer language models can learn positional information without explicit encodings, and this phenomenon is robust across settings but does not extend to masked language models, with the causal attention mechanism being the key factor.
papers.key_findings:
NoPos models achieve competitive perplexity compared to models with explicit positional encodings across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.
Probing experiments show that NoPos models learn an implicit notion of absolute positions in their hidden representations, similar to models with learned positional embeddings.
The success of NoPos models is unique to causal language models; masked language models fail to converge without positional encodings.
Shuffling the prefix tokens leads to a dramatic increase in loss, indicating that the model uses the learned positional information.
The causal attention mask is conjectured to allow the model to infer absolute positions by counting the number of attendable tokens.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models up to 1.3B parameters, and while the trend suggests the findings should hold for larger models, this is not tested.
NoPos models are always slightly worse than models with positional encodings, indicating that the inductive bias of positional encoding is important.
papers.abstract: Causal transformer language models (LMs), such as GPT-3, typically require some form of positional encoding, such as positional embeddings. However, we show that LMs without any explicit positional encoding are still competitive with standard models and that this phenomenon is robust across different datasets, model sizes, and sequence lengths.Probing experiments reveal that such models acquire an implicit notion of absolute positions throughout the network, effectively compensating for the missing information.We conjecture that causal attention enables the model to infer the number of predecessors that each token can attend to, thereby approximating its absolute position.Our findings indicate that causal LMs might derive positional awareness not only from the explicit positioning mechanism but also from the effects of the causal mask.

papers.title: How Do Multilingual Language Models Remember Facts?
papers.research_question: How do factual recall mechanisms in English LLMs generalize to multilingual LLMs, and when does language play a role in recall?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that factual recall mechanisms in English LLMs generalize to multilingual LLMs with variations, and reveals that the last token acts as a function vector encoding relation and language, composed in two stages in decoder-only models.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for factual recall, indicating that knowledge evaluation and editing methods need to be adapted for multilingual settings.
papers.key_findings:
The early MLP site for subject enrichment is present in multilingual LLMs, but the late site involves both MLP and attention, unlike English LLMs where only attention dominates.
Subject information flows similarly to monolingual models, but non-subject token flow differs.
In multilingual decoder-only LLMs, both feed-forward and attention sublayers contribute to object extraction, unlike in English autoregressive LLMs where attention modules dominate.
The last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV) encoding both the relation and the output language.
In decoder-only LLMs, the FV is constructed in two distinct phases: first encoding the relation, then incorporating the language.
future_direction: Developing knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition methods tailored for multilingual LLMs
Studying how the function vector is altered across languages to understand if models think in English
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) store and retrieve vast amounts of factual knowledge acquired during pre-training. Prior research has localized and identified mechanisms behind knowledge recall; however, it has only focused on English monolingual models. The question of how these mechanisms generalize to non-English languages and multilingual LLMs remains unexplored. In this paper, we address this gap by conducting a comprehensive analysis of three multilingual LLMs. First, we show that previously identified recall mechanisms in English largely apply to multilingual contexts, with nuances based on language and architecture. Next, through patching intermediate representations, we localize the role of language during recall, finding that subject enrichment is language-independent, while object extraction is language-dependent. Additionally, we discover that the last token representation acts as a Function Vector (FV), encoding both the language of the query and the content to be extracted from the subject. Furthermore, in decoder-only LLMs, FVs compose these two pieces of information in two separate stages. These insights reveal unique mechanisms in multilingual LLMs for recalling information, highlighting the need for new methodologies -- such as knowledge evaluation, fact editing, and knowledge acquisition -- that are specifically tailored for multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: From Bias to Balance: Exploring and Mitigating Spatial Bias in LVLMs
papers.research_question: What is the spatial bias in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) and how does it affect their semantic understanding when identical visual information is placed at different locations within an image?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that spatial bias in LVLMs stems from a mismatch between vision encoder and LLM attention mechanisms, and proposes Adaptive Global Context Injection (AGCI) to mitigate this bias by injecting global visual context into image tokens.
papers.conclusion: Spatial bias in LVLMs is caused by the disruption of global information flow due to causal attention, and AGCI effectively mitigates this bias without architectural changes.
papers.key_findings:
LVLMs exhibit significant spatial bias, with predictions varying when key visual content is placed at different locations.
The bias originates from the loss of global image context due to causal attention in LLMs, not from the vision encoder.
AGCI improves spatial robustness and average accuracy on probing tasks across multiple LVLMs.
AGCI also enhances performance on downstream tasks including science QA, hallucination benchmarks, and text VQA.
Larger models also show spatial bias, and AGCI is effective for them as well.
papers.limitation:
The probing experiments focus on a 3x3 spatial grid, which may not capture more fine-grained or irregular spatial variations.
Due to computational constraints, the evaluation does not include very large models such as Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B.
future_direction: Investigating whether spatial bias persists or evolves in larger-scale models.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of multimodal tasks, yet their robustness to spatial variations remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we present a systematic study of the spatial bias of LVLMs, focusing on how models respond when identical key visual information is placed at different locations within an image. Through a carefully designed probing dataset, we demonstrate that current LVLMs often produce inconsistent outputs under such spatial shifts, revealing a fundamental limitation in their spatial-semantic understanding. Further analysis shows that this phenomenon originates not from the vision encoder, which reliably perceives and interprets visual content across positions, but from the unbalanced design of position embeddings in the language model component. In particular, the widely adopted position embedding strategies, such as RoPE, introduce imbalance during cross-modal interaction, leading image tokens at different positions to exert unequal influence on semantic understanding. To mitigate this issue, we introduce Balanced Position Assignment (BaPA), a simple yet effective mechanism that assigns identical position embeddings to all image tokens, promoting a more balanced integration of visual information. Extensive experiments show that BaPA enhances the spatial robustness of LVLMs without retraining and further boosts their performance across diverse multimodal benchmarks when combined with lightweight fine-tuning. Further analysis of information flow reveals that BaPA yields balanced attention, enabling more holistic visual understanding.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Multimodal Fine-Tuning: Spatial Features
papers.research_question: How do language backbone representations adapt during multimodal fine-tuning, and when do vision-specific capabilities emerge?
papers.core_contribution: They present a mechanistic analysis of multimodal fine-tuning using stage-wise model diffing, showing how language models learn spatial reasoning through feature reorientation and specialized attention heads.
papers.conclusion: Multimodal adaptation is structured and interpretable, with spatial reasoning emerging through feature reorientation and specialized attention heads.
papers.key_findings:
Vision-preferring features emerge or reorient during multimodal fine-tuning.
A selective subset of these features reliably encodes spatial relations.
These spatial features are causally driven by a small group of mid-layer attention heads.
Stage-wise model diffing can isolate adapted features and reveal when and where spatially-grounded multimodal features arise.
Ablating these spatial features selectively impairs spatial reasoning while leaving general VQA performance unchanged.
papers.limitation:
More detailed ablation and steering studies are needed to fully validate causality.
Experiments are limited to a single model (LLaVA-More with LLaMA-3.1-8B backbone), so generality is unclear.
future_direction: Applying the method to other backbones and larger corpora to assess generality.
papers.abstract: Contemporary Vision-Language Models (VLMs) achieve strong performance on a wide range of tasks by pairing a vision encoder with a pre-trained language model, fine-tuned for visual-text inputs. Yet despite these gains, it remains unclear how language backbone representations adapt during multimodal training and when vision-specific capabilities emerge. In this work, we present the first mechanistic analysis of VLM adaptation. Using stage-wise model diffing, a technique that isolates representational changes introduced during multimodal fine-tuning, we reveal how a language model learns to "see". We first identify vision-preferring features that emerge or reorient during fine-tuning. We then show that a selective subset of these features reliably encodes spatial relations, revealed through controlled shifts to spatial prompts. Finally, we trace the causal activation of these features to a small group of attention heads. Our findings show that stage-wise model diffing reveals when and where spatially grounded multimodal features arise. It also provides a clearer view of modality fusion by showing how visual grounding reshapes features that were previously text-only. This methodology enhances the interpretability of multimodal training and provides a foundation for understanding and refining how pretrained language models acquire vision-grounded capabilities.

papers.title: Learning Interpretable Spatial Operations in a Rich 3D Blocks World
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language instructions to complex spatial actions in a 3D blocks world, and can we learn an inventory of interpretable spatial operations from such data?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a new dataset for 3D spatial language grounding with richer concepts and a new interpretable neural model that learns spatial operations as a set of basis functions.
papers.conclusion: This work presents a new model that learns interpretable spatial operations and a new corpus of 3D spatial language to advance research in action understanding.
papers.key_findings:
The new dataset introduces richer spatial language concepts (e.g., mirroring, twisting, balancing) and is more challenging than previous 2D datasets.
