We replace the standard MLP projection layer in REPA with a simple convolution layer and introduce a spatial normalization layer for the external representation. Surprisingly, our simple method (implemented in $<$4 lines of code), termed iREPA, consistently improves convergence speed of REPA, across a diverse set of vision encoders, model sizes, and training variants (such as REPA, REPA-E, Meanflow, JiT etc). %, etc. Our work motivates revisiting the fundamental working mechanism of representational alignment and how it can be leveraged for improved training of generative models. The code and project page are available at https://end2end-diffusion.github.io/irepa

papers.title: The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably re-discover known algorithms for solving those tasks, and under what conditions do they discover familiar algorithmic solutions?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on modular addition can discover qualitatively different algorithms (Clock, Pizza, and others), with the algorithm learned depending on hyperparameters like attention rate and width, revealing algorithmic phase transitions and the need for tools to characterize algorithmic phase spaces.
papers.conclusion: Algorithmic discoveries in neural networks are not inevitable; even simple tasks admit a diversity of solutions, motivating the development of tools to characterize the algorithmic phase space of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Networks can learn either the previously described Clock algorithm or a new, less intuitive Pizza algorithm for modular addition.
The Pizza algorithm uses averaging and absolute value operations, while the Clock algorithm uses multiplication via attention.
Models sometimes implement multiple, parallel copies of an algorithm (ensembling) for robustness.
Sharp algorithmic phase transitions between Clock and Pizza occur as model hyperparameters (attention rate, width) are varied.
Non-circular algorithms also exist, especially in deeper networks or with low attention rates.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on a single learning problem (modular addition), and scaling the techniques to more complex models and real-world tasks requires significant additional work.
future_direction: How to find, classify, and interpret unfamiliar algorithms in a systematic way.
How to disentangle multiple, parallel algorithm implementations in the presence of ensembling.
papers.abstract: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably rediscover known algorithms for solving those tasks? Several recent studies, on tasks ranging from group arithmetic to in-context linear regression, have suggested that the answer is yes. Using modular addition as a prototypical problem, we show that algorithm discovery in neural networks is sometimes more complex. Small changes to model hyperparameters and initializations can induce the discovery of qualitatively different algorithms from a fixed training set, and even parallel implementations of multiple such algorithms. Some networks trained to perform modular addition implement a familiar Clock algorithm; others implement a previously undescribed, less intuitive, but comprehensible procedure which we term the Pizza algorithm, or a variety of even more complex procedures. Our results show that even simple learning problems can admit a surprising diversity of solutions, motivating the development of new tools for characterizing the behavior of neural networks across their algorithmic phase space.

papers.title: Emergent Structured Representations Support Flexible In-Context Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether large language models functionally rely on structured, human-like conceptual representations for reasoning during in-context concept inference.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs dynamically construct and use a structured, latent conceptual subspace during in-context inference, and this subspace is causally involved in predictions.
papers.conclusion: LLMs construct and use abstract structured representations for in-context inference, offering a mechanistic window into the computational basis of their adaptive behavior.
papers.key_findings:
A conceptual subspace emerges in middle to late layers, with persistent structure across contexts.
Causal mediation analysis shows this subspace is functionally central to model predictions.
Attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace.
The subspace becomes more stable with increasing numbers of demonstrations.
The subspace supports cross-context generalization via a functionally aligned relational structure.
papers.limitation:
Smaller models rely less consistently on the subspace mechanism, exhibiting more diffuse, non-subspace-specific strategies.
Findings are based on a specific reverse dictionary task and may not generalize to all reasoning contexts.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit emergent behaviors suggestive of human-like reasoning. While recent work has identified structured, human-like conceptual representations within these models, it remains unclear whether they functionally rely on such representations for reasoning. Here we investigate the internal processing of LLMs during in-context concept inference. Our results reveal a conceptual subspace emerging in middle to late layers, whose representational structure persists across contexts. Using causal mediation analyses, we demonstrate that this subspace is not merely an epiphenomenon but is functionally central to model predictions, establishing its causal role in inference. We further identify a layer-wise progression where attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace, which is subsequently leveraged by later layers to generate predictions. Together, these findings provide evidence that LLMs dynamically construct and use structured, latent representations in context for inference, offering insights into the computational processes underlying flexible adaptation.

papers.title: Improving Multilingual Language Models by Aligning Representations through Steering
papers.research_question: How can multilingual alignment in LLMs be achieved efficiently by targeting a single layer through representation steering, and what does this reveal about internal structures?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a lightweight method to enhance multilingual LLMs by steering representations at a single layer, achieving performance competitive with translation systems while requiring fewer resources.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that activation-level steering is an efficient tool for improving multilingual capabilities, providing insights into internal representations and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Single-layer steering significantly improves multilingual performance over baselines like prompt optimization and SFT.
Steering vectors can be shared across structurally similar languages, enabling zero-shot cross-linguistic transfer.
The method approaches the performance of Google Translate, with DPO steering trailing by only 3.08%.
High-resource languages dominate the representation space, and steering helps align low-resource languages.
Steering is most effective in early layers for multilingual models like Aya23, while for models like Llama2, it varies by language resource level.
papers.limitation:
probing by sweeping across all model layers is not scalable for LLMs and is impractical for real-world applications
the learnable steering vector is constrained by its fixed linear direction, limiting its capacity to capture intricate mapping relationships
experiments were focused on single layer and language, lacking multi-objective training
future_direction: Developing context-aware steering mechanisms that adapt dynamically to each prompt
Learning steering vectors by individual tokens rather than fixed vectors
Multi-objective training for simultaneous multi-language and multi-layer steering
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how Large Language Models (LLMs) represent non-English tokens -- a question that remains underexplored despite recent progress. We propose a lightweight intervention method using representation steering, where a learned vector is added to the residual stream at a single model layer to enhance multilingual performance. Through extensive experiments across seven competitive baselines -- including prompt optimization, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), in-context learning, cross-lingual transfer, and translation-based methods-we show that our approach consistently outperforms most alternatives. In particular, it achieves performance on par with production-grade translation systems while requiring far fewer resources. We further explore the complementarity between our method and SFT, demonstrating that steering offers a direct, efficient way to realign internal representations. These findings underscore the potential of activation-level interventions as a powerful tool for improving the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Triangulation as an Acceptance Rule for Multilingual Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we validate mechanistic explanations for multilingual models to ensure they are causal and invariant across languages and scripts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces triangulation, an acceptance rule for mechanistic interpretability that requires necessity, sufficiency, and invariance across predicate-preserving environments to filter spurious circuits.
papers.conclusion: Triangulation offers a concrete step toward rigorous, transferable mechanistic explanations by requiring cross-environment consistency, allowing circuits that pass to be interpreted with greater confidence as capturing language-agnostic mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Triangulation provides a falsifiable standard for mechanistic claims that filters spurious circuits passing single-environment tests but failing cross-lingual invariance.
Triangulation can be extended to multimodal settings by holding the image fixed and varying the prompt language.
Triangulation enables separation of circuits into visual, linguistic, and spurious categories based on cross-environment invariance.
The method is grounded in causal abstraction theory and provides an approximate transformation score over interchange interventions.
Triangulation requires explicit cue-only falsifiers to reject mechanisms that rely on surface cues rather than predicate information.
papers.limitation:
Multiple circuits may satisfy triangulation if their effects are redundant; triangulation identifies sufficient mechanisms but does not guarantee uniqueness.
The quality of reference families is decisive, and poor-quality families can mislead by either accepting spurious circuits or rejecting genuine circuits.
Causal interventions at scale are computationally expensive, and prioritization strategies are advisable for practical deployment.
When using LLM judges to verify predicate preservation, circularity risks arise if the judge correlates with the model under study.
papers.abstract: Multilingual language models achieve strong aggregate performance yet often behave unpredictably across languages, scripts, and cultures. We argue that mechanistic explanations for such models should satisfy a \emph{causal} standard: claims must survive causal interventions and must \emph{cross-reference} across environments that perturb surface form while preserving meaning. We formalize \emph{reference families} as predicate-preserving variants and introduce \emph{triangulation}, an acceptance rule requiring necessity (ablating the circuit degrades the target behavior), sufficiency (patching activations transfers the behavior), and invariance (both effects remain directionally stable and of sufficient magnitude across the reference family). To supply candidate subgraphs, we adopt automatic circuit discovery and \emph{accept or reject} those candidates by triangulation. We ground triangulation in causal abstraction by casting it as an approximate transformation score over a distribution of interchange interventions, connect it to the pragmatic interpretability agenda, and present a comparative experimental protocol across multiple model families, language pairs, and tasks. Triangulation provides a falsifiable standard for mechanistic claims that filters spurious circuits passing single-environment tests but failing cross-lingual invariance.

papers.title: Enhancing Multimodal Large Language Models Complex Reason via Similarity Computation
papers.research_question: How can the complex reasoning ability of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) be improved by efficiently utilizing image information and filtering out irrelevant image tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that image tokens semantically related to text have information flow convergence and higher attention scores in the LLM decoder, and proposes Simignore, a method to filter irrelevant image tokens based on similarity computation, which improves complex reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Simignore method, which computes similarity between image and text embeddings to filter irrelevant tokens, enhances the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Image tokens semantically related to text prompts are more likely to have information flow convergence and receive higher attention scores in the LLM decoder.
Filtering out irrelevant image tokens based on similarity between image and text embeddings improves the accuracy of LVLMs on complex reasoning tasks.
The performance improvement depends on the number of tokens ignored, with an optimal number (e.g., 124 out of 576 for LLaVA1.5-7B) yielding the best results.
Important image tokens (with high similarity to text) are crucial for complex reasoning, while unimportant tokens can be ignored to improve performance and reduce computation.
Cosine similarity performs better than Euclidean and Manhattan distance for computing the similarity between image and text embeddings in this task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not adaptively choose the number of image tokens to ignore.
The internal mechanisms of how image and textual information work together to facilitate complex reasoning are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring strategies for adaptively choosing the number of image tokens to ignore.
Investigating the internal mechanisms of the model to more fully understand how image and textual information work together.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have experienced rapid growth, and numerous different models have emerged. The interpretability of LVLMs remains an under-explored area. Especially when faced with more complex tasks such as chain-of-thought reasoning, its internal mechanisms still resemble a black box that is difficult to decipher. By studying the interaction and information flow between images and text, we noticed that in models such as LLaVA1.5, image tokens that are semantically related to text are more likely to have information flow convergence in the LLM decoding layer, and these image tokens receive higher attention scores. However, those image tokens that are less relevant to the text do not have information flow convergence, and they only get very small attention scores. To efficiently utilize the image information, we propose a new image token reduction method, Simignore, which aims to improve the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs by computing the similarity between image and text embeddings and ignoring image tokens that are irrelevant and unimportant to the text. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for complex reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Computation Mechanism Behind LLM Position Generalization
papers.research_question: How do large language models (LLMs) computationally process positional information to enable position generalization, such as tolerance to position perturbations and length generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that LLMs learn a disentanglement of attention logits into positional and semantic components, with a linear correlation of 0.959, and identifies a pattern in intermediate features that enables this effect, providing computational explanations for position generalization.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that attention logits in LLMs can be approximately disentangled into independent positional and semantic components, providing computational explanations for position generalization and insights for controlling these phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
Attention logits can be approximated by a 3-axis linear decomposition with high correlation.
Attention logits can be disentangled into a sum of positional relevance and semantic importance components.
A pattern in slow-rotating dimensions of query and key vectors enables this disentanglement, which is learned rather than inherent.
LLMs exhibit robustness to position perturbations in text, feature order, and position encoding, with minimal impact on perplexity and downstream task accuracy.
The disentanglement mechanism explains how length generalization techniques work by keeping attention outputs in-distribution.
papers.limitation:
The study primarily evaluates position robustness involving text order and length generalizations, but real-world language processing tasks often involve more complex positional dependencies.
The extent to which models actively leverage this property during training is unclear.
future_direction: Future research could delve deeper into the specific architectural choices and training data patterns that contribute to this robustness.
Future explanations on how such a mechanism is acquired during training dynamics could greatly enhance the work.
papers.abstract: Most written natural languages are composed of sequences of words and sentences. Similar to humans, large language models (LLMs) exhibit flexibility in handling textual positions - a phenomenon we term position generalization. They can understand texts with position perturbations and generalize to longer texts than those encountered during training with the latest techniques. These phenomena suggest that LLMs handle positions tolerantly, but how LLMs computationally process positional relevance remains largely unexplored. This work connects the linguistic phenomenon with LLMs' computational mechanisms. We show how LLMs enforce certain computational mechanisms for the aforementioned tolerance in position perturbations. Despite the complex design of the self-attention mechanism, this work reveals that LLMs learn a counterintuitive disentanglement of attention logits. Their values show a 0.959 linear correlation with an approximation of the arithmetic sum of positional relevance and semantic importance. Furthermore, we identify a prevalent pattern in intermediate features, which we prove theoretically enables this effect. The pattern, which is different from how randomly initialized parameters would behave, suggests that it is a learned behavior rather than a natural result of the model architecture. Based on these findings, we provide computational explanations and criteria for LLMs' position flexibilities. This work takes a pioneering step in linking position generalization with modern LLMs' internal mechanisms.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Tracing the Roots of Facts in Multilingual Language Models: Independent, Shared, and Transferred Knowledge
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how multilingual language models acquire and represent factual knowledge across languages, specifically examining the factors affecting probing performance, whether fact representations are shared or independent across languages, and how cross-lingual representations are formed.
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes methods for distinguishing three types of fact representations in multilingual language models (language-independent, cross-lingual shared, and cross-lingual transferred) and reveals the challenges in cross-lingual factual knowledge transfer.
papers.conclusion: Our research establishes the groundwork for further studies in understanding cross-lingual factual knowledge representation and highlights the challenges in achieving effective cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge from high-resource to low-resource languages in ML-LMs.
papers.key_findings:
Factual probing performance across languages shows moderate correlation with training data volume and strong negative correlation with mask token count.
There are localized knowledge sharing patterns among geographically proximate languages.
ML-LMs exhibit both language-independent and cross-lingual fact representations, even for the same fact.
Active fact neurons in low-resource languages are more active and distributed in shallow layers compared to high-resource languages.
Cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge does occur but is limited, and many correctly predicted facts in low-resource languages can be attributed to simple inference patterns rather than true transfer.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to encoder-based models (mBERT and XLM-R) and may not generalize to large decoder-based multilingual models.
future_direction: Enhance the cross-lingual fact representation learning in ML-LMs.
Develop a more precise factual probing dataset.
papers.abstract: Acquiring factual knowledge for language models (LMs) in low-resource languages poses a serious challenge, thus resorting to cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LMs (ML-LMs).In this study, we ask how ML-LMs acquire and represent factual knowledge.Using the multilingual factual knowledge probing dataset, mLAMA, we first conducted a neuron investigation of ML-LMs (specifically, multilingual BERT).We then traced the roots of facts back to the knowledge source (Wikipedia) to identify the ways in which ML-LMs acquire specific facts.We finally identified three patterns of acquiring and representing facts in ML-LMs: languageindependent, cross-lingual shared and transferred, and devised methods for differentiating them.Our findings highlight the challenge of maintaining consistent factual knowledge across languages, underscoring the need for better fact representation learning in ML-LMs. 1

papers.title: Understanding the role of FFNs in driving multilingual behaviour in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in large language models drive multilingual behavior, and what are the patterns of multilingual processing across layers and model sizes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the metric 'activation flatness' and analyzes FFN sublayers (detectors and combinators) to reveal distinct patterns of multilingual processing, identifying the phenomenon of 'over-layerization' where increasing layer depth without other adjustments can degrade performance.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals distinct patterns in FFN sublayers for multilingual processing, with detectors becoming more peaked and language-specific in later layers, and combinators showing multilingual behavior in middle layers, while also identifying over-layerization in certain model configurations.
papers.key_findings:
FFN representations are more sparse near the input and output layers across all models.
Detector activations become more peaked (less flat) through the layers, while combinator activations show a distinct drop in flatness around layer 20 regardless of model size.
Early detector layers are multilingual and process shallow features, becoming more language-specific near the output.
Combinator layers are mostly multilingual in the middle layers, with the final layers becoming language-specific, especially in larger models.
The 2.9B parameter model exhibits 'over-layerization', where increased layer depth without corresponding adjustments leads to degraded generation quality compared to the 7.5B model.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies only on model snapshots (activations), which does not fully capture the complexities of LLMs; probing tasks or attention matrices could provide a more comprehensive understanding.
The investigation is limited to the XGLM model family, and findings may not generalize to other LLM architectures or implementations.
The analysis is limited to a set of predefined languages and test sets, which may not fully represent linguistic diversity.
future_direction: Investigate whether flatter activation patterns are easier to adapt in QLoRA fine-tuning.
Extend the analysis to more languages and explore cross-linguistic variation in more detail.
papers.abstract: Multilingualism in Large Language Models (LLMs) is an yet under-explored area. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the multilingual capabilities of a family of a Large Language Model, examining its architecture, activation patterns, and processing mechanisms across languages. We introduce novel metrics to probe the model's multilingual behaviour at different layers and shed light on the impact of architectural choices on multilingual processing. Our findings reveal different patterns of multilinugal processing in the sublayers of Feed-Forward Networks of the models. Furthermore, we uncover the phenomenon of "over-layerization" in certain model configurations, where increasing layer depth without corresponding adjustments to other parameters may degrade model performance. Through comparisons within and across languages, we demonstrate the interplay between model architecture, layer depth, and multilingual processing capabilities of LLMs trained on multiple languages.

papers.title: Are Structural Concepts Universal in Transformer Language Models? Towards Interpretable Cross-Lingual Generalization
papers.research_question: Can explicitly aligning conceptual correspondence between languages enhance cross-lingual generalization in transformer language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that structural concepts (word classes and grammatical relations) are implicitly alignable across languages in transformer LMs, and proposes a meta-learning method to explicitly align these concepts, improving zero-shot and few-shot cross-lingual generalization without updating the LM parameters.
papers.conclusion: Explicitly aligning conceptual correspondence between languages via meta-learning improves cross-lingual generalization, achieving competitive performance and narrowing the gap between languages, particularly for low-resource ones.
papers.key_findings:
Structural concepts (word classes and grammatical relations) can be identified based on prototypes in a relatively low-dimensional space of LM representations.
These structural concepts are highly alignable across languages in both encoder-only (mBERT) and decoder-only (LLaMA) models, as measured by RSA and Procrustes analysis.
A meta-learning-based method to align conceptual spaces achieves competitive results with state-of-the-art methods on syntactic analysis tasks, especially benefiting low-resource languages.
The method reduces the performance gap between high-resource and low-resource languages.
The approach provides insights into cross-lingual in-context learning and can be integrated with prompting to improve generalization.
papers.limitation: Variations in alignability between language pairs may stem from insufficient UD treebank data for approximating prototypes and degenerate representation spaces for certain languages due to inadequate pretraining data or tokenization deficiencies.
future_direction: Expanding the approach to other aspects of language to better accommodate linguistic diversity using self-supervised knowledge.
Exploring more expressive probing models to extract structural concepts, especially grammatical relations, from models like LLaMA.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have exhibited considerable cross-lingual generalization abilities, whereby they implicitly transfer knowledge across languages. However, the transfer is not equally successful for all languages, especially for low-resource ones, which poses an ongoing challenge. It is unclear whether we have reached the limits of implicit cross-lingual generalization and if explicit knowledge transfer is viable. In this paper, we investigate the potential for explicitly aligning conceptual correspondence between languages to enhance cross-lingual generalization. Using the syntactic aspect of language as a testbed, our analyses of 43 languages reveal a high degree of alignability among the spaces of structural concepts within each language for both encoder-only and decoder-only LLMs. We then propose a meta-learning-based method to learn to align conceptual spaces of different languages, which facilitates zero-shot and few-shot generalization in concept classification and also offers insights into the cross-lingual in-context learning phenomenon. Experiments on syntactic analysis tasks show that our approach achieves competitive results with state-of-the-art methods and narrows the performance gap between languages, particularly benefiting those with limited resources.

papers.title: Probing Contextual Language Models for Common Ground with Visual\n Representations
papers.research_question: To what extent are contextual representations of concrete nouns aligned with corresponding visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a probing method to measure the alignment between contextual language representations and visual features, finding that language representations provide a strong signal for retrieving image patches and that context plays an important role.
papers.conclusion: Contextual language models are useful for discerning between visual representations, but there is a large gap between model and human performance, indicating room for improvement in grounding language models.
papers.key_findings:
Contextual language models (e.g., BERT) significantly outperform non-contextual embeddings (e.g., GloVe) in instance-level retrieval of image patches.
Language representations alone can retrieve image patches of the correct object category with high recall (84-90%).
Contextual information, especially adjectives, improves instance retrieval accuracy.
Visually grounded language models (e.g., VILBERT-MT) slightly outperform text-only models in instance retrieval.
All examined models lag significantly behind human performance in instance retrieval.
papers.limitation: The examined models significantly underperform human subjects in instance retrieval.
papers.abstract:
The success of large-scale contextual language models has attracted great
interest in probing what is encoded in their representations. In this work, we
consider a new question: to what extent contextual representations of concrete
nouns are aligned with corresponding visual representations? We design a
probing model that evaluates how effective are text-only representations in
distinguishing between matching and non-matching visual representations. Our
findings show that language representations alone provide a strong signal for
retrieving image patches from the correct object categories. Moreover, they are
effective in retrieving specific instances of image patches; textual context
plays an important role in this process. Visually grounded language models
slightly outperform text-only language models in instance retrieval, but
greatly under-perform humans. We hope our analyses inspire future research in
understanding and improving the visual capabilities of language models.

papers.title: High-Dimensional Interlingual Representations of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do multilingual large language models develop a universal interlingua representation, or present a partially aligned construct toward certain languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework and the Interlingual Local Overlap (ILO) metric to analyze interlingual representations in multilingual LLMs, and shows that selectively freezing early layers during single-language fine-tuning preserves interlingual alignment and improves cross-lingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: Interlingual semantic alignment is crucial for scalable multilingual learning, and the proposed framework and ILO metric provide effective tools for evaluating and preserving this alignment in multilingual LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual LLMs exhibit inconsistent cross-lingual alignments, with stronger alignment between high-resource languages and within the same linguistic family or region.
Single-language fine-tuning disrupts interlingual alignment, particularly in early layers, leading to degraded cross-lingual generalization.
Selectively freezing early layers (and other alignment-critical parameters) during single-language fine-tuning preserves interlingual alignment and significantly improves cross-lingual transfer performance.
The proposed ILO score effectively quantifies the degree of interlingual alignment by measuring the local neighborhood structure of high-dimensional representations.
Interlingual overlaps that transcend familial and regional boundaries are observed in intermediate model layers, while early and late layers show clustering by resource level and linguistic features.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained on massive multilingual datasets hint at the formation of interlingual constructs--a shared subspace in the representation space. However, evidence regarding this phenomenon is mixed, leaving it unclear whether these models truly develop unified interlingual representations, or present a partially aligned constructs. We explore 31 diverse languages varying on their resource-levels, typologies, and geographical regions; and find that multilingual LLMs exhibit inconsistent cross-lingual alignments. To address this, we propose an interlingual representation framework identifying both the shared interlingual semantic subspace and fragmented components, existed due to representational limitations. We introduce Interlingual Local Overlap (ILO) score to quantify interlingual alignment by comparing the local neighborhood structures of high-dimensional representations. We utilize ILO to investigate the impact of single-language fine-tuning on the interlingual representations in multilingual LLMs. Our results indicate that training exclusively on a single language disrupts the alignment in early layers, while freezing these layers preserves the alignment of interlingual representations, leading to improved cross-lingual generalization. These results validate our framework and metric for evaluating interlingual representation, and further underscore that interlingual alignment is crucial for scalable multilingual learning.

papers.title: Contributions of Transformer Attention Heads in Multi- and Cross-lingual Tasks
papers.research_question: What are the effects of pruning attention heads in multilingual Transformer-based models on cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks, and how can important heads be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that pruning a subset of attention heads in multilingual Transformer models (mBERT and XLM-R) generally improves performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks, and introduces a gradient-based method to rank and identify which heads to prune.
papers.conclusion: Pruning attention heads in multilingual Transformer models generally improves performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks, and the gradient-based method effectively identifies heads to prune, offering better model interpretability and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning attention heads in mBERT and XLM-R generally has positive effects on model performance in cross-lingual and multi-lingual sequence labeling tasks (POS, NER, SF).
A gradient-based method can effectively rank attention heads by importance, and pruning the lowest-ranked heads leads to performance improvements.
The important attention heads for a task are shared across languages, as evidenced by high correlation in head rankings across different languages.
Pruning attention heads is beneficial even when training data in the target language is limited, making models more applicable to resource-poor languages.
In multi-source language settings, pruning attention heads also improves performance, and the gradient-based ranking method can be extended to multiple source languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to sequence labeling tasks (POS, NER, SF) and may not generalize to other cross-lingual tasks.
future_direction: Improving model interpretability in other cross-lingual and multi-lingual tasks, e.g., XNLI and other passage-level classification tasks.
papers.abstract: Weicheng Ma, Kai Zhang, Renze Lou, Lili Wang, Soroush Vosoughi. Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2021.

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: When Alignment Hurts: Decoupling Representational Spaces in Multilingual Models
papers.research_question: Does alignment with a high-resource standard language always benefit related low-resource varieties? The paper challenges this assumption by showing that excessive representational entanglement can hinder generative modeling.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an online variational probing framework for subspace decoupling, providing causal evidence that representational entanglement with a high-resource language hinders generative modeling for low-resource varieties.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates that representational entanglement with a high-resource language is a critical and addressable bottleneck for generative modeling in closely-related, low-resource language varieties, and provides a causal intervention method to mitigate it.
papers.key_findings:
Excessive representational entanglement with Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) hinders generative performance for low-resource Arabic dialects.
Better generative performance correlates with greater representational separability from MSA in the model's internal geometry.
The proposed online subspace decoupling intervention improves dialectal generation by up to +4.9 chrF++ on individual dialects and +2.0 on average compared to standard fine-tuning.
The intervention leads to a trade-off, with a measured decrease in standard-language (MSA) generation performance.
The method is effective across 25 Arabic dialects, demonstrating the generalizability of the representational dominance phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
The MADAR dataset is composed of relatively short sentences, which may not fully capture model behaviors on tasks requiring longer-form generation.
The causal claim is based on intervention experiments within a single language family (Arabic), and generalization to other language families requires further validation.
future_direction: Scalable and Efficient Methods
Inference-Time Interventions
Generalization to Other Languages
papers.abstract: Alignment with high-resource standard languages is often assumed to aid the modeling of related low-resource varieties. We challenge this assumption by demonstrating that excessive representational entanglement with a dominant variety, such as Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) in relation to Arabic dialects, can actively hinder generative modeling. We present the first comprehensive causal study of this phenomenon by analyzing and directly intervening in the internal representation geometry of large language models (LLMs). Our key contribution is an online variational probing framework that continuously estimates the subspace of the standard variety during fine-tuning, enabling projection-based decoupling from this space. While our study uses Arabic as a case due to its unusually rich parallel resources across 25 dialects, the broader motivation is methodological: dialectal MT serves as a controlled proxy for generative tasks where comparable multi-variety corpora are unavailable. Across 25 dialects, our intervention improves generation quality by up to +4.9 chrF++ and +2.0 on average compared to standard fine-tuning, despite a measured tradeoff in standard-language performance. These results provide causal evidence that subspace dominance by high-resource varieties can restrict generative capacity for related varieties. More generally, we unify geometric and information-theoretic probing with subspace-level causal interventions, offering practical tools for improving generative modeling in closely related language families and, more broadly, for controlling representational allocation in multilingual and multi-domain LLMs. Code will be released.

papers.title: Evidence of Learned Look-Ahead in a Chess-Playing Neural Network
papers.research_question: Do neural networks learn to implement algorithms such as look-ahead or search internally, or do they rely on simple heuristics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that the policy network of Leela Chess Zero has learned to perform internal look-ahead, representing future optimal moves and using these representations causally for its output.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents correlational and causal evidence of learned look-ahead in Leela, suggesting that in tactically complex states, some form of look-ahead plays an important role in determining the model's policy.
papers.key_findings:
Activations on the target square of the optimal move two turns into the future (the 3rd move) are unusually important for the network's output, as shown by activation patching.
Attention head L12H12 moves information from the 3rd move target square 'backward in time' to the 1st move target square, and its ablation significantly reduces performance.
Specialized 'piece movement heads' appear to analyze the consequences of future moves; ablating information flow out of the 3rd move target in these heads reduces performance.
A simple bilinear probe trained on the network's activations can predict the optimal move two turns ahead with 92% accuracy.
The convergence of these three lines of evidence strongly suggests learned look-ahead is an important mechanism in the model.
papers.limitation:
The paper does not present a precise description of how look-ahead might be implemented in Leela.
The work focuses on look-ahead along a single line of play and does not test whether Leela compares multiple different lines (search).
The analysis focuses on board states that are unusually complex and thus more likely to require look-ahead, not the entire input distribution.
Chess as a domain might favor look-ahead to an unusually strong extent, limiting generalizability.
future_direction: Understanding the exact implementation of look-ahead in Leela.
Studying whether language models use similarly principled mechanisms when appropriate.
Gaining a better understanding of how look-ahead might be combined with simple heuristics in Leela across the input distribution.
papers.abstract: Do neural networks learn to implement algorithms such as look-ahead or search "in the wild"? Or do they rely purely on collections of simple heuristics? We present evidence of learned look-ahead in the policy network of Leela Chess Zero, the currently strongest neural chess engine. We find that Leela internally represents future optimal moves and that these representations are crucial for its final output in certain board states. Concretely, we exploit the fact that Leela is a transformer that treats every chessboard square like a token in language models, and give three lines of evidence (1) activations on certain squares of future moves are unusually important causally; (2) we find attention heads that move important information "forward and backward in time," e.g., from squares of future moves to squares of earlier ones; and (3) we train a simple probe that can predict the optimal move 2 turns ahead with 92% accuracy (in board states where Leela finds a single best line). These findings are an existence proof of learned look-ahead in neural networks and might be a step towards a better understanding of their capabilities.

papers.title: The inevitability and superfluousness of cell types in spatial cognition
papers.research_question: Does spatial knowledge and spatial cell-like representations arise in non-spatial computational systems, and are these cells necessary for spatial cognition?
papers.core_contribution: Spatial cell-like representations inevitably arise in complex non-spatial systems and are superfluous for spatial cognition, as spatial information is distributed and can be decoded even without them.
papers.conclusion: Spatial cell types may be inevitable and superfluous in complex information processing systems, and the focus on cell types may be misleading.
papers.key_findings:
DNNs for object recognition, even untrained, can decode spatial variables (location, heading, distance to border) from visual inputs.
Many units in these DNNs exhibit firing patterns that meet criteria for place, head-direction, and border cells.
Excluding units classified as spatial cells has minimal impact on spatial decoding performance.
Spatial information is distributed across units, and units most important for decoding are not necessarily those with classic spatial tuning.
These results challenge the necessity and specificity of spatial cell types in spatial cognition.
papers.limitation: The model does not capture all empirical findings of spatial cells and has limited scope and generalizability.
future_direction: Blurring the visual inputs to DNNs to match rodent perception.
Vary environmental settings to verify generalizability.
Vary the environment to assess remapping effects.
papers.abstract: Summary Discoveries of functional cell types, exemplified by the cataloging of spatial cells in the hippocampal formation, are heralded as scientific breakthroughs. We question whether the identification of cell types based on human intuitions has scientific merit and suggest that “spatial cells” may arise in non-spatial computations of sufficient complexity. We show that deep neural networks (DNNs) for object recognition, which lack spatial grounding, contain numerous units resembling place, border, and head-direction cells. Strikingly, even untrained DNNs with randomized weights contained such units and support decoding of spatial information. Moreover, when these “spatial” units are excluded, spatial information can be decoded from the remaining DNN units, which highlights the superfluousness of cell types to spatial cognition. Now that large-scale simulations are feasible, the complexity of the brain should be respected and intuitive notions of cell type, which can be misleading and arise in any complex network, should be relegated to history.

papers.title: Shape Happens: Automatic Feature Manifold Discovery in LLMs via Supervised Multi-Dimensional Scaling
papers.research_question: How can we reliably detect feature manifolds in language models, and do these manifolds actively support reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Supervised Multi-Dimensional Scaling (SMDS), a method for hypothesis-driven manifold analysis, and shows that feature manifolds in LLMs are stable, interpretable, and actively used in reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The findings shed light on the functional role of feature manifolds, supporting a model of entity-based reasoning in which LMs encode and transform structured representations.
papers.key_findings:
Temporal entities form feature manifolds with intuitive structures (e.g., circles, lines, clusters) that are consistent across model architectures and sizes.
Feature manifolds are dynamically adjusted depending on the task and context.
Feature manifolds actively support reasoning, as perturbing them impairs performance and manifold quality correlates with accuracy.
The method extends to other domains (e.g., geography) and to multidimensional manifolds.
Models represent temporal intervals with logarithmic compression, resembling the Weber-Fechner law.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to a set of pre-defined geometric hypotheses.
The datasets are synthetic and may not fully capture the complexity of real-world temporal reasoning.
The intervention experiments, while indicative, do not establish strict causality.
future_direction: Extend SMDS to automatically discover manifold geometries.
Apply SMDS to more complex reasoning tasks.
Investigate how manifolds evolve during training.
papers.abstract: The linear representation hypothesis states that language models (LMs) encode concepts as directions in their latent space, forming organized, multidimensional manifolds. Prior efforts focus on discovering specific geometries for specific features, and thus lack generalization. We introduce Supervised Multi-Dimensional Scaling (SMDS), a model-agnostic method to automatically discover feature manifolds. We apply SMDS to temporal reasoning as a case study, finding that different features form various geometric structures such as circles, lines, and clusters. SMDS reveals many insights on these structures: they consistently reflect the properties of the concepts they represent; are stable across model families and sizes; actively support reasoning in models; and dynamically reshape in response to context changes. Together, our findings shed light on the functional role of feature manifolds, supporting a model of entity-based reasoning in which LMs encode and transform structured representations.

papers.title: Evaluating the Representational Hub of Language and Vision Models
papers.research_question: How do different vision-and-language tasks affect the encoder's ability to learn multimodal representations that are transferable and truly merge the two modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The multimodal encoding skills learned by pre-training on GuessWhat and ReferIt are more stable and transferable than those learned through VQA, and all encoders give more weight to the visual input than the linguistic one.
papers.conclusion: None of the three tasks leads to learning fine-grained multimodal understanding skills that can solve the FOIL task well, but there are differences among tasks: VQA encoder learns less stable and transferable skills, while ReferIt and GuessWhat encoders are more stable and transferable, and the visual modality has higher weight than the linguistic one.
papers.key_findings:
The VQA task is easier to learn but the multimodal encoding skills it learns are less stable and transferable than those learned through ReferIt and GuessWhat.
The ReferIt and GuessWhat encoders perform better on the FOIL diagnostic task than the VQA encoder.
The semantic spaces learned by the ReferIt and GuessWhat encoders are closer to each other than to the VQA encoder's space.
All encoders (except the one fully trained on FOIL) give more weight to the visual modality than the linguistic one in constructing multimodal representations.
The GuessWhat encoder has an advantage when very little FOIL training data is available.
papers.limitation: The differences among tasks could be due to subtle parallelisms with the diagnostic task: ReferIt and GuessWhat may resemble some aspects of FOIL (which revolves around objects), while VQA is more diverse.
future_direction: Evaluate the models on different diagnostic datasets that prioritise skills other than object identification.
papers.abstract: The multimodal models used in the emerging field at the intersection of computational linguistics and computer vision implement the bottom-up processing of the "Hub and Spoke" architecture proposed in cognitive science to represent how the brain processes and combines multi-sensory inputs. In particular, the Hub is implemented as a neural network encoder. We investigate the effect on this encoder of various vision-and-language tasks proposed in the literature: visual question answering, visual reference resolution, and visually grounded dialogue. To measure the quality of the representations learned by the encoder, we use two kinds of analyses. First, we evaluate the encoder pre-trained on the different vision-and-language tasks on an existing diagnostic task designed to assess multimodal semantic understanding. Second, we carry out a battery of analyses aimed at studying how the encoder merges and exploits the two modalities.

papers.title: Convergent World Representations and Divergent Tasks
papers.research_question: What conditions govern the geometry of neural representations and how do they support generalization and adaptation during fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Multi-task training leads to convergent world representations, but divergent tasks can harm the integration of new entities during fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Multi-task training leads to convergent world representations, but divergent tasks can harm fine-tuning integration, suggesting that task properties affect gradient dynamics and representation updates.
papers.key_findings:
Different geometric tasks produce distinct representational geometries in single-task models.
Multi-task training drives convergence of representations across tasks, supporting the Multitask Scaling Hypothesis.
Single-task representational similarity (CKA) partially predicts cross-task generalization after fine-tuning.
Divergent tasks (e.g., distance) actively harm multi-task fine-tuning generalization, performing worse than single-task baselines.
Divergent tasks cause new entities to be encoded in hidden subspaces rather than integrated into the existing representation manifold.
papers.limitation:
The study is correlational and does not establish causality between increasing single-task CKA and improving fine-tuning generalization.
The test of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis is limited to task diversity and does not include different architectures.
future_direction: Investigate why multi-task training drives more linearly surfaced representations.
Study what determines when representations stop evolving during training.
Explore the hypothesis that certain task-architecture pairings induce gradient dynamics that bypass shared representations.
papers.abstract: While neural representations are central to modern deep learning, the conditions governing their geometry and their roles in downstream adaptability remain poorly understood. We develop a framework clearly separating the underlying world, the data generation process and the resulting model representations to study these questions in a controlled setup. 5,075 city coordinates define the world and 7 geometric tasks generate the training data for autoregressive training. We find that different tasks give rise to qualitatively and quantitatively distinct world representation geometries. However, multi-task training drives convergence of world representations: models trained on non-overlapping tasks develop aligned geometric representations, providing controlled evidence for the Multitask Scaling Hypothesis of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis. To study adaptation, we pretrain models on all tasks, then test whether new entities (cities) can be consistently integrated into the representation space via fine-tuning. Surprisingly, we find that despite multi-task pretraining, some tasks, which we call divergent, actively harm the representational integration of new entities and harm generalization. Our results show that training on multiple relational tasks reliably produces convergent world representations, but lurking divergent tasks can catastrophically harm new entity integration via fine-tuning.

papers.title: Probing the Emergence of Cross-lingual Alignment during LLM Training
papers.research_question: How does cross-lingual alignment emerge during the pre-training of multilingual large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates a strong correlation between cross-lingual neuron overlap and zero-shot transfer performance in multilingual LLMs, and reveals non-monotonic alignment dynamics during pre-training with drops in smaller models.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that shared neurons encoding linguistic features are tightly connected to cross-lingual transfer ability, providing insights into multilingual pretraining dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron overlap for linguistic features increases during pre-training but experiences severe drops in smaller model scales like BLOOM560m and BLOOM1b1.
There is a statistically significant, strong correlation between neuron overlap and zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance on tasks like POS tagging and XNLI.
Larger models (e.g., BLOOM1b7) show more monotonic growth in alignment, suggesting a scaling law effect.
Drops in alignment correspond to degradation in both in-language and cross-lingual performance.
The emergence of cross-lingual alignment is not steady and can pass through sub-optimal regions during training.
papers.limitation:
Focus on BLOOM checkpoints with large intervals, so findings might not apply to finer-grained training windows.
Only consider autoregressive models with the same objective and training dataset; varying these may result in different patterns.
Focus on alignment of languages seen during pretraining, leaving generalization to unseen languages for future research.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve remarkable levels of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance. We speculate that this is predicated on their ability to align languages without explicit supervision from parallel sentences. While representations of translationally equivalent sentences in different languages are known to be similar after convergence, however, it remains unclear how such cross-lingual alignment emerges during pre-training of LLMs. Our study leverages intrinsic probing techniques, which identify which subsets of neurons encode linguistic features, to correlate the degree of cross-lingual neuron overlap with the zero-shot cross-lingual transfer performance for a given model. In particular, we rely on checkpoints of BLOOM, a multilingual autoregressive LLM, across different training steps and model scales. We observe a high correlation between neuron overlap and downstream performance, which supports our hypothesis on the conditions leading to effective cross-lingual transfer. Interestingly, we also detect a degradation of both implicit alignment and multilingual abilities in certain phases of the pre-training process, providing new insights into the multilingual pretraining dynamics.

papers.title: Language Representation Projection: Can We Transfer Factual Knowledge across Languages in Multilingual Language Models?
papers.research_question: Can cross-lingual alignment of representation spaces enable factual knowledge transfer across languages? Specifically, can we transfer factual knowledge from English to non-English languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes LRP2, a parameter-free method that projects representations between languages to align representation spaces, which improves factual knowledge retrieval and transfer across languages in multilingual language models.
papers.conclusion: The paper confirms that cross-lingual alignment of representation spaces enables factual knowledge transfer across languages, and proposes LRP2 as an effective method for this transfer.
papers.key_findings:
LRP2 improves factual knowledge retrieval accuracy and cross-lingual transferability for non-English languages.
LRP2 aligns representation spaces: LIRP projects non-English representations to English-like ones, and LSRP projects them back to the non-English space.
LRP2 increases the overlap of knowledge neurons between English and non-English languages, indicating enhanced cross-lingual knowledge transfer.
Cross-lingual knowledge neurons exist in multilingual pretrained language models.
Different languages require different optimal layer configurations for the LIRP and LSRP modules, indicating varying degrees of representation alignment needed.
papers.limitation:
The effectiveness of LRP2 heavily relies on the inherent capabilities of multilingual pretrained language models.
Experiments are limited to two relatively small models due to limited compute resources.
future_direction: Investigate LRP2 on larger language models.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pretrained language models serve as repositories of multilingual factual knowledge. Nevertheless, a substantial performance gap of factual knowledge probing exists between high-resource languages and low-resource languages, suggesting limited implicit factual knowledge transfer across languages in multilingual pretrained language models. This paper investigates the feasibility of explicitly transferring relatively rich factual knowledge from English to non-English languages. To accomplish this, we propose two parameter-free Language Representation Projection modules (LRP2). The first module converts non-English representations into English-like equivalents, while the second module reverts English-like representations back into representations of the corresponding non-English language. Experimental results on the mLAMA dataset demonstrate that LRP2 significantly improves factual knowledge retrieval accuracy and facilitates knowledge transferability across diverse non-English languages. We further investigate the working mechanism of LRP2 from the perspectives of representation space and cross-lingual knowledge neuron.

papers.title: Probing LLMs for Joint Encoding of Linguistic Categories
papers.research_question: How are linguistically related syntactic categories jointly encoded in LLMs, and do these patterns hold across languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence that linguistically related syntactic categories are jointly encoded in LLMs, with similar patterns across languages and between different levels of the linguistic hierarchy.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates joint encoding of linguistic categories in LLMs, supporting the idea that models learn hierarchical and shared representations for syntax across languages.
papers.key_findings:
POS tags that are linguistically related are jointly encoded in both monolingual and multilingual models.
Joint encoding patterns are consistent across English, Italian, and Greek in multilingual models.
Information about linguistic categories can be shared across languages, indicating language-agnostic encoding.
There is evidence of joint encoding between POS tags and dependency relations, suggesting information sharing across tasks.
The cross-neutralization method effectively reveals shared representations without tuning the base models.
papers.limitation:
Limited to encoder-only architectures.
Only three languages are examined.
Limited to syntactic tasks (POS tagging and dependency labeling).
Lack of cross-neutralization effects does not necessarily indicate absence of joint encoding.
future_direction: Extend experiments to more languages, particularly low-resource and typologically distant languages.
Include higher-level semantic tasks such as semantic role labeling and coreference resolution.
Explore other model architectures like encoder-decoder or decoder-only models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit impressive performance on a range of NLP tasks, due to the general-purpose linguistic knowledge acquired during pretraining. Existing model interpretability research (Tenney et al., 2019) suggests that a linguistic hierarchy emerges in the LLM layers, with lower layers better suited to solving syntactic tasks and higher layers employed for semantic processing. Yet, little is known about how encodings of different linguistic phenomena interact within the models and to what extent processing of linguistically-related categories relies on the same, shared model representations. In this paper, we propose a framework for testing the joint encoding of linguistic categories in LLMs. Focusing on syntax, we find evidence of joint encoding both at the same (related part-of-speech (POS) classes) and different (POS classes and related syntactic dependency relations) levels of linguistic hierarchy. Our cross-lingual experiments show that the same patterns hold across languages in multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: Large Language Models Are Partially Primed in Pronoun Interpretation
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) adapt their referential biases in pronoun interpretation in a human-like way when exposed to consistent referential patterns in the local discourse context?
papers.core_contribution: InstructGPT can adapt its syntactic bias in pronoun interpretation from exposure to referential patterns in the local context, but fails to adapt its semantic bias, suggesting LLMs only partially represent semantic knowledge in referential processing.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can adapt to syntactic patterns in pronoun interpretation from local exposure, but not to semantic patterns, indicating a partial and non-human-like representation of semantic knowledge in referential processing.
papers.key_findings:
InstructGPT adapted its syntactic bias (subject vs. non-subject preference) based on recent exposure, showing sensitivity to syntactic patterns in the local discourse.
InstructGPT exhibited a strong, persistent goal bias in pronoun interpretation that was not influenced by exposure to source/goal patterns, unlike human participants.
FLAN-UL2 failed to generate meaningful patterns, answering 'yes' 100% of the time to ambiguous target questions and showing poor comprehension.
The adaptation to syntactic patterns was observed even in the presence of confounding semantic goal bias (Experiment 2a).
The results suggest LLMs may over-represent semantic knowledge (goal bias) or lack the ability to track and adapt to higher-level semantic pattern frequencies across a discourse.
papers.limitation:
The study simulated participants only by manipulating the temperature hyperparameter; more sophisticated prompting methods could be explored.
Direct comparison with psycholinguistic experiments might not be the only method to investigate LLMs' discourse capacity.
The study is strictly behavioral and does not analyze the models' internal representations.
future_direction: Incorporate more detailed prompting to simulate diverse linguistic backgrounds in experimental simulations.
Mitigate the semantic knowledge gap via instruction fine-tuning or chain-of-thought prompting.
Explore a comprehensive list of discourse probing tasks as an alternative method.
papers.abstract: While a large body of literature suggests that large language models (LLMs) acquire rich linguistic representations, little is known about whether they adapt to linguistic biases in a human-like way. The present study probes this question by asking whether LLMs display human-like referential biases using stimuli and procedures from real psycholinguistic experiments. Recent psycholinguistic studies suggest that humans adapt their referential biases with recent exposure to referential patterns; closely replicating three relevant psycholinguistic experiments from Johnson & Arnold (2022) in an in-context learning (ICL) framework, we found that InstructGPT adapts its pronominal interpretations in response to the frequency of referential patterns in the local discourse, though in a limited fashion: adaptation was only observed relative to syntactic but not semantic biases. By contrast, FLAN-UL2 fails to generate meaningful patterns. Our results provide further evidence that contemporary LLMs discourse representations are sensitive to syntactic patterns in the local context but less so to semantic patterns. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/zkx06111/llm_priming.

papers.title: Language over Content: Tracing Cultural Understanding in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do multilingual large language models internally represent and process cultural knowledge, and does linguistic form or semantic content dominate their internal path selection?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that internal activation paths in multilingual LLMs overlap more for semantically equivalent questions asked in the same language about different cultures than for questions asked in different languages about the same culture, indicating that cultural understanding is strongly mediated by language-specific circuits.
papers.conclusion: Query language affects internal path selection more strongly than target culture, and cultural understanding is mainly stored in language-dependent paths. Politically unique contexts like South and North Korea are reflected in the model's internal mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Internal path overlap is greater for same-language, cross-country questions than for cross-language, same-country questions, showing a strong language-specific pattern.
The South Korea–North Korea pair exhibits low path overlap and high variability despite linguistic similarity, indicating distinct internal representation patterns.
Multilingual LLMs rely heavily on language-specific circuits when representing and applying cultural knowledge, prioritizing linguistic form over semantic content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focused on internal path overlap, but interventions or circuit patching could clarify which features drive cultural knowledge processing and how language- and culture-related features interact.
Some country pairs, such as South and North Koreas, show distinct patterns compared to other similar language pairs, yet the reasons remain unclear.
future_direction: Further subdivide cultural knowledge into finer categories and include more languages for a more comprehensive investigation.
Use interventions or circuit patching to clarify which features drive cultural knowledge processing and how language- and culture-related features interact.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used across diverse cultural contexts, making accurate cultural understanding essential. Prior evaluations have mostly focused on output-level performance, obscuring the factors that drive differences in responses, while studies using circuit analysis have covered few languages and rarely focused on culture. In this work, we trace LLMs' internal cultural understanding mechanisms by measuring activation path overlaps when answering semantically equivalent questions under two conditions: varying the target country while fixing the question language, and varying the question language while fixing the country. We also use same-language country pairs to disentangle language from cultural aspects. Results show that internal paths overlap more for same-language, cross-country questions than for cross-language, same-country questions, indicating strong language-specific patterns. Notably, the South Korea-North Korea pair exhibits low overlap and high variability, showing that linguistic similarity does not guarantee aligned internal representation.

papers.title: Counterfactually Probing Language Identity in Multilingual Models
papers.research_question: How is language identity encoded and used in multilingual models, and can counterfactual probing be used to causally manipulate this identity in embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Language identity is linearly encoded in contextual token embeddings of multilingual models and can be causally manipulated via counterfactual probing to affect the language of generated tokens, but not specifically to boost translation-equivalent words, providing evidence for both language-specific and language-general components.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual models like mBERT and XLM-R contain both language-specific and language-general components, and counterfactual probing methods like AlterRep can be fruitfully applied to analyze and manipulate language identity in these models.
papers.key_findings:
Pushing token embeddings towards a target language systematically increases the probability of words from that language in masked language modeling.
Pushing embeddings away from the template language decreases the probability of words from that language.
The intervention does not specifically boost translation-equivalent words more than random words from the target language.
Pushing embeddings in the same direction as the template language has minimal effect on target word probability but increases the overall prior for that language.
The method is robust to both monolingual and synthetic code-mixed training data.
papers.limitation:
INLP extracts only linearly extractable information; more complex non-linear methods might be needed to manipulate non-linearly encoded properties.
The AlterRep procedure is sensitive to parameters like α and the number of INLP iterations, and choosing them is tricky.
The results do not demonstrate practical utility, such as for machine translation.
The work carries the general risks associated with large language models, including environmental impacts.
future_direction: Use the method to explore linguistic typology in multilingual model space.
Apply more complex non-linear erasure methods, such as those proposed by Ravfogel et al. (2022).
Translate the findings into practical applications like machine translation.
papers.abstract: Techniques in causal analysis of language models illuminate how linguistic information is organized in LLMs. We use one such technique, AlterRep, a method of counterfactual probing, to explore the internal structure of multilingual models (mBERT and XLM-R). We train a linear classifier on a binary language identity task, to classify tokens between Language X and Language Y.
