Applying a counterfactual probing procedure, we use the classifier weights to project the embeddings into the null space and push the resulting embeddings either in the direction of Language X or Language Y. Then we evaluate on a masked language modeling task. We find that, given a template in Language X, pushing towards Language Y systematically increases the probability of Language Y words, above and beyond a third-party control language. But it does not specifically push the model towards translation-equivalent words in Language Y. Pushing towards Language X (the same direction as the template) has a minimal effect, but somewhat degrades these models. Overall, we take these results as further evidence of the rich structure of massive multilingual language models, which include both a language-specific and language-general component. And we show that counterfactual probing can be fruitfully applied to multilingual models.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models:belief directions are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context impact the behavior of belief probes (directions predictive of truth) in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the context sensitivity and consistency of belief probes across layers and models, shows belief directions are causal mediators in natural language inference, and introduces a more stable variant of Contrast Consistent Search (CCR).
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that belief directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
papers.key_findings:
Belief probes are generally context sensitive but are also sensitive to irrelevant contexts and can update probabilities incorrectly.
The type of errors made by probes depend on the layer, the model type, and the kind of data.
Belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.
Instruction-tuning makes models more likely to represent prior assertions as true, even if they conflict with the model's own evaluation.
papers.limitation: The difficulty of separating hypothetical LLM 'beliefs' from commonly-held beliefs, as probes might identify features correlated with truth in the training data rather than an objective evaluation of truth.
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as getting at a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions can be described as being conditional on the preceding (related) sentences. Specifically, we quantify the responsiveness of the probes to the presence of (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences, and score the probes on their consistency. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these belief directions influences the position of the hypothesis along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the (type of) model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that belief directions are (one of the) causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: Discourse structure interacts with reference but not syntax in neural\n language models
papers.research_question: Does discourse structure (implicit causality) influence reference and syntactic processing in neural language models, and how does this compare to human behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer language models learn a representational distinction for implicit causality that influences reference resolution but not syntactic attachment, while LSTM language models fail to learn such a distinction, revealing a mismatch between learned representations and behavior in language models.
papers.conclusion: Language models can learn discourse structure (implicit causality) from text, but they do not consistently use this knowledge in behavior, especially for syntactic processing, indicating limitations in how they acquire and utilize linguistic abstractions.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM language models show no influence of implicit causality on reference or syntax.
TransformerXL shows partial implicit causality representation, influencing reference but not syntax.
GPT-2 XL shows robust implicit causality effects on reference, matching human behavior, but not on syntax.
Transformers encode implicit causality in representations for both reference and syntax, but this knowledge does not affect syntactic behavior.
Both transformer models show a strong preference for local agreement in syntax, overriding discourse effects.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to unidirectional models and specific architectures, so mechanistic claims about the relationship between learned linguistic knowledge and model configurations are cautioned.
The representational similarity measure (Pearson's r) may not be optimal for capturing the relevant distinctions, especially for LSTM models.
The models may be unable to learn the syntactic operation of attachment, as suggested by the erasure of number agreement in final layers.
future_direction: Investigate the role of training objectives, such as predicting coherence relations instead of next-word prediction.
Explore the exact role of training data and model architecture in learning linguistic interactions.
Cross-linguistic studies to further understand the limitations of language models in learning syntax.
papers.abstract:
Language models (LMs) trained on large quantities of text have been claimed
to acquire abstract linguistic representations. Our work tests the robustness
of these abstractions by focusing on the ability of LMs to learn interactions
between different linguistic representations. In particular, we utilized
stimuli from psycholinguistic studies showing that humans can condition
reference (i.e. coreference resolution) and syntactic processing on the same
discourse structure (implicit causality). We compared both transformer and long
short-term memory LMs to find that, contrary to humans, implicit causality only
influences LM behavior for reference, not syntax, despite model representations
that encode the necessary discourse information. Our results further suggest
that LM behavior can contradict not only learned representations of discourse
but also syntactic agreement, pointing to shortcomings of standard language
modeling.

papers.title: What does it mean to be language-agnostic? Probing multilingual sentence encoders for typological properties
papers.research_question: How do multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties of languages, and how does this vary with different pretraining strategies?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual sentence encoders capture typological properties, but the encoding differs based on pretraining objectives: models with cross-lingual objectives (LASER, XLM) lose typological information in higher layers and create a shared interlingual space, while models with monolingual objectives (M-BERT, XLM-R) retain typological information in all layers and partition the space into language-specific subspaces.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between universality and language-specific information in multilingual encoders, and pretraining objectives influence how typological information is encoded.
papers.key_findings:
All encoders capture some typological properties (word order, pronouns, negation).
M-BERT and XLM-R outperform LASER and XLM on lexical and morphological properties.
Typological information is localizable in lower layers of LASER and XLM, but spread across all layers in M-BERT and XLM-R.
Cross-lingual training leads to more language-agnostic representations but at the cost of losing language-specific typological information in higher layers.
XLM generalizes to languages unseen during pretraining, capturing their typological properties.
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders have seen much success in cross-lingual model transfer for downstream NLP tasks. Yet, we know relatively little about the properties of individual languages or the general patterns of linguistic variation that they encode. We propose methods for probing sentence representations from state-of-the-art multilingual encoders (LASER, M-BERT, XLM and XLM-R) with respect to a range of typological properties pertaining to lexical, morphological and syntactic structure. In addition, we investigate how this information is distributed across all layers of the models. Our results show interesting differences in encoding linguistic variation associated with different pretraining strategies.

papers.title: Sensorimotor Regularities as Alignment between Humans and Large Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent might LLMs encode the sensorimotor regularities that humans leverage in concept representation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an evaluation framework based on sensorimotor regularities (image schemas) to assess and improve human-LLM alignment at the conceptual level, and demonstrates its utility through empirical analysis and a downstream study.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes a foundation for evaluating and improving human-LLM alignment at the conceptual level.
papers.key_findings:
Three contemporary LLMs (LlaMa-2-7b, LlaMa-2-70b, gpt-4-1106) encode highly human-like sensorimotor gestalts (image schema distributions).
The models exhibit reduced alignment when mapping these gestalts to specific concepts (conceptual associations).
The models do not systematically combine image schemas in ways consistent with human patterns (image schema co-occurrences).
Augmenting GPT-4 with targeted sensorimotor priors derived from its misalignments yields sentence continuations rated by humans as more conceptually clear, contextually contingent, and human-like.
papers.limitation:
The human baseline is limited to 24 participants, which may not fully represent the diversity of human conceptualizations.
The analysis focused on a specific domain (technology learning), limiting generalizability to other domains.
The downstream evaluation used a single creative writing task, which may not capture the full range of potential applications.
The approach relies on manual annotation of image schemas, which is time-consuming and subjective.
future_direction: Expand the human baseline to more diverse populations and larger sample sizes.
Extend the framework to other abstract conceptual domains beyond technology learning.
Automate the annotation of image schemas to scale the evaluation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) do not construct conceptual representations in ways that align with human cognition, posing risks for human-AI interaction. While LLMs solely rely on linguistic distributional knowledge, humans leverage both linguistic and sensorimotor knowledge. To systematically assess human-LLM alignment in concept representations, we propose a novel evaluation framework based on sensorimotor regularities, operationalized as image schemas—multimodal gestalts derived from repeated sensorimotor experiences. Investigating linguistic manifestations of such schemas, we systematically identify human-LLM alignments and misalignments in the encoding of sensorimotor regularities. Results indicate that three contemporary disembodied LLMs encode highly human-like sensorimotor gestalts. However, these models exhibit reduced alignment when mapping such gestalts to concepts, and they do not systematically combine these gestalts in ways consistent with human patterns. We identify each LLM’s misalignments with human patterns in image schema distribution, conceptual associations, and image schema co-occurrences. Building on these findings, we augment gpt-4-1106 with targeted sensorimotor priors derived from its identified misalignments with human patterns. In a downstream user study, this augmentation yields sentence continuations rated by humans as significantly more conceptually clear, contextually contingent, and human-like than baseline outputs. Our work establishes a foundation for evaluating and improving human-LLM alignment at the conceptual level.

papers.title: Visual symbolic mechanisms: Emergent symbol processing in vision language models
papers.research_question: Do Vision Language Models (VLMs) employ emergent symbolic mechanisms, similar to those found in language models, to solve the binding problem for visual scenes? How do VLMs bind features to objects in multi-object scenes?
papers.core_contribution: This paper identifies a set of emergent symbolic mechanisms in VLMs that use content-independent spatial indices (position IDs) to bind visual features to objects, and demonstrates that binding errors in VLMs are directly caused by failures in these mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: VLMs employ emergent symbolic mechanisms for visual binding that use spatial position as a content-independent scaffold, and improving these mechanisms could reduce the binding failures that limit current VLM performance.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs employ a three-stage architecture with ID retrieval, ID selection, and feature retrieval attention heads that use position IDs (spatial indices) to bind features to objects.
Position IDs use a relative, rather than absolute, spatial coding scheme.
These symbolic mechanisms generalize beyond synthetic stimuli to complex, photorealistic images (PUG) and real-world images (COCO).
Position IDs are localized within the image patches corresponding to each object.
Binding errors in VLMs, such as in scenes with shared features (low entropy), are directly linked to failures in the position ID representation and can be mitigated by patching in robust position IDs from high-entropy scenes.
papers.limitation: The extent to which the identified mechanisms are truly emergent, and the role of architectural inductive biases (e.g., position embeddings) in driving their emergence, remains an open question.
future_direction: Investigate the role of architectural inductive biases in the emergence of visual symbolic mechanisms.
Improve binding performance via architectural innovations (e.g., object-centric architectures) or training strategies that strengthen symbolic mechanisms (e.g., spatial pointing tasks).
papers.abstract: To accurately process a visual scene, observers must bind features together to represent individual objects. This capacity is necessary, for instance, to distinguish an image containing a red square and a blue circle from an image containing a blue square and a red circle. Recent work has found that language models solve this 'binding problem' via a set of symbol-like, content-independent indices, but it is unclear whether similar mechanisms are employed by Vision Language Models (VLMs). This question is especially relevant, given the persistent failures of VLMs on tasks that require binding. Here, we identify a previously unknown set of emergent symbolic mechanisms that support binding specifically in VLMs, via a content-independent, spatial indexing scheme. Moreover, we find that binding errors, when they occur, can be traced directly to failures in these mechanisms. Taken together, these results shed light on the mechanisms that support symbol-like processing in VLMs, and suggest possible avenues for reducing the number of binding failures exhibited by these models.

papers.title: Shapley Head Pruning: Identifying and Removing Interference in Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Can we reduce interference in multilingual transformers by identifying and pruning language-specific attention heads, thereby improving performance without adding parameters?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Shapley Head Pruning, a method that uses Shapley Values to identify and remove language-specific attention heads that cause interference in multilingual transformers, thereby improving cross-lingual performance without parameter updates.
papers.conclusion: The method effectively identifies language-specific components and improves cross-lingual performance through pruning, and suggests future work on linguistic features and pre-training.
papers.key_findings:
Attention Head Shapley Values vary across languages, indicating language-specific and language-agnostic heads.
Pruning heads with negative Shapley Values improves performance on XNLI and UDPOS without updating parameters.
The method outperforms random pruning and gradient-based pruning baselines.
Some attention heads show clear language-agnostic patterns (e.g., synonym linking), while others are language-specific.
Zero-shot pruning using English Shapley Values also improves performance for many languages.
papers.limitation:
Computational cost of Shapley Values is high compared to gradient-based methods.
Reliance on attention visualization, which is debated as a sound analytical tool.
future_direction: Exploring the relationship between linguistic features, training data volume, and the language-specificity of attention heads.
Reducing cross-lingual interference introduced by language-specific components during pre-training, such as pruning during pre-training or utilizing sparsely activated networks.
papers.abstract: Multilingual transformer-based models demonstrate remarkable zero and few-shot transfer across languages by learning and reusing language-agnostic features. However, as a fixed-size model acquires more languages, its performance across all languages degrades. Those who attribute this interference phenomenon to limited model capacity address the problem by adding additional parameters, despite evidence that transformer-based models are overparameterized. In this work, we show that it is possible to reduce interference by instead identifying and pruning language-specific attention heads. First, we use Shapley Values, a credit allocation metric from coalitional game theory, to identify attention heads that introduce interference. Then, we show that pruning such heads from a fixed model improves performance for a target language on both sentence classification and structural prediction. Finally, we provide insights on language-agnostic and language-specific attention heads using attention visualization.

papers.title: Far from the Shallow: Brain-Predictive Reasoning Embedding through Residual Disentanglement
papers.research_question: How can reasoning-specific components in LLM representations be isolated, and how do these isolated reasoning embeddings align with human brain activity during language comprehension?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a residual disentanglement method to isolate reasoning-specific embeddings from LLM hidden states, and uses these embeddings to provide neural evidence for abstract reasoning computations during language comprehension, showing distinct spatiotemporal brain alignment.
papers.conclusion: The work provides compelling neural evidence for an abstract reasoning computation during language comprehension and offers a robust framework for mapping distinct cognitive functions from artificial models to the human brain.
papers.key_findings:
Residual disentanglement yields four nearly orthogonal embeddings for lexicon, syntax, meaning, and reasoning.
The isolated reasoning embedding accounts for unique variance in neural activity not explained by other linguistic features and recruits visual regions beyond classical language areas.
The neural signature for reasoning peaks later (~350-400ms) than signals for lexicon, syntax, and meaning, consistent with a processing hierarchy.
Standard, non-disentangled LLM embeddings are biased toward linguistically shallow features (lexicon, syntax), masking the contributions of deeper cognitive processing like reasoning.
The method provides a framework for mapping distinct cognitive functions from artificial models to the human brain.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on ECoG data provides limited spatial coverage, with insufficient sampling in frontal regions crucial for reasoning.
The role of layers beyond the reasoning saturation layer (around layer 30 in Qwen2.5-14B) remains unclear; they may encode more abstract representations.
future_direction: Integrate complementary modalities such as fMRI to improve spatial resolution.
Explore larger models optimized for multi-step reasoning to reveal stronger or more specialized reasoning signals.
Investigate how higher-level representations in deeper layers (beyond reasoning saturation) might align with cortical hierarchies or large-scale cognitive organization.
papers.abstract: Understanding how the human brain progresses from processing simple linguistic inputs to performing high-level reasoning is a fundamental challenge in neuroscience. While modern large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to model neural responses to language, their internal representations are highly "entangled," mixing information about lexicon, syntax, meaning, and reasoning. This entanglement biases conventional brain encoding analyses toward linguistically shallow features (e.g., lexicon and syntax), making it difficult to isolate the neural substrates of cognitively deeper processes. Here, we introduce a residual disentanglement method that computationally isolates these components. By first probing an LM to identify feature-specific layers, our method iteratively regresses out lower-level representations to produce four nearly orthogonal embeddings for lexicon, syntax, meaning, and, critically, reasoning. We used these disentangled embeddings to model intracranial (ECoG) brain recordings from neurosurgical patients listening to natural speech. We show that: 1) This isolated reasoning embedding exhibits unique predictive power, accounting for variance in neural activity not explained by other linguistic features and even extending to the recruitment of visual regions beyond classical language areas. 2) The neural signature for reasoning is temporally distinct, peaking later (~350-400ms) than signals related to lexicon, syntax, and meaning, consistent with its position atop a processing hierarchy. 3) Standard, non-disentangled LLM embeddings can be misleading, as their predictive success is primarily attributable to linguistically shallow features, masking the more subtle contributions of deeper cognitive processing.

papers.title: Can you map it to English? The Role of Cross-Lingual Alignment in Multilingual Performance of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does an LLM's ability to align representations of non-English inputs to English impact its performance on NLU tasks, and does misalignment causally explain failures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that cross-lingual alignment with English in middle layers is associated with and causally affects LLM performance on multilingual NLU tasks.
papers.conclusion: Cross-lingual semantic alignment in localized middle layers contributes causally to non-English correctness in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Transfer Success (TS) instances exhibit higher cross-lingual alignment with English than Transfer Failure (TF) instances.
Activation patching of English activations into non-English forward passes can correct incorrect predictions, indicating causal role of alignment.
Middle layers (e.g., layers 16-25) are critical for alignment and effective patching.
Control patching experiments show that semantic alignment, not just target token bias, drives corrections in specific middle layers.
Alignment peaks in middle layers and varies by language typology, with closer languages to English showing higher alignment.
papers.limitation:
Scope restricted to discriminative NLU tasks.
Benchmarks may have translation artifacts due to human translation from English.
Only analyzes bilingual alignment with English, not between other languages.
future_direction: Exploring targeted steering at inference time to leverage English activations for enhancing performance on non-English languages.
Studying potential downsides such as inflated confidence and erasure of valuable local, non-English knowledge.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can answer prompts in many languages, despite being trained predominantly on English; yet, the mechanisms driving this generalization remain poorly understood. This work asks: How does an LLM's ability to align representations of non-English inputs to English impact its performance on natural language understanding (NLU) tasks? We study the role of representation alignment in instance-level task decisions, complementing prior analyses conducted both at the language level and task-independently. We introduce the Discriminative Alignment Index ($\DALI$) to quantify instance-level alignment across 24 languages other than English and three distinct NLU tasks. Results show that incorrect NLU predictions are strongly associated with lower representation alignment with English in the model's middle layers. Through activation patching, we show that incorrect predictions in languages other than English can be fixed by patching their parallel English activations in the middle layers, thereby demonstrating the causal role of representation (mis)alignment in cross-lingual correctness.

papers.title: The Other Mind: How Language Models Exhibit Human Temporal Cognition
papers.research_question: How do large language models exhibit human-like temporal cognition, specifically whether they spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point and adhere to the Weber-Fechner law?
papers.core_contribution: Larger LLMs spontaneously exhibit human-like temporal cognition, establishing a subjective reference point and adhering to the Weber-Fechner law, which emerges from multi-level convergence at neuronal, representational, and informational levels.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit human-like temporal cognition through multi-level convergence, suggesting cognition is a subjective construction of the external world. This points to the risk of alien cognitive frameworks and the need for AI alignment paradigms that guide internal world-building.
papers.key_findings:
In similarity judgment tasks, larger models spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point (ca. 2025) and their perception of time logarithmically compresses as years recede from this point, adhering to the Weber-Fechner law.
A subgroup of temporal-preferential neurons in the FFN exhibits minimal activation at the subjective reference point and implements a logarithmic coding scheme similar to biological systems.
Representations of years undergo hierarchical construction: from basic numerical values in shallow layers to abstract temporal orientation organized around a reference point in deep layers.
Pre-trained embedding models reveal that the training corpus possesses an inherent, non-linear temporal structure, providing raw material for the model's internal construction of temporal cognition.
The findings support an experientialist perspective where LLM cognition is a subjective construction of the external world by its internal representational system, leading to potential convergence with or divergence from human cognition.
future_direction: Evolve AI alignment beyond behavioral control to a paradigm that actively guides the formation of a model's internal world from its source.
Monitor models' emergent representational and cognitive patterns and enable intervention across the chain of cognition.
Curate the AI's environment with harmless or formalized verifiable information exposures.
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance, they exhibit certain cognitive patterns similar to those of humans that are not directly specified in training data. This study investigates this phenomenon by focusing on temporal cognition in LLMs. Leveraging the similarity judgment task, we find that larger models spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point and adhere to the Weber-Fechner law, whereby the perceived distance logarithmically compresses as years recede from this reference point. To uncover the mechanisms behind this behavior, we conducted multiple analyses across neuronal, representational, and informational levels. We first identify a set of temporal-preferential neurons and find that this group exhibits minimal activation at the subjective reference point and implements a logarithmic coding scheme convergently found in biological systems. Probing representations of years reveals a hierarchical construction process, where years evolve from basic numerical values in shallow layers to abstract temporal orientation in deep layers. Finally, using pre-trained embedding models, we found that the training corpus itself possesses an inherent, non-linear temporal structure, which provides the raw material for the model's internal construction. In discussion, we propose an experientialist perspective for understanding these findings, where the LLMs' cognition is viewed as a subjective construction of the external world by its internal representational system. This nuanced perspective implies the potential emergence of alien cognitive frameworks that humans cannot intuitively predict, pointing toward a direction for AI alignment that focuses on guiding internal constructions. Our code is available at https://TheOtherMind.github.io.

papers.title: Circuit Mechanisms for Spatial Relation Generation in Diffusion Transformers
papers.research_question: How do Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) generate correct spatial relations between objects as specified in text prompts, and how do the underlying circuit mechanisms differ depending on the choice of text encoder?
papers.core_contribution: The circuit mechanisms for spatial relation generation in Diffusion Transformers differ drastically depending on the text encoder: with random embeddings, a two-stage circuit with specialized cross-attention heads emerges; with a pretrained T5 encoder, a different circuit leverages information fusion in text tokens.
papers.conclusion: The choice of text encoder determines the circuit mechanism for spatial relation generation in Diffusion Transformers, and improvements to embedding models may be more critical than DiT modifications for robust spatial relation generation in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
With random token embeddings (RTE), the DiT implements a two-stage circuit: a 'spatial relation head' reads relation words and interacts with positional embeddings to create spatial gradients, and an 'object generation head' reads shape words to generate objects at the tagged locations.
With the T5 text encoder, spatial relation and object information are fused into single tokens (e.g., shape2), and the DiT reads this combined information via a different circuit, extracting relation factors from the token's embedding.
Although both RTE- and T5-based DiTs achieve similar high in-domain accuracy, their robustness to out-of-domain prompt perturbations differs significantly, with T5-DiT being much more sensitive to small changes like adding filler words.
The spatial relation head in RTE-DiT works by aligning sinusoidal positional embeddings of image tokens with relation word embeddings via the QK circuit, producing spatial gradients that act as positional tags.
In T5-DiT, variance partitioning shows that spatial relation information is encoded in the contextual embedding of object tokens, and the DiT's MLP projection amplifies this relation information.
papers.limitation: The study uses a controlled synthetic dataset, which may not capture the complexity of real-world images and prompts.
future_direction: Generalizing the circuit discovery approach to other relational reasoning tasks beyond spatial relations.
Developing more general methods for supervised feature finding in representation spaces, as an alternative to linear variance partitioning.
papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have greatly advanced text-to-image generation, but models still struggle to generate the correct spatial relations between objects as specified in the text prompt. In this study, we adopt a mechanistic interpretability approach to investigate how a DiT can generate correct spatial relations between objects. We train, from scratch, DiTs of different sizes with different text encoders to learn to generate images containing two objects whose attributes and spatial relations are specified in the text prompt. We find that, although all the models can learn this task to near-perfect accuracy, the underlying mechanisms differ drastically depending on the choice of text encoder. When using random text embeddings, we find that the spatial-relation information is passed to image tokens through a two-stage circuit, involving two cross-attention heads that separately read the spatial relation and single-object attributes in the text prompt. When using a pretrained text encoder (T5), we find that the DiT uses a different circuit that leverages information fusion in the text tokens, reading spatial-relation and single-object information together from a single text token. We further show that, although the in-domain performance is similar for the two settings, their robustness to out-of-domain perturbations differs, potentially suggesting the difficulty of generating correct relations in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Low-Dimensional Structure in the Space of Language Representations is\n Reflected in Brain Responses
papers.research_question: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks, and is this low-dimensional structure reflected in human brain responses to natural language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language representations from various models and tasks lie in a low-dimensional space, and that this structure can predict how well each representation maps to brain responses, revealing a hierarchy in the brain's language processing.
papers.conclusion: The low-dimensional structure of language representations is reflected in the brain, and the representation embedding method captures this structure, linking computational models to neural processing.
papers.key_findings:
The space of language representations has a low-dimensional structure, with the first dimension explaining 22% of variance.
Language model layers follow a trajectory from word embeddings to next-word embeddings, with syntactic and semantic tasks clustering in the middle.
The first dimension of the representation embedding space corresponds to a hierarchy in the brain's language processing, from auditory cortex to higher-level semantic areas.
The representation embeddings can predict which representations best explain brain responses in different regions.
Some pairs of representations are difficult to distinguish based on brain responses, such as GloVe and its next-word embedding due to fMRI temporal imprecision.
papers.limitation: The temporal imprecision of fMRI data limits the ability to distinguish between representations that are close in time, such as GloVe and its next-word embedding.
papers.abstract:
How related are the representations learned by neural language models,
translation models, and language tagging tasks? We answer this question by
adapting an encoder-decoder transfer learning method from computer vision to
investigate the structure among 100 different feature spaces extracted from
hidden representations of various networks trained on language tasks. This
method reveals a low-dimensional structure where language models and
translation models smoothly interpolate between word embeddings, syntactic and
semantic tasks, and future word embeddings. We call this low-dimensional
structure a language representation embedding because it encodes the
relationships between representations needed to process language for a variety
of NLP tasks. We find that this representation embedding can predict how well
each individual feature space maps to human brain responses to natural language
stimuli recorded using fMRI. Additionally, we find that the principal dimension
of this structure can be used to create a metric which highlights the brain's
natural language processing hierarchy. This suggests that the embedding
captures some part of the brain's natural language representation structure.

papers.title: Language-Specific Layer Matters: Efficient Multilingual Enhancement for Large Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently enhance the multilingual capabilities of large vision-language models by identifying and fine-tuning language-specific layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PLAST, a method to efficiently enhance multilingual capabilities of LVLMs by identifying language-specific layers and fine-tuning them with translation pairs.
papers.conclusion: PLAST effectively enhances multilingual performance of LVLMs and achieves superior efficiency compared to full-parameter tuning methods by fine-tuning only language-specific layers.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific neurons in shallow layers are crucial for multilingual understanding in LVLMs.
PLAST improves multilingual performance with only 14% of parameters tuned, achieving significant efficiency gains.
PLAST generalizes to low-resource languages and complex visual reasoning tasks.
Fine-tuning both FFN and attention sub-layers within selected layers yields better performance than tuning only one.
PLAST outperforms full-parameter fine-tuning and other parameter-efficient methods like LoRA in both performance and efficiency.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models up to 13B parameters due to computing resources.
Performance trade-offs exist across different languages, potentially due to imbalances in multilingual training data.
future_direction: Explore PLAST on larger-scale models (larger than 13B).
Investigate data-centric strategies such as data selection and augmentation to further improve multilingual capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in understanding visual information with human languages but also exhibit an imbalance in multilingual capabilities. In this work, we delve into the multilingual working pattern of LVLMs and identify a salient correlation between the multilingual understanding ability of LVLMs and language-specific neuron activations in shallow layers. Building on this insight, we introduce PLAST, a training recipe that achieves efficient multilingual enhancement for LVLMs by Precise LAnguage-Specific layers fine-Tuning. PLAST first identifies layers involved in multilingual understanding by monitoring language-specific neuron activations. These layers are then precisely fine-tuned with question-translation pairs to achieve multilingual alignment. Our empirical results on MM-Bench and MMMB demonstrate that PLAST effectively improves the multilingual capabilities of LVLMs and achieves significant efficiency with only 14% of the parameters tuned. Further analysis reveals that PLAST can be generalized to low-resource and complex visual reasoning tasks, facilitating the language-specific visual information engagement in shallow layers.

papers.title: Different types of syntactic agreement recruit the same units within large language models
papers.research_question: We investigate whether different syntactic phenomena recruit shared or distinct components in LLMs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that syntactic agreement phenomena recruit overlapping units in large language models, suggesting that agreement forms a functional category, and this pattern holds across languages with overlap correlating with syntactic similarity.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal that syntactic agreement constitutes a meaningful category within LLMs' representational spaces, with shared units across agreement types and languages, organized by syntactic similarity.
papers.key_findings:
Syntax-responsive units are consistently identified across sentence instances for each syntactic phenomenon and causally support model performance.
Different types of syntactic agreement (e.g., subject-verb, anaphor, determiner-noun) recruit overlapping sets of units in English.
The overlap among agreement units is higher than with non-agreement phenomena, indicating agreement as a shared functional category.
This pattern replicates in Russian and Chinese, with agreement units showing cross-lingual overlap.
Cross-lingual unit overlap for subject-verb agreement increases with syntactic similarity across 57 languages.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on top-n% unit localization may overlook more distributed syntactic representations.
Analyses are primarily correlational, though causal involvement is demonstrated via ablation.
Focus on benchmarks comparing grammatical to ungrammatical sentences, which may not capture full grammatical knowledge.
future_direction: Apply the approach to other syntactic phenomena, including infrequent structures, ambiguities, and long-distance dependencies.
Extend experiments to other languages with BLiMP-like benchmarks, such as Dutch or Turkish.
Investigate the relationship between syntax and semantics in model representations.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can reliably distinguish grammatical from ungrammatical sentences, but how grammatical knowledge is represented within the models remains an open question. We investigate whether different syntactic phenomena recruit shared or distinct components in LLMs. Using a functional localization approach inspired by cognitive neuroscience, we identify the LLM units most responsive to 67 English syntactic phenomena in seven open-weight models. These units are consistently recruited across sentences containing the phenomena and causally support the models' syntactic performance. Critically, different types of syntactic agreement (e.g., subject-verb, anaphor, determiner-noun) recruit overlapping sets of units, suggesting that agreement constitutes a meaningful functional category for LLMs. This pattern holds in English, Russian, and Chinese; and further, in a cross-lingual analysis of 57 diverse languages, structurally more similar languages share more units for subject-verb agreement. Taken together, these findings reveal that syntactic agreement-a critical marker of syntactic dependencies-constitutes a meaningful category within LLMs' representational spaces.

papers.title: Learning Representations of Spatial Displacement through Sensorimotor\n Prediction
papers.research_question: How can compact representations of spatial displacement be learned from motor sequences using sensorimotor prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a method using RNNs to encode motor sequences into compact representations that capture spatial displacement through sensorimotor prediction, resulting in topologically organized representations.
papers.conclusion: The method successfully learns compact representations of spatial displacement from motor sequences, with the representation space maintaining continuity from sensorimotor prediction.
papers.key_findings:
Sensorimotor prediction guides the learning of motor sequence representations that are organized topologically in terms of spatial displacement.
The representation space hm captures dimensions such as longitudinal and lateral displacement and orientation change.
For continuous environments with large rotation amplitudes, the representation space curves, forming circular shapes for orientation.
The method works for both forward and holonomic agents, handling redundant motor spaces.
In simple discrete environments, an inverse model is needed for topological organization, but not in continuous environments.
papers.limitation: The study is based on simulation and uses distance sensors which implicitly contain spatial information, limiting generalization to other sensor types.
future_direction: Apply the approach to vision sensors where spatial information is not explicit.
Use the learned representation hm as a latent space for controlling motor commands via an inverse model.
Apply the representations in Reinforcement Learning to solve navigation tasks.
papers.abstract:
Robots act in their environment through sequences of continuous motor
commands. Because of the dimensionality of the motor space, as well as the
infinite possible combinations of successive motor commands, agents need
compact representations that capture the structure of the resulting
displacements. In the case of an autonomous agent with no a priori knowledge
about its sensorimotor apparatus, this compression has to be learned. We
propose to use Recurrent Neural Networks to encode motor sequences into a
compact representation, which is used to predict the consequence of motor
sequences in term of sensory changes. We show that sensory prediction can
successfully guide the compression of motor sequences into representations that
are organized topologically in term of spatial displacement.

papers.title: Shared Global and Local Geometry of Language Model Embeddings
papers.research_question: What geometric similarities exist in token embeddings across large language models, both globally and locally?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that token embeddings of language models share global and local geometric similarities, and based on this, introduces EMB2EMB to transfer steering vectors between models.
papers.conclusion: The embeddings of language models share similar global and local geometric structures, which enables the transfer of steering vectors across models via a simple linear transformation.
papers.key_findings:
Token embeddings across models from the same family share similar relative orientations (global similarity).
Local geometry, characterized by Locally Linear Embeddings (LLE) weights and intrinsic dimension, is also similar across models.
Tokens with lower intrinsic dimensions form semantically coherent clusters, while those with higher intrinsic dimensions do not.
Steering vectors can be transferred between models using a linear transformation (EMB2EMB), enabling control of one model with vectors from another.
papers.limitation:
The intrinsic dimension measure is sensitive to hyperparameters (neighbor count, variance threshold).
The semantic coherence analysis may not work well for models with many special tokens or non-English tokens (as in Gemma2).
future_direction: Investigating the relationship between the geometry of embeddings and hidden states.
papers.abstract: Researchers have recently suggested that models share common representations. In our work, we find numerous geometric similarities across the token embeddings of large language models. First, we find ``global'' similarities: token embeddings often share similar relative orientations. Next, we characterize local geometry in two ways: (1) by using Locally Linear Embeddings, and (2) by defining a simple measure for the intrinsic dimension of each embedding. Both characterizations allow us to find local similarities across token embeddings. Additionally, our intrinsic dimension demonstrates that embeddings lie on a lower dimensional manifold, and that tokens with lower intrinsic dimensions often have semantically coherent clusters, while those with higher intrinsic dimensions do not. Based on our findings, we introduce EMB2EMB, a simple application to linearly transform steering vectors from one language model to another, despite the two models having different dimensions.

papers.title: Discriminating Spatial and Temporal Relevance in Deep Taylor\n Decompositions for Explainable Activity Recognition
papers.research_question: How can spatial and temporal relevance be discriminated in deep Taylor decompositions for explainable activity recognition in 3D CNNs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a discriminative method to separate and visualize spatial and temporal relevance in deep Taylor decompositions for explainable activity recognition in 3D CNNs.
papers.conclusion: Introduces a method for separating and visualizing spatial and temporal components in deep Taylor explanations for 3D CNNs, providing more insight into salient motion than general relevance maps.
papers.key_findings:
The original deep Taylor explanation for video tasks ambiguously combines spatial and temporal relevance, making it difficult to distinguish motion-based relevance.
Subtracting spatial relevance (obtained from frame-only inputs) from the original explanation exposes temporal relevance attributed to motion.
The method highlights key frames and regions where motion is salient, such as the body during pull-ups or the tennis ball during serving.
Spatial relevance primarily focuses on edges and background objects, which can obscure motion relevance in the original explanation.
The proposed method is an approximation, as shown by inequalities in relevance sums and changes in model predictions for individual frames.
papers.limitation: The method is an approximation, as the sum of spatial and temporal relevance does not equal the original relevance, and spatial relevance for non-dominant classes differs from dominant classes.
future_direction: Formalize a method for exposing true spatial relevance in the frame, moving beyond the current approximation.
papers.abstract:
Current techniques for explainable AI have been applied with some success to
image processing. The recent rise of research in video processing has called
for similar work n deconstructing and explaining spatio-temporal models. While
many techniques are designed for 2D convolutional models, others are inherently
applicable to any input domain. One such body of work, deep Taylor
decomposition, propagates relevance from the model output distributively onto
its input and thus is not restricted to image processing models. However, by
exploiting a simple technique that removes motion information, we show that it
is not the case that this technique is effective as-is for representing
relevance in non-image tasks. We instead propose a discriminative method that
produces a na\"ive representation of both the spatial and temporal relevance of
a frame as two separate objects. This new discriminative relevance model
exposes relevance in the frame attributed to motion, that was previously
ambiguous in the original explanation. We observe the effectiveness of this
technique on a range of samples from the UCF-101 action recognition dataset,
two of which are demonstrated in this paper.

papers.title: Brain-Language Model Alignment: Insights into the Platonic Hypothesis and Intermediate-Layer Advantage
papers.research_question: Do brains and language models converge toward the same internal representations of the world? The paper reviews evidence to test the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and the Intermediate-Layer Advantage.
papers.core_contribution: This review of 25 fMRI-based studies provides converging evidence that models and brains may share abstract representational structures, supporting the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and the Intermediate-Layer Advantage.
papers.conclusion: Framing alignment through the dual lenses of the PRH and the Intermediate-Layer Advantage provides a theoretical scaffold for designing future experiments, benchmarks, and models that more directly probe shared human–artificial representational structure.
papers.key_findings:
Alignment tends to be stronger for larger, higher-performing models and those trained on more tasks, supporting the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.
Cross-modal training reliably enhances alignment by pushing models toward modality-independent conceptual representations.
Intermediate layers of language models show the strongest alignment with brain activity, supporting the Intermediate-Layer Advantage.
Fine-tuning (including instruction-tuning and brain-tuning) can improve alignment, but the evidence is not uniformly positive.
Multimodal models, especially vision-language models, align better with brain activity than unimodal models.
papers.limitation: The studies analysed differ in metrics, datasets, and alignment protocols. Such heterogeneity implies that effects of scale or layer depth should be treated as qualitative patterns rather than quantitative laws.
future_direction: Designing future experiments, benchmarks, and models that more directly probe shared human–artificial representational structure.
papers.abstract: Do brains and language models converge toward the same internal representations of the world? Recent years have seen a rise in studies of neural activations and model alignment. In this work, we review 25 fMRI-based studies published between 2023 and 2025 and explicitly confront their findings with two key hypotheses: (i) the Platonic Representation Hypothesis -- that as models scale and improve, they converge to a representation of the real world, and (ii) the Intermediate-Layer Advantage -- that intermediate (mid-depth) layers often encode richer, more generalizable features. Our findings provide converging evidence that models and brains may share abstract representational structures, supporting both hypotheses and motivating further research on brain-model alignment.

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: Depth-Wise Emergence of Prediction-Centric Geometry in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do decoder-only large language models transform context into predictions, and how does representational geometry reorganize across depth to enable selective causal control over token prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Decoder-only LLMs exhibit a depth-wise transition from context-processing to prediction-forming phases, with late-layer representations implementing a structured geometric code where angular organization parametrizes prediction similarity and norms encode context-specific information, providing a mechanistic-geometric account of prediction formation.
papers.conclusion: The paper reconciles geometric and intervention-based approaches by showing that late-layer angular geometry is causally operative for prediction, while early-layer geometry is descriptive but not causally relevant, highlighting the importance of targeting causally meaningful geometric degrees of freedom for model interpretation and control.
papers.key_findings:
Early layers are sensitive to input-centric interventions, while late layers are sensitive to prediction-centric interventions, indicating a functional dissociation.
There is a sharp depth-wise transition from context-processing to prediction-forming computation, accompanied by a reorganization of representational geometry.
In late layers, angular distance between representations correlates with prediction similarity (symmetric KL divergence), while Euclidean distance does not.
Purely angular interventions are effective in late layers but not in early layers, whereas norm interventions are ineffective throughout, showing that angular geometry is causally relevant for prediction.
The geometry of late-layer representations is organized such that angular structure parametrizes prediction distributions, while representation norms encode context-specific information that does not determine prediction.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single class of tasks and model architectures; unclear how broadly the identified geometric schema generalizes across tasks, modalities, or training regimes.
The relationship between early-layer context geometry (e.g., dimensionality expansion) and the emergence of prediction-aligned angular codes is not yet understood.
Analysis emphasizes representations averaged across contexts and does not address context-dependent dynamics in multi-step or algorithmic tasks.
future_direction: Understanding architectural and optimization biases that favor angular coding in prediction-forming layers.
Exploring geometry-aware, layer-specific adapters for model control.
Generalizing the findings across tasks, modalities, and training regimes, and studying context-dependent dynamics in multi-step tasks.
papers.abstract: We show that decoder-only large language models exhibit a depth-wise transition from context-processing to prediction-forming phases of computation accompanied by a reorganization of representational geometry. Using a unified framework combining geometric analysis with mechanistic intervention, we demonstrate that late-layer representations implement a structured geometric code that enables selective causal control over token prediction. Specifically, angular organization of the representation geometry parametrizes prediction distributional similarity, while representation norms encode context-specific information that does not determine prediction. Together, these results provide a mechanistic-geometric account of the dynamics of transforming context into predictions in LLMs.

papers.title: Wavelet-based Positional Representation for Long Context
papers.research_question: How can we design a positional encoding method that effectively extrapolates to longer contexts without limiting the attention field, by leveraging wavelet transforms with multiple scales?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a wavelet-based positional representation method that uses multiple scales to improve extrapolation to long contexts without constraining the attention field, outperforming RoPE and ALiBi.
papers.conclusion: The wavelet-based positional representation method demonstrates superior performance in extrapolation tasks compared to traditional methods, and it offers the advantage of not constraining the receptive field.
papers.key_findings:
RoPE can be interpreted as a wavelet transform with a fixed scale, which may explain its poor extrapolation performance.
ALiBi uses multiple window sizes (scales) but limits the receptive field, which hinders long-range dependencies.
The proposed wavelet-based method with multiple scales and shifts achieves lower perplexity than RoPE and ALiBi in both short and long context experiments.
The method is effective for extrapolation without non-overlapping inference and does not limit the attention field.
The choice of wavelet function (e.g., Ricker, Gaussian) and the configuration of scale and shift parameters are important for performance.
papers.limitation: The computational overhead of calculating relative positions may impose a bottleneck, despite memory reduction techniques.
future_direction: Reducing the computational overhead of calculating relative positions.
Pre-training with larger datasets and evaluating on more benchmarks (e.g., LongRangeArena).
papers.abstract: In the realm of large-scale language models, a significant challenge arises when extrapolating sequences beyond the maximum allowable length. This is because the model's position embedding mechanisms are limited to positions encountered during training, thus preventing effective representation of positions in longer sequences. We analyzed conventional position encoding methods for long contexts and found the following characteristics. (1) When the representation dimension is regarded as the time axis, Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) can be interpreted as a restricted wavelet transform using Haar-like wavelets. However, because it uses only a fixed scale parameter, it does not fully exploit the advantages of wavelet transforms, which capture the fine movements of non-stationary signals using multiple scales (window sizes). This limitation could explain why RoPE performs poorly in extrapolation. (2) Previous research as well as our own analysis indicates that Attention with Linear Biases (ALiBi) functions similarly to windowed attention, using windows of varying sizes. However, it has limitations in capturing deep dependencies because it restricts the receptive field of the model. From these insights, we propose a new position representation method that captures multiple scales (i.e., window sizes) by leveraging wavelet transforms without limiting the model's attention field. Experimental results show that this new method improves the performance of the model in both short and long contexts. In particular, our method allows extrapolation of position information without limiting the model's attention field.

papers.title: How Distributed are Distributed Representations? An Observation on the Locality of Syntactic Information in Verb Agreement Tasks
papers.research_question: Where is syntactic information localized in transformer representations for French object-past participle agreement tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Syntactic information is encoded locally in transformer representations in a way consistent with French grammar, as shown through probing and causal analysis.
papers.conclusion: Transformers process French object-past participle agreement in a linguistically-motivated manner, and this work is a step towards understanding inner representations.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic information is encoded locally within context tokens and not distributed globally across the sentence.
Masking linguistically relevant tokens (antecedent and relative pronoun) degrades prediction performance, indicating a causal link.
Number information is encoded in a small number of dimensions but redundantly across the representation.
Probing accuracy is high in context tokens and drops in prefix and suffix, showing localized encoding.
Transformers rely on tokens consistent with French grammar for agreement prediction.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a specific linguistic phenomenon (object-past participle agreement) in French and could be extended to other languages and phenomena.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other linguistic phenomena and languages.
papers.abstract: This work addresses the question of the localization of syntactic information encoded in the transformers representations. We tackle this question from two perspectives, considering the object-past participle agreement in French, by identifying, first, in which part of the sentence and, second, in which part of the representation syntactic information is encoded. The results of our experiments using probing, causal analysis and feature selection method, show that syntactic information is encoded locally in a way consistent with the French grammar.

papers.title: Probing Multimodal Large Language Models for Global and Local Semantic Representations
papers.research_question: How is global and local semantic information encoded in decoder-only Multimodal Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Intermediate layers of decoder-only MLLMs encode more global semantic information, while top layers focus excessively on local token features, diminishing global encoding ability.
papers.conclusion: The upper layers in MLLMs focus too much on the next token's semantic features, resulting in loss of global information, which should inform future pre-training improvements.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers of MLLMs perform best on global image-text entailment tasks.
Top layers may excessively focus on local information, leading to diminished ability to encode global information.
In object recognition, upper layers show improved performance when provided with category cues, indicating a focus on local features.
The findings are consistent across different MLLMs and various prompts, indicating robustness.
future_direction: Improving pre-training processes and architecture designs of MLLMs to better encode global information.
papers.abstract: The advancement of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has greatly accelerated the development of applications in understanding integrated texts and images. Recent works leverage image-caption datasets to train MLLMs, achieving state-of-the-art performance on image-to-text tasks. However, there are few studies exploring which layers of MLLMs make the most effort to the global image information, which plays vital roles in multimodal comprehension and generation. In this study, we find that the intermediate layers of models can encode more global semantic information, whose representation vectors perform better on visual-language entailment tasks, rather than the topmost layers. We further probe models regarding local semantic representations through object recognition tasks. We find that the topmost layers may excessively focus on local information, leading to a diminished ability to encode global information. Our code and data are released via https://github.com/kobayashikanna01/probing_MLLM_rep.

papers.title: Language and spatial frames of reference: The effect of verbal interference.
papers.abstract: People think about spatial frames of reference (FoRs) in accord with the spatial system of their native language.It has been claimed that this correlation reflects a causal influence of language on thought.We tested this claim.Earlier studies have shown that whereas English speakers favor an egocentric FoR, there is a pre-linguistic predisposition favoring a geocentric FoR.We reasoned that if language plays a central on-line role in spatial cognition, verbal interference should disrupt egocentric responding and reveal the underlying geocentric bias.We conducted a standard spatial rotation task on English speakers, with and without verbal interference.Under verbal interference, compared with no interference, we found less egocentric responding, as predicted, and an increase in error.However, in contrast with prediction, the amount of geocentric responding did not differ across the two conditions.These results suggest that language does not play an on-line role in overriding a geocentric bias.

papers.title: Does Environmental Experience Shape Spatial Cognition? Frames of Reference Among Ancash Quechua Speakers (Peru)
papers.abstract: Previous studies have shown that language contributes to humans' ability to orient using landmarks and shapes their use of frames of reference (FoRs) for memory. However, the role of environmental experience in shaping spatial cognition has not been investigated. This study addresses such a possibility by examining the use of FoRs in a nonverbal spatial memory task among residents of an Andean community in Peru. Participants consisted of 97 individuals from Ancash Quechua-speaking households (8-77 years of age) who spoke Quechua and/or Spanish and varied considerably with respect to the extent of their experience in the surrounding landscape. The results demonstrated that environmental experience was the only factor significantly related to the preference for allocentric FoRs. The study thus shows that environmental experience can play a role alongside language in shaping habits of spatial representation, and it suggests a new direction of inquiry into the relationships among language, thought, and experience.

papers.title: Spatial reasoning in bilingual Mexico: Delimiting the influence of language
papers.abstract: What is the relation been spatial language and cognition?Across speech communities, linguistic preferences for particular spatial frames of reference (FoR) predict nonlinguistic spatial reasoning strategies.This has been taken to imply a powerful influence of language on reasoning, but extra-linguistic factors may also matter.We present evidence from a bilingual community in Juchitn, Mexico, where the two languages contrast in how they encode space.In our spatial reasoning task, the population overall showed a mixed profile of FoR use.This naturally occurring variability provided a laboratory for asking, at a fine-grained level, what factors predict individuals' spatial reasoning.Contrary to suggestions in the literature, we found no effects of language dominance or of the language used for the task.Instead, reliance on an egocentric strategy for the non-linguistic task was predicted by mastery of egocentric spatial vocabulary.These results delimit the influence of language on spatial reasoning.

papers.title: Semantic Typology and Spatial Conceptualization
papers.abstract: This project collected linguistic data for spatial relations across a typologically and genetically varied set of languages.In the linguistic analysis, we focus on the ways in which propositions may be functionally equivalent across the linguistic communities while nonetheless representing semantically quite distinctive frames of reference.Running nonlinguistic experiments on subjects from these language communities, we find that a population's cognitive frame of reference correlates with the linguistic frame of reference within the same referential domain.*INTRODUCTION.This study examines the relationship between language and cognition through a crosslinguistic and crosscultural study of spatial reference.Beginning with a crosslinguistic survey of spatial reference in language use, we find systematic variation that contradicts usual assumptions about what must be universal.However, the available number of general spatial systems for describing spatial arrays can be sorted into a few distinctive frames of reference.We focus on two frames of reference: the ABSOLUTE, based on fixed bearings such as north and south, and the RELATIVE, based on projections from the human body such as 'in front (of me)', 'to the left'.In assessing language use, it is not enough to rely on descriptions of languages that are based on conventional elicitation techniques as these may not fully reflect actual socially anchored conventions.We have developed and used director/matcher language games which facilitate interactive discourse between native speakers about spatial relations in tabletop space.The standardized nature of these games allows more exact comparison across languages than is usually possible with conventionally collected discourse.Having observed the variation of language use across communities, we further ask whether there is corresponding conceptual variation-the question of the linguistic relativity of thought.For this, we developed nonlinguistic experiments to determine the speaker's cognitive representations independently of the linguistic data collection.The findings from these experiments clearly demonstrate that a community's use of linguistic coding reliably correlates with the way the individual conceptualizes and memorizes spatial distinctions for nonlinguistic purposes.Because we find linguistic relativity effects in a domain that seems basic to human experience and is directly linked to universally shared perceptual mechanisms, it seems likely that similar correlations between language and thought will be found in other domains as well.1.A CROSSLINGUISTIC AND CROSSCULTURAL STUDY OF SPATIAL REFERENCE.The primary goal of our project is to test, refine, and reformulate hypotheses about language and human cognition drawing on in-depth information from a broad sample of non-* This article developed from a presentation entitled 'Cultural variation in spatial conceptualization'

papers.title: Language, Culture and Spatial Cognition: Bringing anthropology to the table
papers.abstract: Languages vary in their semantic partitioning of the world. This has led to speculation that language might shape basic cognitive processes. Spatial cognition has been an area of research in which linguistic relativity – the effect of language on thought – has both been proposed and rejected. Prior studies have been inconclusive, lacking experimental rigor or appropriate research design. Lacking detailed ethnographic knowledge as well as failing to pay attention to intralanguage variations, these studies often fall short of defining an appropriate concept of language, culture, and cognition. Our study constitutes the first research exploring (1) individuals speaking different languages yet living (for generations) in the same immediate environment and (2) systematic intralanguage variation. Results show that language does not shape spatial cognition and plays at best the secondary role of foregrounding alternative possibilities for encoding spatial arrangements.

papers.title: Moving Forward in Space and Time: How Strong is the Conceptual Link between Spatial and Temporal Frames of Reference?
papers.abstract: People often use spatial vocabulary to describe temporal relations, and this increasingly has motivated attempts to map spatial frames of reference (FoRs) onto time. Recent research suggested that speech communities, which differ in how they conceptualize space, may also differ in how they conceptualize time and, more specifically, that the preferences for spatial FoRs should carry over to the domain of time. Here, we scrutinize this assumption (a) by reviewing data from recent studies on temporal references, (b) by comparing data we had collected in previous studies on preferences for spatial and temporal FoRs in four languages, (c) by analyzing new data from dynamic spatial tasks that resemble the temporal tasks more closely, and (d) by assessing the co-variation of individual preferences of English speakers across space and time. While the first set of data paints a mixed picture, the latter three do not support the assumption of a close link between referencing preferences across domains. We explore possible reasons for this lack of consistency and discuss implications for research on temporal references.

papers.title: Changes in spatial frames of reference use in Iwaidja in different intergenerational contexts
papers.abstract: Abstract Research into sociocultural factors affecting the use of spatial frames of reference (FoR) has begun to move away from characterizing FoR choice as inherent to each language, instead emphasizing variation within speech communities, but has so far paid little attention to variation in individual speaker’s FoR use with different addressees. This paper reports on differences in two senior adults’ use of FoRs in Iwaidja when addressing a peer compared to addressing a child. Performing the Man and Tree task, the speakers made frequent use of geocentric descriptions with their peers, and substantially fewer geocentric descriptions with a child. The study was conducted in a complex multilingual speech environment where younger generations’ language use is shifting away from Iwaidja towards English and to other Australian languages. Factors motivating the different FoR choices in child-directed speech may include elements of parentese and accommodation to the children’s incomplete acquisition of Iwaidja. The children’s contact with English, particularly through schooling, may affect the adults’ expectations of the children’s acquisition of frames of reference in English. Drawing attention to the impact of the addressee in spatial speech, this study adds to understanding sociocultural elements of spatial reference in the context of language contact and shift.

papers.title: Variation in spatial concepts: Different frames of reference on different axes
papers.abstract: Spatial language and cognition vary across contexts. In some groups, people tend to use egocentric space (e.g. left, right) to encode the locations of objects, while in other groups, people use allocentric space (e.g. upriver, downriver) to describe the same spatial scene. These different spatial Frames of Reference (FoRs) characterize both the way people talk about spatial relations and the way they think about them, even when they are not using language. These patterns of spatial language and spatial thinking tend to covary, but the root causes of this variation are unclear. Here we propose that this variation in FoR use reflects variation in the spatial discriminability of the relevant spatial continua. In an initial test of this proposal, we compared FoR use across spatial axes that are known to differ in discriminability. In two non-verbal tests, a group of indigenous Bolivians used different FoRs on different spatial axes; on the lateral axis, where egocentric (left-right) discrimination is difficult, their behavior was predominantly allocentric; on the sagittal axis, where egocentric (front-back) discrimination is relatively easy, their behavior was predominantly egocentric. These findings support the spatial discriminability hypothesis, which may explain variation in spatial concepts not only across axes, but also across groups, between individuals, and over development.

papers.title: Extending Spatial Frames of Reference to Temporal Concepts
