Extend the analysis to other model components such as MLPs.
Further explore advanced probing methods.
papers.abstract: Despite excelling on multimodal benchmarks, vision-language models (VLMs) largely remain a black box. In this paper, we propose a novel interpretability framework to systematically analyze the internal mechanisms of VLMs, focusing on the functional roles of attention heads in multimodal reasoning. To this end, we introduce CogVision, a dataset that decomposes complex multimodal questions into step-by-step subquestions designed to simulate human reasoning through a chain-of-thought paradigm, with each subquestion associated with specific receptive or cognitive functions such as high-level visual reception and inference. Using a probing-based methodology, we identify attention heads that specialize in these functions and characterize them as functional heads. Our analysis across diverse VLM families reveals that these functional heads are universally sparse, vary in number and distribution across functions, and mediate interactions and hierarchical organization. Furthermore, intervention experiments demonstrate their critical role in multimodal reasoning: removing functional heads leads to performance degradation, while emphasizing them enhances accuracy. These findings provide new insights into the cognitive organization of VLMs and suggest promising directions for designing models with more human-aligned perceptual and reasoning abilities.

papers.title: How do Multimodal Foundation Models Encode Text and Speech? An Analysis of Cross-Lingual and Cross-Modal Representations
papers.research_question: How do multimodal foundation models encode text and speech? Specifically, how do they represent semantically equivalent sentences across languages and modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes cross-lingual and cross-modal representations in multimodal foundation models, finding that cross-modal similarity increases over layers, length adaptation helps but is limited to high-resource languages, speech has larger cross-lingual differences than text, and the modality gap is often larger than the language gap.
papers.conclusion: While multimodal foundation models present a unified architecture, they do not inherently create fully unified semantic representations. Representational gaps such as speech-text length mismatches, weak representations for low-resource languages, and tokenizer bottlenecks persist.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-modal representations converge over model layers, except in the initial layers which are specialized for text or speech processing.
Length adaptation mechanisms (e.g., pooling, Q-Former) are crucial for reducing the cross-modal gap, but their effectiveness is primarily limited to high-resource languages.
Speech exhibits larger cross-lingual differences than text, likely due to greater variability in acoustic features and recording conditions.
For models not explicitly trained for modality-agnostic representations (Seamless, SALMONN), the modality gap is more prominent than the language gap.
Tokenizer fragmentation for languages with diverse scripts (e.g., in SALMONN) leads to inflated initial similarity scores that drop in subsequent layers.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on the FLEURS dataset, which is created from Wikipedia texts, may limit generalizability to other domains like informal or spoken texts.
The study focuses only on speech and text modalities; exploring other modalities like images is out of scope.
Only three multimodal foundation models are analyzed; newer models like Qwen-Audio and Llama 3 are not covered.
Six of the 30 analyzed languages are not shared between SONAR and the other models, creating a non-fully overlapping experimental setup.
Findings are based on intrinsic analyses (SVCCA on activations); other explainability methods or downstream task performance could provide complementary insights.
papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models aim to create a unified representation space that abstracts away from surface features like language syntax or modality differences. To investigate this, we study the internal representations of three recent models, analyzing the model activations from semantically equivalent sentences across languages in the text and speech modalities. Our findings reveal that: 1) Cross-modal representations converge over model layers, except in the initial layers specialized at text and speech processing. 2) Length adaptation is crucial for reducing the cross-modal gap between text and speech, although current approaches' effectiveness is primarily limited to high-resource languages. 3) Speech exhibits larger cross-lingual differences than text. 4) For models not explicitly trained for modality-agnostic representations, the modality gap is more prominent than the language gap.

papers.title: The Vector Grounding Problem
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded in the world, i.e., have intrinsic meaning, despite being trained only on text data without direct interaction with the world?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that large language models can achieve referential grounding (intrinsic meaning) through selection processes in training that endow internal states with representational functions, even without multimodality or embodiment.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can, in principle and in some cases in practice, have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded, thus solving the Vector Grounding Problem and possessing intrinsic meaning independently of human interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Distinguishes referential grounding from other forms (sensorimotor, relational, communicative, epistemic) and argues referential grounding is the only kind essential to solving the Vector Grounding Problem.
Proposes that referential grounding requires two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories: causal-informational relations to the world and a history of selection that endows internal states with the function of carrying this information.
Argues that post-training (e.g., preference tuning for factual accuracy) can establish selection processes that confer world-involving representational functions to LLM internal states.
Suggests that pre-training might, under specific conditions, also lead to world-involving representational functions through implicit extra-linguistic success conditions in the training data.
Contends that in-context learning could, in principle, allow LLMs to acquire world-involving representational functions during inference without parameter updates.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce seemingly meaningful outputs, yet they are trained on text alone without direct interaction with the world. This leads to a modern variant of the classical symbol grounding problem in AI: can LLMs' internal states and outputs be about extra-linguistic reality, independently of the meaning human interpreters project onto them? We argue that they can. We first distinguish referential grounding -- the connection between a representation and its worldly referent -- from other forms of grounding and argue it is the only kind essential to solving the problem. We contend that referential grounding is achieved when a system's internal states satisfy two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories of representation: (1) they stand in appropriate causal-informational relations to the world, and (2) they have a history of selection that has endowed them with the function of carrying this information. We argue that LLMs can meet both conditions, even without multimodality or embodiment.

papers.title: Cross-neutralising: Probing for joint encoding of linguistic information in multilingual models
papers.research_question: How are linguistic properties encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in multilingual models like M-BERT and XLM-R?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that multilingual models jointly encode typological linguistic properties across languages, and this can be probed using the cross-neutralising method.
papers.conclusion: Typological feature values are encoded jointly across languages in multilingual models and can be localized via language centroids.
papers.key_findings:
Self-neutralising by subtracting language centroids removes typological information, reducing probing accuracy to chance levels.
Cross-neutralising shows that performance deteriorates for languages sharing the same typological feature value, indicating joint encoding.
This joint encoding pattern is observed in both M-BERT and XLM-R models.
The effect is consistent across different layers of the models.
Language centroids capture specific feature values in a localizable way across languages.
papers.limitation: When probing performance before neutralising is low (<75% accuracy), it is unclear what information the language centroids capture, limiting the interpretation of results.
future_direction: Correlate typological feature encoding with downstream task performance
Use cross-neutralising for selective generalization in models based on typology
Apply the method to other scenarios like multimodal models
papers.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders are widely used to transfer NLP models across languages. The success of this transfer is, however, dependent on the model's ability to encode the patterns of cross-lingual similarity and variation. Yet, little is known as to how these models are able to do this. We propose a simple method to study how relationships between languages are encoded in two state-of-the-art multilingual models (i.e. M-BERT and XLM-R). The results provide insight into their information sharing mechanisms and suggest that linguistic properties are encoded jointly across typologically-similar languages in these models.

papers.title: TopoLM: brain-like spatio-functional organization in a topographic language model
papers.research_question: Can a spatial smoothness principle lead to brain-like topographic organization in a transformer language model, and does it predict the functional organization observed in the human language system?
papers.core_contribution: Introducing a spatial smoothness loss in a transformer language model leads to brain-like topographic organization of semantically interpretable clusters without sacrificing task performance or brain alignment.
papers.conclusion: The spatial smoothness principle leads to topographic organization consistent with the spatio-functional organization of linguistic processing in the brain.
papers.key_findings:
TopoLM develops semantically interpretable clusters that match the functional organization in the brain's language system.
TopoLM predicts the emergence of a spatially organized cortical language system and fine-grained linguistic feature clusters observed in human cortex.
The spatial organization comes at virtually no cost to task performance or brain alignment, with TopoLM performing similarly to a non-topographic baseline on benchmarks.
TopoLM shows brain-like verb- and noun-selective clusters, specific to concrete over abstract words, replicating neuroimaging findings.
The non-topographic baseline does not show such clustering, indicating the spatial loss is necessary for brain-like organization.
papers.limitation: TopoLM is a feed-forward model with multiple layers, and the topographic maps are specific to each layer, so there is no coherent tissue across the entire system as in the brain. This limits modeling of tissue perturbations such as micro-stimulation.
future_direction: Using TopoLM to discover new candidates for spatial clustering in linguistic processing and inform the selection of optimal stimuli for further neuroimaging experiments.
papers.abstract: Neurons in the brain are spatially organized such that neighbors on tissue often exhibit similar response profiles. In the human language system, experimental studies have observed clusters for syntactic and semantic categories, but the mechanisms underlying this functional organization remain unclear. Here, building on work from the vision literature, we develop TopoLM, a transformer language model with an explicit two-dimensional spatial representation of model units. By combining a next-token prediction objective with a spatial smoothness loss, representations in this model assemble into clusters that correspond to semantically interpretable groupings of text and closely match the functional organization in the brain's language system. TopoLM successfully predicts the emergence of the spatio-functional organization of a cortical language system as well as the organization of functional clusters selective for fine-grained linguistic features empirically observed in human cortex. Our results suggest that the functional organization of the human language system is driven by a unified spatial objective, and provide a functionally and spatially aligned model of language processing in the brain.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: On the Entity-Level Alignment in Crosslingual Consistency
papers.research_question: What factors give rise to crosslingual consistency in multilingual LLMs, and do failures in entity alignment cause inconsistencies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first systematic analysis linking crosslingual consistency to entity-level alignment, introduces two prompting methods (SUBSUB and SUBINJ) that improve factual recall and consistency, and uses mechanistic interpretability to show these methods enhance entity representation alignment through pivot-language processing.
papers.conclusion: Entity alignment is a key factor underlying crosslingual consistency in multilingual LLMs, and the proposed prompting methods offer effective and practical strategies for improving multilingual factual prediction by enhancing this alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Crosslingual consistency is strongly correlated with entity alignment across all studied models.
Consistent factual recall rarely occurs without correctly aligning either the subject or object entities between two languages.
The proposed prompting methods SUBSUB and SUBINJ, which incorporate English translations of subjects, substantially improve factual recall accuracy and consistency, especially in English-centric models.
Mechanistic analysis using Logit Lens shows that SUBSUB and SUBINJ interventions reinforce entity representation alignment in the model's internal conceptual space.
The model's conceptual space is biased towards high-resource languages like English, explaining why using English subject translations is more effective than using other languages.
papers.limitation: Inconsistency can also stem from failure in the processing stage – i.e., the model lacks the factual knowledge so it cannot retrieve the correct object in the conceptual space, which is beyond the scope of this paper.
papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) are expected to recall factual knowledge consistently across languages. However, the factors that give rise to such crosslingual consistency -- and its frequent failure -- remain poorly understood. In this work, we hypothesize that these inconsistencies may arise from failures in entity alignment, the process of mapping subject and object entities into a shared conceptual space across languages. To test this, we assess alignment through entity-level (subject and object) translation tasks, and find that consistency is strongly correlated with alignment across all studied models, with misalignment of subjects or objects frequently resulting in inconsistencies. Building on this insight, we propose SubSub and SubInj, two effective methods that integrate English translations of subjects into prompts across languages, leading to substantial gains in both factual recall accuracy and consistency. Finally, our mechanistic analysis reveals that these interventions reinforce the entity representation alignment in the conceptual space through model's internal pivot-language processing, offering effective and practical strategies for improving multilingual factual prediction.

papers.title: Language models align with brain regions that represent concepts across modalities
papers.research_question: Do language models align with brain regions that represent concepts consistently across different input modalities (text and images)?
papers.core_contribution: Language models predict brain activity better in regions with high semantic consistency across modalities, even when those regions are not language-selective, suggesting LMs develop cross-modal conceptual representations.
papers.conclusion: Language models align with brain regions that represent concepts consistently across modalities, indicating that LMs may internally develop cross-modal conceptual representations.
papers.key_findings:
Brain regions with higher semantic consistency (responding similarly to concepts across text and image paradigms) are better predicted by LM representations.
This correlation holds even in brain regions with weak language selectivity.
Representational similarity between LMs and semantically consistent brain regions is significant and increases for vision-language models when using both text and image stimuli.
Both language-only and vision-language models show alignment with semantically consistent brain regions.
papers.limitation:
The picture paradigm correlation is lower and skewed by visual cortex areas that encode images but not necessarily concepts.
The study uses an inter-participant noise ceiling due to lack of repeated trials, which may not capture all variability.
papers.abstract: Cognitive science and neuroscience have long faced the challenge of disentangling representations of language from representations of conceptual meaning. As the same problem arises in today's language models (LMs), we investigate the relationship between LM--brain alignment and two neural metrics: (1) the level of brain activation during processing of sentences, targeting linguistic processing, and (2) a novel measure of meaning consistency across input modalities, which quantifies how consistently a brain region responds to the same concept across paradigms (sentence, word cloud, image) using an fMRI dataset (Pereira et al., 2018). Our experiments show that both language-only and language-vision models predict the signal better in more meaning-consistent areas of the brain, even when these areas are not strongly sensitive to language processing, suggesting that LMs might internally represent cross-modal conceptual meaning.

papers.title: Language Steering for Multilingual In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: Does language identity occupy structured directions in activation space, and can a simple activation offset improve multilingual in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces language vectors, a training-free method that improves multilingual in-context learning by steering activations, and shows that language identity occupies structured directions in activation space.
papers.conclusion: Language vectors improve multilingual in-context learning and encode meaningful linguistic structure, supporting the hypothesis that language identity occupies structured directions in activation space.
papers.key_findings:
Language vectors improve performance over baselines across tasks and languages.
Vectors encode linguistic structure, with related languages clustering together.
Vectors transfer across tasks, indicating they capture language-specific rather than task-specific information.
Steering is most effective in early to middle layers.
The method is training-free and requires no parameter updates.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameters are selected per language via validation performance, which requires held-out data and may not generalize to new languages or domains.
Evaluation is limited to instruction-tuned decoder-only models.
Certain task transfers fail (e.g., MSVAMP to XNLI).
future_direction: Extending the approach to languages without parallel data.
Applying language vectors to generative tasks such as summarization.
Predicting steering effectiveness without exhaustive hyperparameter search.
papers.abstract: While multilingual large language models have gained widespread adoption, their performance on non-English languages remains substantially inferior to English. This disparity is particularly evident in in-context learning scenarios, where providing demonstrations in English but testing on non-English inputs leads to significant performance degradation. In this paper, we hypothesize that LLMs develop a universal semantic space for understanding languages, where different languages are encoded as distinct directions within this space. Based on this hypothesis, we propose language vectors -- a training-free language steering approach that leverages activation differences between source and target languages to guide model behavior. We steer the model generations by adding the vector to the intermediate model activations during inference. This is done to make the model's internal representations shift towards the target language space without any parameter updates. We evaluate our method across three datasets and test on a total of 19 languages on three different models. Our results show consistent improvements on multilingual in-context learning over baselines across all tasks and languages tested. Beyond performance gains, hierarchical clustering of steering vectors reveals meaningful linguistic structure aligned with language families. These vectors also successfully transfer across tasks, demonstrating that these representations are task-agnostic.

papers.title: Diverging views on the role of structured representations in linguistics and language modeling
papers.research_question: How do language models compare to human language processing in terms of structured representations, and what is their role in the science of language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that language models struggle with structured representations central to human language, and suggests that for language models to be effective models of language, structured representations must be incorporated as computational objects.
papers.conclusion: Language models need to conceptualize structured representations as computational objects to better align with human language and contribute to the science of language.
papers.key_findings:
Language models trained on next-word prediction may not learn structure-dependent representations necessary for human language.
Models like ChatGPT show insensitivity to Binding Principle C, incorrectly allowing co-reference in prohibited contexts.
Language models do not make a qualitative distinction between possible and impossible languages, treating them similarly unlike humans.
The internal representational infrastructure for possible and impossible languages overlaps in models, indicating no fundamental difference.
Incorporating structured representations as primary computational targets could enhance language models' utility as models of language.
future_direction: Incorporate structured representations as computational objects in language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent years have seen dramatic advances in the linguistic abilities of language models, leading some authors to argue that they can be treated as models of language. Against this background, we provide a cognitive perspective on the place of language models in the science of language, with a particular focus on the role of structured representations. Evidence from linguistics, psychology and cognitive neuroscience shows that structured representations occupy a central place in the human mind. Structured representations constrain how linguistic forms map onto meanings, thereby determining the boundaries of possible human languages. In language modeling, instead, the place of structured representations is often peripheral. They are seen as optional end point of modeling, to be induced as a consequence of the objective the model tries to optimize – that is, next-word prediction. Because structured relations and representations are not necessarily useful for predicting the next word in a sequence, it is not guaranteed that the model’s internal organization will come to encode those representations. Indeed, contemporary language models struggle to use structured representations functionally to map form onto meaning, and to determine whether they should consider their input as a possible human language or not. Building on classic insights in linguistics and (computational) cognitive science, we suggest that any use of language models as models of language requires conceptualizing the role of structured representations as computational objects.

papers.title: When Meanings Meet: Investigating the Emergence and Quality of Shared Concept Spaces during Multilingual Language Model Training
papers.research_question: How do shared, language-agnostic concept spaces emerge and develop during the multilingual pretraining of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Shared concept spaces emerge early in multilingual pretraining and remain relatively stable, but alignment with these spaces is language-dependent and influenced by training data composition.
papers.conclusion: Shared concept spaces emerge early and are progressively refined during multilingual pretraining, with alignment depending on language and data composition. Targeted multi-aligned data can improve alignment for low-resource languages.
papers.key_findings:
Shared concept spaces arise early in pretraining and continue to refine throughout training.
Alignment with shared concept spaces depends on language similarity and training data proportion.
Cross-lingual concept patching can shift model behavior, such as selecting dominant senses for polysemous words or translating cross-lingual homographs instead of copying them.
The model initially prefers copying input words over translating them, a behavior learned early.
Patching from averaged representations across languages (the 'seen' setting) is often as effective as patching from English-only representations for inducing concepts in English output.
papers.limitation:
Focuses primarily on a single, relatively small model (EuroLLM-1.7B), though provides supporting evidence on two others.
Analysis is restricted to nouns; behavior of other word classes is not studied.
Inherits biases from the Multi-SimLex dataset, such as ambiguous translations for polysemous words.
Focuses only on the simple task of word-level translation; findings may not generalize to more complex tasks.
future_direction: Investigate how representations for other word classes (beyond nouns) behave.
Study the emergence and behavior of language-agnostic spaces for more complex multilingual tasks like sentence-level translation or reasoning.
papers.abstract: Training Large Language Models (LLMs) with high multilingual coverage is becoming increasingly important -- especially when monolingual resources are scarce. Recent studies have found that LLMs process multilingual inputs in shared concept spaces, thought to support generalization and cross-lingual transfer. However, these prior studies often do not use causal methods, lack deeper error analysis or focus on the final model only, leaving open how these spaces emerge during training. We investigate the development of language-agnostic concept spaces during pretraining of EuroLLM through the causal interpretability method of activation patching. We isolate cross-lingual concept representations, then inject them into a translation prompt to investigate how consistently translations can be altered, independently of the language. We find that shared concept spaces emerge early} and continue to refine, but that alignment with them is language-dependent}. Furthermore, in contrast to prior work, our fine-grained manual analysis reveals that some apparent gains in translation quality reflect shifts in behavior -- like selecting senses for polysemous words or translating instead of copying cross-lingual homographs -- rather than improved translation ability. Our findings offer new insight into the training dynamics of cross-lingual alignment and the conditions under which causal interpretability methods offer meaningful insights in multilingual contexts.

papers.title: A Joint Matrix Factorization Analysis of Multilingual Representations
papers.research_question: How do multilingual language models encode morphosyntactic features in their layers? Are the findings robust in low-resource settings? Do morphosyntactic typology and downstream task performance reflect in the factorization outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a joint matrix factorization tool for analyzing multilingual representations and finds that morphosyntactic encoding varies across layers, influenced by language properties, and the tool's outputs correlate with phylogenetic trees and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The joint matrix factorization tool provides insights into multilingual representations, showing layer-wise variations in morphosyntactic encoding and correlations with linguistic properties and task performance.
papers.key_findings:
Encoding of morphosyntactic information decreases from lower to upper layers in multilingual models.
Language-specific factors like writing system and number of unique characters influence encoding.
Multilingual representations show distinct patterns in languages with low proximity.
Low-resource languages benefit from related languages in the model.
Factorization outputs yield hierarchical clusters resembling phylogenetic trees and predict cross-lingual task performance.
papers.limitation:
Only used RoBERTa and XLM-R models, not other available models like BERT or T5.
Downsampled Wikipedia data for equal representation, which may not reflect full-scale training.
Analysis limited to morphosyntactic features, not other linguistic aspects.
future_direction: Extend analysis tool to examine representations learned by multimodal models.
Expand scope to include other linguistic aspects such as semantics and pragmatics.
papers.abstract: We present an analysis tool based on joint matrix factorization for comparing latent representations of multilingual and monolingual models. An alternative to probing, this tool allows us to analyze multiple sets of representations in a joint manner. Using this tool, we study to what extent and how morphosyntactic features are reflected in the representations learned by multilingual pre-trained models. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of over 33 languages and 17 morphosyntactic categories. Our findings demonstrate variations in the encoding of morphosyntactic information across upper and lower layers, with category-specific differences influenced by language properties. Hierarchical clustering of the factorization outputs yields a tree structure that is related to phylogenetic trees manually crafted by linguists. Moreover, we find the factorization outputs exhibit strong associations with performance observed across different cross-lingual tasks. We release our code to facilitate future research.

papers.title: The Mechanistic Emergence of Symbol Grounding in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does symbol grounding emerge in language models, specifically what are the loci and mechanisms driving this emergence?
papers.core_contribution: Symbol grounding emerges in middle-layer computations via aggregate attention heads that retrieve environmental grounds to predict linguistic forms, generalizing across Transformers and state-space models but not LSTMs.
papers.conclusion: Symbol grounding can mechanistically emerge in autoregressive language models, with practical implications for predicting and potentially controlling the reliability of generation.
papers.key_findings:
Grounding concentrates in middle-layer computations.
Grounding is implemented through an aggregate mechanism where attention heads aggregate environmental ground to support prediction of linguistic forms.
This phenomenon replicates in multimodal dialogue and across architectures (Transformers and state-space models) but not in unidirectional LSTMs.
Grounding cannot be fully explained by co-occurrence statistics.
Causal interventions show that aggregate heads are critical for grounding.
papers.limitation: Full-scale VLMs present additional complications such as large numbers of visual tokens and redundant artifact tokens, making systematic identification and intervention at scale a nontrivial challenge.
future_direction: Investigate how grounding mechanisms interact with other emergent phenomena, such as in-context learning and reasoning.
Scale the analysis to larger models and more naturalistic settings.
papers.abstract: Symbol grounding (Harnad, 1990) describes how symbols such as words acquire their meanings by connecting to real-world sensorimotor experiences. Recent work has shown preliminary evidence that grounding may emerge in (vision-)language models trained at scale without using explicit grounding objectives. Yet, the specific loci of this emergence and the mechanisms that drive it remain largely unexplored. To address this problem, we introduce a controlled evaluation framework that systematically traces how symbol grounding arises within the internal computations through mechanistic and causal analysis. Our findings show that grounding concentrates in middle-layer computations and is implemented through the aggregate mechanism, where attention heads aggregate the environmental ground to support the prediction of linguistic forms. This phenomenon replicates in multimodal dialogue and across architectures (Transformers and state-space models), but not in unidirectional LSTMs. Our results provide behavioral and mechanistic evidence that symbol grounding can emerge in language models, with practical implications for predicting and potentially controlling the reliability of generation.

papers.title: The Same But Different: Structural Similarities and Differences in Multilingual Language Modeling
papers.research_question: When two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? When two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs use shared internal circuitry for similar syntactic processes across languages, even in independently trained monolingual models, and employ language-specific components (e.g., feed-forward networks) for language-specific morphological processes.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds that cross-lingual structural similarity is represented within LLMs using shared circuits that invoke the same algorithm independent of language, and that language-specific processing is localized to play a causal role only in languages that require it.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual models use a single circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs.
Monolingual models trained independently on English and Chinese each adopt nearly the same circuit for the IOI task, suggesting consistency in how LLMs learn to handle this aspect of language modeling.
For tasks requiring language-specific morphological processes (e.g., past tense marking in English), multilingual models invoke a largely overlapping circuit but employ language-specific components as needed, such as feed-forward networks in English only for morphological marking.
The circuits identified for the IOI task align with prior work, indicating that the same mechanism is shared between English and Chinese within a multilingual model.
Heads specifically responsible for past tense disambiguation are activated in English but not in Chinese, and they suppress present-tense verbs in English.
papers.limitation: Results are limited to specific tasks and datasets, requiring future work for replication and generalization.
future_direction: Replicate and generalize findings to more tasks and datasets.
Explore cross-disciplinary collaborations to gain fresh perspectives on linguistic universality using LLMs.
Investigate whether circuit overlap can be exploited for improving cross-lingual transfer and safety.
papers.abstract: We employ new tools from mechanistic interpretability in order to ask whether the internal structure of large language models (LLMs) shows correspondence to the linguistic structures which underlie the languages on which they are trained. In particular, we ask (1) when two languages employ the same morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using shared internal circuitry? and (2) when two languages require different morphosyntactic processes, do LLMs handle them using different internal circuitry? Using English and Chinese multilingual and monolingual models, we analyze the internal circuitry involved in two tasks. We find evidence that models employ the same circuit to handle the same syntactic process independently of the language in which it occurs, and that this is the case even for monolingual models trained completely independently. Moreover, we show that multilingual models employ language-specific components (attention heads and feed-forward networks) when needed to handle linguistic processes (e.g., morphological marking) that only exist in some languages. Together, our results provide new insights into how LLMs trade off between exploiting common structures and preserving linguistic differences when tasked with modeling multiple languages simultaneously.

papers.title: Why Can GPT Learn In-Context? Language Models Implicitly Perform Gradient Descent as Meta-Optimizers
papers.research_question: What is the working mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) in GPT models? The paper investigates whether ICL can be understood as implicit finetuning, where the attention mechanism performs a form of gradient descent.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent, leading to the understanding that in-context learning is a form of implicit finetuning. Inspired by this, the paper designs a momentum-based attention mechanism that improves performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning can be understood as implicit finetuning via a meta-optimization process, and this understanding can inspire model design, as demonstrated by the momentum-based attention.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer attention has a dual form with gradient descent, which explains in-context learning as implicit finetuning.
Empirical comparisons show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning in terms of predictions, attention outputs, attention weights, and attention to training tokens.
Momentum-based attention, designed by analogy with gradient descent with momentum, improves performance on language modeling and in-context learning tasks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to Transformer-based models and does not consider other architectures.
The dual form is derived using a relaxed linear attention approximation, and the mechanism of standard attention without approximation may be more complex.
Experiments are limited to models up to 2.7B parameters and only classification tasks, leaving larger models and other task types for future work.
future_direction: Study in-context learning for non-Transformer architectures.
Investigate the mechanism of standard Transformer attention without the linear approximation.
Extend the analysis to larger models and other tasks like open-ended generation.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models have shown surprising in-context learning (ICL) ability. With a few demonstration input-label pairs, they can predict the label for an unseen input without parameter updates. Despite the great success in performance, its working mechanism still remains an open question. In this paper, we explain language models as meta-optimizers and understand in-context learning as implicit finetuning. Theoretically, we figure out that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent. On top of it, we understand ICL as follows: GPT first produces meta-gradients according to the demonstration examples, and then these meta-gradients are applied to the original GPT to build an ICL model. We comprehensively compare the behaviors of in-context learning and explicit finetuning on real tasks to provide empirical evidence that supports our understanding. Experimental results show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning from multiple perspectives. Inspired by the dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, we design a momentum-based attention by analogy with gradient descent with momentum. The improved performance over vanilla attention further supports our understanding from another perspective, and more importantly, shows the potential to utilize our understanding for future model design. The code is available at \url{https://aka.ms/icl}.

papers.title: From Monolingual to Bilingual: Investigating Language Conditioning in Large Language Models for Psycholinguistic Tasks
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages, and how does language identity (monolingual vs bilingual prompting) affect their output behavior and internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models condition their psycholinguistic behavior and internal representations on the language identity specified in the prompt, with differences between monolingual and bilingual prompting, offering insights into cross-linguistic cognition in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results demonstrate that LLMs are not language-neutral. Instead, they respond to and encode language-specific cues in both their outputs and internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Both models adapt their outputs based on the linguistic identity embedded in the prompt.
Qwen shows greater sensitivity to prompt language and sharper behavioral distinctions between Dutch and Chinese than Llama.
Probing reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more linearly decodable in deeper layers.
Chinese prompts yield stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch prompts.
Bilingual prompting can introduce interference or noise, especially for low-resource languages like Dutch.
papers.limitation:
Focus on only three languages (English, Dutch, Chinese), limiting generalizability.
Only two LLMs are evaluated.
Tasks represent only a narrow slice of the psycholinguistic space.
future_direction: Expanding to include languages with different scripts, phonological systems, or morphological complexity (e.g., Arabic, Hindi, Finnish).
Incorporating a broader set of psycholinguistic phenomena, such as lexical decision making, semantic priming, syntactic ambiguity resolution, and metaphor comprehension.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong linguistic capabilities, but little is known about how they encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages. We investigate whether and how LLMs exhibit human-like psycholinguistic responses under different linguistic identities using two tasks: sound symbolism and word valence. We evaluate two models, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, under monolingual and bilingual prompting in English, Dutch, and Chinese. Behaviorally, both models adjust their outputs based on prompted language identity, with Qwen showing greater sensitivity and sharper distinctions between Dutch and Chinese. Probing analysis reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more decodable in deeper layers, with Chinese prompts yielding stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch. Our results demonstrate that language identity conditions both output behavior and internal representations in LLMs, providing new insights into their application as models of cross-linguistic cognition.

papers.title: Geometry without Position? When Positional Embeddings Help and Hurt Spatial Reasoning
papers.research_question: To what extent do positional embeddings determine the geometric structure of visual representations, and under what conditions do they facilitate or hinder spatial reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Positional embeddings act as geometric priors that shape the spatial structure of vision transformer representations, and geometric consistency across views depends on the consistency of positional embeddings rather than visual content alone.
papers.conclusion: Positional embeddings critically regulate spatial interactions and geometric consistency in vision transformer representations, and future designs should consider positional embedding consistency for multi-view tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Positional embeddings function as geometric priors that shape the spatial structure of ViT representations.
Geometric consistency across views depends primarily on the consistency of positional embeddings, not visual content.
Removing or shuffling positional embeddings degrades spatial anchoring and correspondence.
A simple, training-free token re-indexing that aligns positional embeddings across views can restore geometric correspondence.
Models like VGGT implicitly learn to reconcile positional embeddings across views to achieve robust multi-view representations.
papers.limitation: The analysis isolates the representational role of positional embeddings at inference time and does not capture how a model would behave if positional mechanisms were changed during training.
future_direction: Future positional designs that incorporate geometric constraints, such as multi-view alignment or scene-aware positional embedding systems.
Moving beyond purely image-space positional frames to better bridge image-space indexing with scene-space structure.
papers.abstract: This paper revisits the role of positional embeddings (PEs) within vision transformers (ViTs) from a geometric perspective. We show that PEs are not mere token indices but effectively function as geometric priors that shape the spatial structure of the representation. We introduce token-level diagnostics that measure how multi-view geometric consistency in ViT representation depends on consitent PEs. Through extensive experiments on 14 foundation ViT models, we reveal how PEs influence multi-view geometry and spatial reasoning. Our findings clarify the role of PEs as a causal mechanism that governs spatial structure in ViT representations. Our code is provided in https://github.com/shijianjian/vit-geometry-probes

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: The Case for Translation-Invariant Self-Attention in Transformer-Based\n Language Models
papers.research_question: How are positional information encoded in transformer-based language models, and can translation-invariant self-attention be an effective alternative to conventional position embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes translation-invariant self-attention (TISA), a new positional encoding method that satisfies six design criteria and improves performance on GLUE tasks with very few added parameters.
papers.conclusion: Translation invariance emerges in state-of-the-art language models, and TISA is a positional encoding method that satisfies all six design criteria and improves downstream performance.
papers.key_findings:
Position embeddings in transformer-based language models become increasingly translation-invariant during training, and this invariance correlates with model performance.
Adding TISA to ALBERT improves performance on GLUE tasks with minimal parameter increase.
TISA can be used with or without conventional position embeddings, though performance is better when combined.
papers.limitation:
Lack of computational resources to pretrain TISA-only models from scratch
TISA alone (without position embeddings) does not perform as well as when combined with position embeddings
future_direction: Applying TISA to transformer models in other domains like speech, motion synthesis, and computer vision
Exploring two-stage training with TISA, pre-training on short sequences and then scaling to longer ones
papers.abstract:
Mechanisms for encoding positional information are central for
transformer-based language models. In this paper, we analyze the position
embeddings of existing language models, finding strong evidence of translation
invariance, both for the embeddings themselves and for their effect on
self-attention. The degree of translation invariance increases during training
and correlates positively with model performance. Our findings lead us to
propose translation-invariant self-attention (TISA), which accounts for the
relative position between tokens in an interpretable fashion without needing
conventional position embeddings. Our proposal has several theoretical
advantages over existing position-representation approaches. Experiments show
that it improves on regular ALBERT on GLUE tasks, while only adding orders of
magnitude less positional parameters.

papers.title: Deconstructing Positional Information: From Attention Logits to Training Biases
papers.research_question: How do different positional encoding schemes (additive vs. multiplicative) mediate the interaction between token content and position, and what causes the performance paradox and single-head deposit pattern in RoPE?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified Toeplitz-matrix framework to analyze positional encodings, discovers the single-head deposit pattern in RoPE, and provides a theoretical explanation showing this pattern is an intrinsic property of RoPE's multiplicative structure.
papers.conclusion: The Toeplitz framework provides a powerful lens for understanding positional encodings, and the deposit pattern explains RoPE's performance paradox. Controlled mixing of positional signals is a promising strategy for achieving robust, distributed representations.
papers.key_findings:
RoPE's multiplicative structure enables superior performance on tasks requiring content-position coupling but leads to a single-head deposit pattern where positional information is concentrated in one early-layer head.
Additive positional encodings (Absolute, T5, ALiBi) do not exhibit the deposit pattern and show different learning dynamics.
The deposit pattern is an intrinsic property of RoPE, caused by exponential amplification of gradient signals during training, leading to extreme specialization.
Hybrid architectures like Multi-Latent Attention (MLA) can mitigate the deposit pattern and improve robustness by mixing positional signals.
RoPE's strong inductive bias suppresses the formation of latent positional representations observed in models with additive or no PE.
papers.limitation:
The connection between the deposit pattern and RoPE's known struggles with length extrapolation requires direct empirical validation.
Future work should probe the limits of these positional mechanisms on more complex, algorithmic tasks such as sequence reversal or Dyck language recognition.
future_direction: Direct empirical validation of the link between the deposit pattern and length extrapolation.
Testing positional mechanisms on more complex, algorithmic tasks.
More complex controlled analysis of positional mechanisms in transformers.
papers.abstract: Positional encodings enable Transformers to incorporate sequential information, yet their theoretical understanding remains limited to two properties: distance attenuation and translation invariance. Because natural language lacks purely positional data, the interplay between positional and semantic information is still underexplored. We address this gap by deconstructing the attention-logit computation and providing a structured analysis of positional encodings, categorizing them into additive and multiplicative forms. The differing properties of these forms lead to distinct mechanisms for capturing positional information. To probe this difference, we design a synthetic task that explicitly requires strong integration of positional and semantic cues. As predicted, multiplicative encodings achieve a clear performance advantage on this task. Moreover, our evaluation reveals a hidden training bias: an information aggregation effect in shallow layers that we term the single-head deposit pattern. Through ablation studies and theoretical analysis, we proved that this phenomenon is inherent in multiplicative encodings. These findings deepen the understanding of positional encodings and call for further study of their training dynamics.

papers.title: Conceptual structure coheres in human cognition but not in large language models
papers.research_question: Does conceptual structure in large language models cohere across different probing tasks as it does in humans, or do human and LLM conceptual representations differ in robustness?
papers.core_contribution: Human conceptual structure is robust across different tasks and cultures, but large language models exhibit less coherence in conceptual structure across different probing tasks, indicating a lack of a stable conceptual core.
papers.conclusion: Human conceptual structure is robust to differences in task, language, and culture, while contemporary LLMs lack such coherence, highlighting a fundamental difference between human cognition and current machine language models.
papers.key_findings:
Human conceptual structure estimates from three different tasks (feature listing, triadic comparisons, pairwise ratings) are highly coherent (squared Procrustes correlations between 0.72 and 0.96).
LLM conceptual structure estimates vary depending on the probing task; for GPT-3, the squared Procrustes correlations between different task embeddings are lower (e.g., 0.72 between feature listing and triplet, 0.47 between feature listing and pairwise, 0.25 between triplet and pairwise).
LLM conceptual structure from verified feature lists aligns moderately well with human feature norms (squared Procrustes correlation 0.89), but other LLM-derived embeddings align less well.
Chain-of-thought prompting improves alignment with human conceptual structure for some models but does not achieve human-level coherence.
Embeddings from internal representations (e.g., GPT-3 hidden layers, word2vec, CLIP) do not cohere well with each other or with human embeddings.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a constrained set of 30 concepts from two domains; a larger scale study might reveal different results.
The LLM simulations did not employ advanced prompting techniques like tree-of-thought or self-consistency, which might improve coherence.
LLMs lack multimodal sensory experience that humans have, which might affect conceptual organization.
future_direction: Conduct a larger scale study on larger concept sets.
Investigate the use of advanced prompting techniques (e.g., tree-of-thought, self-consistency) to improve conceptual coherence in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Neural network models of language have long been used as a tool for developing hypotheses about conceptual representation in the mind and brain. For many years, such use involved extracting vector-space representations of words and using distances among these to predict or understand human behavior in various semantic tasks. Contemporary large language models (LLMs), however, make it possible to interrogate the latent structure of conceptual representations using experimental methods nearly identical to those commonly used with human participants. The current work utilizes three common techniques borrowed from cognitive psychology to estimate and compare the structure of concepts in humans and a suite of LLMs. In humans, we show that conceptual structure is robust to differences in culture, language, and method of estimation. Structures estimated from LLM behavior, while individually fairly consistent with those estimated from human behavior, vary much more depending upon the particular task used to generate responses--across tasks, estimates of conceptual structure from the very same model cohere less with one another than do human structure estimates. These results highlight an important difference between contemporary LLMs and human cognition, with implications for understanding some fundamental limitations of contemporary machine language.

papers.title: When Can Transformers Ground and Compose: Insights from Compositional Generalization Benchmarks
papers.research_question: When and how can transformer models ground language to a visual world and compose object attributes to solve compositional generalization tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Simple transformer-based models (GroCoT) can achieve strong compositional generalization on grounded navigation tasks, with the main challenge being target identification. A simpler task (RefEx) reveals that even a single self-attention layer can ground and compose attributes, and its computations can be fully interpreted.
papers.conclusion: Transformer models are capable of grounded compositional generalization, and their success can be understood through analysis of their attention mechanisms, as demonstrated on both complex benchmarks and a simplified interpretable task.
papers.key_findings:
GroCoT, a simple transformer-based model, outperforms specialized architectures on ReaSCAN and GSRR benchmarks.
The primary difficulty in ReaSCAN is target identification, not navigation or sequence generation.
The C2 test split in ReaSCAN is unfair; with a corrected setup, transformers can generalize to deeper command structures.
A one-layer, one-head attention-only transformer can solve the RefEx task and generalize to novel compositions of object attributes.
The computations of the attention-only transformer on RefEx can be fully described via a precise mathematical construction of its learned parameters.
papers.abstract: Humans can reason compositionally whilst grounding language utterances to the real world. Recent benchmarks like ReaSCAN (Wu et al., 2021) use navigation tasks grounded in a grid world to assess whether neural models exhibit similar capabilities. In this work, we present a simple transformer-based model that outperforms specialized architectures on ReaSCAN and a modified version (Qiu et al., 2021) of gSCAN (Ruis et al., 2020). On analyzing the task, we find that identifying the target location in the grid world is the main challenge for the models. Furthermore, we show that a particular split in ReaSCAN, which tests depth generalization, is unfair. On an amended version of this split, we show that transformers can generalize to deeper input structures. Finally, we design a simpler grounded compositional generalization task, RefEx, to investigate how transformers reason compositionally. We show that a single self-attention layer with a single head generalizes to novel combinations of object attributes. Moreover, we derive a precise mathematical construction of the transformer’s computations from the learned network. Overall, we provide valuable insights about the grounded compositional generalization task and the behaviour of transformers on it, which would be useful for researchers working in this area.

papers.title: How Language Directions Align with Token Geometry in Multilingual LLMs
papers.research_question: Where and how is language information encoded within transformer layers? Does the pretraining language distribution structurally reshape the geometry of multilingual representations?
papers.core_contribution: Language information in multilingual LLMs is linearly separable from the first transformer block and remains stable across layers, and the alignment between language directions and vocabulary embeddings is shaped by pretraining data composition, indicating structural imprinting.
papers.conclusion: Language representation in LLMs is distinguished by latent representational structures formed during pretraining, established early and preserved across layers, highlighting the importance of balanced language composition for fairness and robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Language information becomes sharply separated in the first transformer block (+76.4±8.2%p from Layer 0→1) and remains almost fully linearly separable throughout model depth.
The alignment between language directions and vocabulary embeddings is strongly tied to the language composition of the training data, with Chinese-inclusive models showing 4.21× higher alignment for Chinese compared to English-centric models.
Chinese reaches maximal separability in deeper layers, whereas Spanish and German converge earlier, showing typological effects.
Linear probes achieve 99.8±0.1% accuracy on average, with only a 0.58±0.12%p gap relative to MLP probes, indicating linear separability.
Match@Peak remains low for Latin-script languages, suggesting language directions capture abstract features beyond token identity.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to five languages and may not generalize to all languages or scripts.
future_direction: expanding the analysis to additional languages and scripts
evaluating the influence of tokenizer design
conducting interventional studies
papers.abstract: Multilingual LLMs demonstrate strong performance across diverse languages, yet there has been limited systematic analysis of how language information is structured within their internal representation space and how it emerges across layers. We conduct a comprehensive probing study on six multilingual LLMs, covering all 268 transformer layers, using linear and nonlinear probes together with a new Token--Language Alignment analysis to quantify the layer-wise dynamics and geometric structure of language encoding. Our results show that language information becomes sharply separated in the first transformer block (+76.4$\pm$8.2 percentage points from Layer 0 to 1) and remains almost fully linearly separable throughout model depth. We further find that the alignment between language directions and vocabulary embeddings is strongly tied to the language composition of the training data. Notably, Chinese-inclusive models achieve a ZH Match@Peak of 16.43\%, whereas English-centric models achieve only 3.90\%, revealing a 4.21$\times$ structural imprinting effect. These findings indicate that multilingual LLMs distinguish languages not by surface script features but by latent representational structures shaped by the training corpus. Our analysis provides practical insights for data composition strategies and fairness in multilingual representation learning. All code and analysis scripts are publicly available at: https://github.com/thisiskorea/How-Language-Directions-Align-with-Token-Geometry-in-Multilingual-LLMs.

papers.title: Rethinking Cross-lingual Alignment: Balancing Transfer and Cultural Erasure in Multilingual LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the trade-off between knowledge transfer and cultural localization in cross-lingual alignment, and how can we design alignment techniques to balance this trade-off?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a holistic evaluation framework (transfer-localization plane) to measure the trade-off between knowledge transfer and cultural erasure in cross-lingual alignment, and proposes a novel inference-time method (Surgical Steering) that disentangles universal and localized steering at different layers to better balance the two objectives.
papers.conclusion: Cultural knowledge is suppressed but partially recoverable through targeted steering; however, some cultural nuances are irretrievably lost, highlighting a persistent and perhaps unavoidable cost of cross-lingual alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Current cross-lingual alignment methods consistently improve factual transfer at the direct cost of cultural localization across all six languages studied.
Universal factual transfer and culturally-specific knowledge are optimally steerable at different model layers (transfer in middle layers, localization in deeper layers).
Surgical Steering, which applies English steering at a middle layer and localization steering at a deeper layer, achieves a better balance between transfer and localization than applying either alone.
Cultural knowledge is not permanently erased by alignment but is suppressed and can be partially recovered through targeted, layer-specific interventions.
The fundamental trade-off between transfer and localization persists, indicating that some cultural nuances are irretrievably lost during the alignment process.
papers.limitation:
The fundamental trade-off persists; models with stronger alignment are less responsive to steering, indicating that some cultural nuances are irrevocably lost during the alignment process.
English bias is not completely removed even with steering; the post-trained CLA models never fully return to the point of the unaligned baseline.
papers.abstract: Cross-lingual alignment (CLA) aims to align multilingual representations, enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) to seamlessly transfer knowledge across languages. While intuitive, we hypothesize, this pursuit of representational convergence can inadvertently cause "cultural erasure", the functional loss of providing culturally-situated responses that should diverge based on the query language. In this work, we systematically analyze this trade-off by introducing a holistic evaluation framework, the transfer-localization plane, which quantifies both desirable knowledge transfer and undesirable cultural erasure. Using this framework, we re-evaluate recent CLA approaches and find that they consistently improve factual transfer at the direct cost of cultural localization across all six languages studied. Our investigation into the internal representations of these models reveals a key insight: universal factual transfer and culturally-specific knowledge are optimally steerable at different model layers. Based on this finding, we propose Surgical Steering, a novel inference-time method that disentangles these two objectives. By applying targeted activation steering to distinct layers, our approach achieves a better balance between the two competing dimensions, effectively overcoming the limitations of current alignment techniques.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 1, Learning Hierarchical Language Structures
papers.research_question: How do language models perform deep reasoning over hierarchical structures, and can we understand their inner workings using synthetic context-free grammars (CFGs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers can learn complex context-free grammars and that their hidden states linearly encode non-terminal information, while attention patterns mimic dynamic programming algorithms for parsing.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn complex hierarchical structures defined by CFGs, and their internal representations and attention patterns align with dynamic programming algorithms for parsing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers (GPT variants) can accurately learn and generate strings from synthetic CFGs that require dynamic programming to parse.
Hidden states of the trained transformers linearly encode non-terminal ancestor information almost perfectly.
Attention patterns in the trained models resemble the information flow of dynamic programming, with boundary-based attention.
Relative and rotary positional embeddings are crucial for learning harder CFGs, outperforming absolute positional embeddings.
Training with perturbed data (10% noise) improves robustness to corrupted prefixes.
papers.limitation: The chosen CFGs are synthetic and may not encompass all CFGs; the results are specific to the designed CFG families.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models are effective but complex, and understanding their inner workings and reasoning mechanisms is a significant challenge. Previous research has primarily explored how these models handle simple tasks like name copying or selection, and we extend this by investigating how these models perform recursive language structure reasoning defined by context-free grammars (CFGs). We introduce a family of synthetic CFGs that produce hierarchical rules, capable of generating lengthy sentences (e.g., hundreds of tokens) that are locally ambiguous and require dynamic programming to parse. Despite this complexity, we demonstrate that generative models like GPT can accurately learn and reason over CFG-defined hierarchies and generate sentences based on it. We explore the model's internals, revealing that its hidden states precisely capture the structure of CFGs, and its attention patterns resemble the information passing in a dynamic programming algorithm. This paper also presents several corollaries, including showing why absolute positional embeddings is inferior to relative and rotary embeddings; uniform attention alone is surprisingly effective (motivating our follow-up work on Canon layers); encoder-only models (e.g., BERT, DeBERTa) struggle with deep structure reasoning on CFGs compared to autoregressive models (e.g., GPT); and injecting structural or syntactic noise into pretraining data markedly improves robustness to corrupted language prompts.

papers.title: Representations in vision and language converge in a shared, multidimensional space of perceived similarities
papers.research_question: Do vision and language share a common representational format, and is this format captured by large language model (LLM) embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that human similarity judgments for images and sentences converge on a shared, modality-agnostic representational structure, which predicts brain activity in visual cortex and is best captured by LLM-based computational models.
papers.conclusion: The findings support a shared relational space for vision and language that captures behaviorally relevant structure across sensory modalities and is well modeled by LLM-based systems.
papers.key_findings:
Visual and linguistic similarity judgments are strongly correlated (Spearman ⍴ = 0.781).
Both visual and linguistic similarity judgments predict brain activity in mid- and high-level visual regions.
LLM-trained recurrent convolutional neural networks (RCNNs) better capture the behavioral similarity structure than category-trained RCNNs or AlexNet.
The shared representational structure is grounded in relational properties of the world and is not dependent on first-order visual experience.
The alignment between linguistic judgments and brain activity persists even when participants have not seen the corresponding images.
papers.limitation: The study does not test how behavioral representational geometries align with neural activity during sentence reading.
future_direction: Future research should address the distinct representational dimensions projected from each modality to form a richer representation.
Future research should investigate whether this relational similarity structure is a universal principle extending to other domains like sound or motion perception.
Future fMRI studies of sentence reading are needed to see if similarity judgments predict activity patterns in visual regions during reading.
papers.abstract: Humans can effortlessly describe what they see, yet establishing a shared representational format between vision and language remains a significant challenge. Emerging evidence suggests that human brain representations in both vision and language are well predicted by semantic feature spaces obtained from large language models (LLMs). This raises the possibility that sensory systems converge in their inherent ability to transform their inputs onto shared, embedding-like representational space. However, it remains unclear how such a space manifests in human behaviour. To investigate this, sixty-three participants performed behavioural similarity judgements separately on 100 natural scene images and 100 corresponding sentence captions from the Natural Scenes Dataset. We found that visual and linguistic similarity judgements not only converge at the behavioural level but also predict a remarkably similar network of fMRI brain responses evoked by viewing the natural scene images. Furthermore, computational models trained to map images onto LLM-embeddings outperformed both category-trained and AlexNet controls in explaining the behavioural similarity structure. These findings demonstrate that human visual and linguistic similarity judgements are grounded in a shared, modality-agnostic representational structure that mirrors how the visual system encodes experience. The convergence between sensory and artificial systems suggests a common capacity of how conceptual representations are formed-not as arbitrary products of first order, modality-specific input, but as structured representations that reflect the stable, relational properties of the external world.

papers.title: On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages: a Case Study on the Subject-verb Agreement Task
papers.research_question: How universal are the circuits implemented by language models for solving the same task across different languages? Specifically, the paper investigates whether the circuits for subject-verb agreement are similar in English and Spanish.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that the circuits for subject-verb agreement in English and Spanish in Gemma models are highly consistent, driven by an attention head that writes a language-independent subject number signal into the residual stream, which is read by downstream MLP neurons. This direction can causally steer the model's predictions across languages.
papers.conclusion: The circuits for subject-verb agreement are highly consistent across English and Spanish in Gemma models, with a language-independent subject number direction written by an attention head and read by MLP neurons, which can causally steer predictions across languages.
papers.key_findings:
The circuits for subject-verb agreement in English and Spanish are highly consistent in Gemma 2B.
A specific attention head (L13H7 in Gemma 2B) writes a subject number signal as a direction in the residual stream.
